Unlike the cramped triage cubicles at the campus health center, this room had a wide, wheelchair-accessible examination lane designed so Jordan didn't even have to transfer out of his chair. Better still, after Jordan signed a standard clinic release form at the front desk, the optometrist—a warm, soft-spoken man in his forties named **Dr. Patel**—invited Aubrie and Madison to sit in the two visitor chairs right inside the room while the rest of the group waited in the lobby.

Dr. Patel swung the heavy black phoropter into position in front of Jordan's face and dimmed the overhead lights.

"Alright, Jordan," Dr. Patel said clearly, already briefed by Nurse Collins' referral notes to speak facing him and give him a beat to respond with a thumbs-up for *'One'* or two fingers for *'Two'*. "We know your baseline vision without correction is below 20/200. Let's start bringing that chart into focus. Which is clearer—one, or two?"

At first, the glowing square on the far wall was the same familiar, hopeless smear of white and gray milk that Jordan had stared at his entire life. Dr. Patel clicked a heavy dial. Then another. And another.

Suddenly, the amorphous gray blob in the center of the light box shrank, its fuzzy edges pulling inward like a telescope lens locking onto a distant star.

Jordan gasped silently, his breath catching in his throat.

"How about now?" Dr. Patel asked gently, clicking a finer cylinder adjustment into place. "One... or two?"

Jordan raised two fingers, his hand trembling slightly. Looking through the circular apertures of the phoropter, he wasn't looking at a smudge anymore. For the first time in eighteen years, he was looking at crisp, jet-black letters with razor-sharp serifs across a room:

E  F  P
T  O  Z
L  P  E  D

"Can you type what you see on the fourth line for me?" Dr. Patel asked.

Jordan's hands dropped to the keyboard of his Vanguard Pro resting on his lap. Without even needing to hunch down to the keys, he typed into EchoType and hit execute:

<aac>P E C F D. And the line below it is E D F C Z P.</aac>

Across the room in the dim light, Madison clapped both hands over her mouth to stifle an excited squeal, and Aubrie wiped a tear from her cheek.

"Twenty-twenty," Dr. Patel said, a broad, satisfied smile creasing his face as he swung the phoropter arm back—returning the room to its familiar soft blur, though Jordan's heart was now racing with hope. "You have significant compound myopic astigmatism, Jordan—minus-4.75 in the right eye, minus-5.00 in the left—which is why everything past arm's length has been a complete blur. The great news is that your retinas and optic nerves are completely healthy. All you need is the right glass in front of your eyes."

Dr. Patel turned to his desktop printer, pulled a crisp, heavyweight prescription slip off the tray, and signed the bottom with a blue fountain pen.

"Now, because we are a clinical medical practice rather than a retail optical chain, any frames ordered through our office have to be sent out to our regional wholesale lab in Roanoke, which takes ten to fourteen business days," Dr. Patel explained, handing the signed paper prescription directly to Jordan. "With your university lectures already underway, I don't want you sitting in the back of an astronomy hall waiting two weeks to see the projector."

"Can we take his prescription somewhere local that cuts lenses on the spot?" Madison asked eagerly, leaning forward in her chair.

"You sure can," Dr. Patel smiled. "Right after you finish your audiology evaluation next door with Dr. Vance, walk back across to the **Pepper Plaza Transit Center** and hop on the northbound **Route 1** bus heading back up North Franklin Street. Get off at **Strickland Farm Shopping Center**—right across the four-lane boulevard from **New River Valley Mall**. There's a big retail optical store in Strickland Farm called **LensWorks Optical** that has a full one-hour surfacing and edging lab right inside the building. Hand them this signed prescription, pick out your frames, and they'll have single-vision high-index polycarbonate lenses cut and mounted for you in under an hour."

Jordan looked down at the signed slip of paper in his hand—the official medical document bearing his chosen name, **Jordan Fuller**, and the exact mathematical numbers that would unlock the visible universe. Tucking it carefully into the zippered front pocket of his laptop bag, he gave Dr. Patel an earnest, grateful nod before Aubrie and Madison rolled with him toward the connecting door to Audiology.

### Part 8: The Audiologist's Verdict & The Ride Home in High Definition

**Date:** 2014-08-29 at 14:25 America/New_York

![Seated upright in his wheelchair in the accessible front bay of a Blue Ridge Transit bus bathed in golden late-afternoon Virginia sunlight, Jordan Fuller wears his brand-new rectangular eyeglasses, behind-the-ear digital hearing aids, and maroon CPI T-shirt while holding his CPI Poly Pass and looking out the wide panoramic window in awe at the soaring gray Ironstone collegiate-gothic towers of Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute and the Blue Ridge Mountains in 20/20 high definition, as Aubrie Jean Kelly, Madison Grace Miller, and Zoë Wren Brooks smile beside him.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e001/c009/s005/ride-home-in-high-definition.jpg)

#### 2:25 PM — The Audiologist's Verdict

With Dr. Patel's signed eyeglass prescription tucked safely into his laptop bag, Jordan rolled through the connecting interior door into the Audiology Suite next door, accompanied by Aubrie, Zoë, and Mark while the rest of the crew waited in the front reception lounge.

**Dr. Elena Vance**, the clinic's lead doctor of audiology, greeted them with a warm, practiced calm and guided Jordan's wheelchair up the flush threshold ramp into a double-walled, sound-attenuated acoustic booth. For the next forty minutes, Dr. Vance conducted a comprehensive battery of diagnostic tests: pure-tone air- and bone-conduction audiometry, tympanometry, otoacoustic emissions, and speech-threshold recognition.

When Dr. Vance opened the heavy acoustic door and invited Jordan, Aubrie, Zoë, and Mark around her consultation desk, she thoughtfully rolled her articulated diagnostic monitor arm right to the front edge of the desk—within eighteen inches of Jordan's face—and zoomed the interface to three hundred percent so he could read the steep, downward-plunging red and blue lines on the audiogram clearly even before his glasses were cut.

"Nurse Collins' instinct at the campus clinic was spot-on, Jordan," Dr. Vance said, positioning herself directly in front of him and speaking in a clear, measured cadence so he could pair her lip movements with his residual low-frequency hearing. "Your middle ear structures and eardrums are completely normal. What we are looking at here is severe-to-profound, rapidly progressive bilateral sensorineural hearing loss."

She used a stylus to trace the steep drop-off on the zoomed-in chart above 500 Hertz.

"Inside your cochlea—the snail-shaped inner ear organ—the microscopic sensory hair cells responsible for converting high- and mid-frequency sound vibrations into electrical signals are degenerating," Dr. Vance explained with quiet clinical honesty. "That is why you can still hear low-frequency rumbles, like a bus engine or a deep bass tone, while human speech consonants like *S*, *F*, *T*, and *K* sound like muffled static underwater. And based on your otoacoustic emission results today, those remaining hair cells are continuing to deteriorate."

Jordan's hands rested on his Vanguard Pro keyboard. With Aubrie's hand resting warmly on his shoulder and the clinical truth laid out plainly in front of him, the panic that had seized him on Wednesday didn't return. Instead, he wanted the engineering truth.

<aac>Nurse Collins said it will eventually result in total deafness,</aac> Jordan typed, triggering EchoType. <aac>Will hearing aids stop it?</aac>

"I'm glad you asked that directly, because I never sugarcoat the physics for my patients," Dr. Vance replied, respecting his intelligence immediately. "Conventional hearing aids are essentially miniature acoustic amplifiers—they make sounds louder for the surviving hair cells to pick up. Right now, while you still have residual low- and mid-frequency hair cells, programmable high-output behind-the-ear hearing aids paired with your university FM classroom lapel system will give you an immediate, massive boost for your fall semester classes."

She pulled up a second high-contrast diagram on the close-up monitor—an illustration showing a sleek external processor behind the ear connected to a small circular magnetic transmitter coil resting against the side of the head above the ear, sending digital signals directly to an internal electrode array coiled inside the cochlea.

"However," Dr. Vance continued carefully, "because your condition is progressive, simply cranking up acoustic volume on dying hair cells has a hard ceiling. Within the next six to twelve months, as those hair cells finish dropping off, conventional hearing aids won't be enough. The permanent solution—and the gold standard for your exact audiological profile, because your auditory nerves themselves are 100% intact—is **bilateral cochlear implants**."

Zoë leaned forward slightly in her chair, her eyes scanning the schematic on the monitor. "Because a cochlear implant bypasses the damaged hair cells entirely and stimulates the spiral ganglion nerves directly with electrical pulses."

"Spot on," Dr. Vance smiled at Zoë before looking back at Jordan. "Instead of shouting louder at broken microphones, a cochlear implant replaces the microphones with a direct digital interface to your auditory nerve. Today, I am fitting you with a pair of programmed clinical bridge hearing aids and syncing them to your CPI FM receiver so you can hear your professors and your friends right now. At the same time, I am logging today's baseline audiogram to open your formal candidacy file with the cochlear implant surgical team at Star City Roanoke General. When your natural thresholds cross that final line, we won't let you fall into silence—we'll upgrade the hardware."

Dr. Vance reached into a sterile tray and carefully fitted the two calibrated behind-the-ear bridge processors over Jordan's ears, nestling the soft silicone domes into his ear canals before clicking them on at a gentle initial gain.

A soft, musical three-tone chime sounded directly inside Jordan's head—higher, crisper, and cleaner than anything he had heard since he was a small child.

Then Aubrie spoke beside him.

"Can you hear me, J?"

Jordan's breath caught. For years, voices had been dull, muffled thuds buried under cotton. Now, he heard the delicate, airy *"s"* and *"h"* in her whisper, the soft rustle of her sleeve against his armrest, and the quiet hum of the clinic's air conditioning.

His fingers trembled slightly on the keys before he pressed execute.

<aac>Your voice is so warm,</aac> his terminal spoke into the room, as a single tear slipped down his cheek. <aac>I didn't know it sounded like that.</aac>

***

#### 3:15 PM — LensWorks at Strickland Farm

Stepping out of the **Montgomery Vision and Hearing Clinic** and crossing back over to the sawtooth bus bays of the **Pepper Plaza Transit Center** opposite the **Montgomery County Courthouse**, Jordan stopped his wheelchair under the glass transit shelter and tilted his head toward the open sky.

His vision beyond arm's length was still a soft watercolor blur—for another hour, at least—but through his newly fitted behind-the-ear bridge hearing aids, the acoustic world of downtown Christiansburg had come alive with astonishing depth and direction.

Two hours ago, when they had disembarked at Pepper Plaza, the town had sounded like a flat, underwater hum. Now, Jordan could hear the distinct chirping of sparrows in the courthouse oaks across Roanoke Street, the crisp click of Hannah's sandals on the concrete platform, the rhythmic *tick-tick-tick* of the crosswalk beacon at the corner, and the clear, bright cadence of all eight of his friends talking around him at once—without having to cup his hand behind his ear a single time.

"How's the sound out here in the wild, mate?" Sarah asked, grinning as she leaned against the shelter glass beside Lauren.

Jordan didn't have to strain or guess what she had said. Smiling wide, he typed on his Vanguard Pro and hit execute:

<aac>I can hear every single consonant in your Australian accent. And I can hear the bus coming up Roanoke Street before I can even see it.</aac>

Sure enough, ten seconds later, a northbound sixty-foot **Blue Ridge Transit** articulated coach glided into the **Pepper Plaza Transit Center** bay, its amber LED sign alternating between 1 CPI and 1 via S MAIN ST.

When the front air suspension kneeled—producing a crisp, high-frequency pneumatic *pssshhh* that Jordan heard in crystal stereo—and the front-door aluminum ramp flipped onto the curb, Jordan flashed his **CPI Poly Pass** to the driver, rolled smoothly aboard into the forward wheelchair bay, and let Mark click the four floor retractors into place.

This time, they weren't heading straight back to campus. They were using **Route 1** the way thousands of CPI students and local residents used it every day—hopping ten minutes north up **North Franklin Street (Business US-460)** across the grade-separated railroad bridge into northern Christiansburg's commercial retail district, where **New River Valley Mall** rose on the west side of the four-lane boulevard and the sprawling open-air **Strickland Farm Shopping Center** stretched out on the east side.

"Next stop, **Strickland Farm**," Mark announced as Hannah pulled the yellow stop-request cord just past the overpass.

The sixty-foot coach pulled into the North Franklin Street curbside stop directly in front of **Strickland Farm Shopping Center**. Within twenty seconds of the brakes setting, Jordan rolled down the front ramp onto the wide concrete sidewalk, and the nine-person phalanx strolled down the sunlit shopping-center promenade toward a wide glass storefront crowned with bold blue-and-silver channel letters:

LENSWORKS OPTICAL — GLASSES IN ABOUT AN HOUR

As the automatic glass doors slid open and a cheerful entrance chime rang overhead, a quiet realization washed over Jordan: **this was the first time in his eighteen years of life he had ever gone shopping in a store with friends.**

Inside, the showroom was bright and welcoming, lined with illuminated floor-to-ceiling display walls holding hundreds of eyeglass frames, while along the back wall, a massive interior picture window looked directly into the store's on-site surfacing and edging laboratory, where technicians in white coats operated automated computer-guided lens grinders.

"Welcome to LensWorks!" a friendly optician in a neat polo shirt greeted them from the counter.

Instead of hanging back behind someone else, Jordan rolled right up to the accessible low section of the counter, reached into his laptop bag, and handed Dr. Patel's signed prescription slip to the optician himself.

<aac>Hi. My optometrist just gave me this prescription. He said you can make polycarbonate glasses in about an hour?</aac> Jordan's "Sydney" voice asked clearly.

"Minus-4.75 and minus-5.00 in high-index thin polycarbonate with anti-reflective coating? We have those blanks in stock right back there in our lab, Jordan," the optician smiled, keying the numbers into his terminal. "We can have them edged, polished, and mounted in forty-five minutes. Go ahead and pick out your frames with your crew!"

What followed was twenty minutes of pure, joyful chaos that Jordan knew he would remember for the rest of his life. With his new hearing aids picking up every laugh and commentary across the showroom, Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Sarah, Jessica, and Mark appointed themselves his personal styling committee.

"Okay, absolutely not those round wire ones—you look like an eighteenth-century tax collector," Madison laughed, gently plucking a pair of brass circles off his nose.

"Try the thick black horn-rims," Sarah suggested, holding a mirror up in front of Jordan's wheelchair even though he had to lean within four inches of the glass to see his own reflection. "Very indie rock."

"Negative," Zoë declared, adjusting her own glasses as she inspected the structural hinges along the menswear wall. "With Jordan's facial geometry and the fact that he will be wearing behind-the-ear audio processors, thick acetate temples will create excessive pressure behind the pinna. He requires a lightweight, spring-hinged titanium or gunmetal frame with low-profile temple arms."

"Leave it to Zoë to turn frame shopping into a mechanical engineering thesis," Mark grinned—until Aubrie reached onto the center shelf right where Zoë was pointing and lifted down a sleek, lightweight pair of **dark gunmetal-and-tortoiseshell rectangular frames** with thin, flexible titanium arms.

Aubrie carefully slid them onto Jordan's face, tucking the slim arms comfortably beside his new hearing aids without a millimeter of crowding.

The entire circle of eight friends went quiet for a beat.

"Oh," Aubrie breathed, her cheeks warming slightly as she looked down at him. "Yeah. Those are the ones."

"One hundred percent," Madison agreed instantly, nodding with wide blue eyes. "Pack it up, team, we have a winner."

"Very sharp, brother," Mark nodded approvingly, while Lauren gave an enthusiastic two thumbs-up.

After Jordan paid at the counter using the medical-accommodation stipend voucher Ms. Higgins and Nurse Collins had linked to his student account, the optician carried the gunmetal frames through the door into the glass-walled laboratory. For the next forty minutes, while Madison, Sarah, and Lauren ducked next door to grab warm soft pretzels and iced lemonades for the group at the outdoor patio tables, Zoë, Mark, and Aubrie stood with Jordan right in front of the laboratory window—describing the mesmerizing dance of the robotic diamond-wheel edger as jets of cooling water sprayed across Jordan's polycarbonate lenses, shaving them to the exact millimeter contour of his frames.

Then, at four-fifteen, the lab door swung open. The optician walked out holding a black velvet-lined dispensing tray and called across the showroom:

"Order ready for **Jordan Fuller**!"

Jordan's heart gave a triumphant leap. Nobody had to tap his shoulder or translate for him—**he had heard a stranger call his chosen name across a busy store with his own ears.**

He wheeled over to the accessible fitting table, surrounded by his eight friends. The optician sanitized the nose pads, leaned down with a warm smile, and gently slid the finished frames onto Jordan's face, adjusting the temple tips behind his ears.

"Go ahead and open your eyes, Jordan."

Jordan blinked once. Then twice.

The world exploded into breathtaking, impossible detail.

He didn't just see shapes and smeared puddles of color anymore. He looked up at **Aubrie** standing right in front of him, and for the first time since she had opened the door of Room 214 on Saturday morning, he saw the delicate individual flecks of warm gold and hazel-brown in her eyes, the fine weave of the fabric in her maroon sweater, and the tiny dimple at the corner of her smile. He looked around the semi-circle at **Madison's** bright blue eyes, **Zoë's** sharp, proud smile, **Lauren's** auburn hair, **Hannah** and **Mark** standing arm-in-arm, **Sarah's** beaming grin, and six-foot-three **Jessica** towering warmly at the back of the group.

Then he looked past them through the plate-glass storefront window of LensWorks Optical, straight across the parking lot of **Strickland Farm Shopping Center** and across four-lane North Franklin Street, where he could read every single crisp letter on the marquee of **New River Valley Mall** a quarter-mile away.

His fingers moved slowly to his keyboard, his eyes returning to Aubrie's face.

<aac>I can see your eyelashes,</aac> his "Sydney" voice said softly into the showroom. <aac>I can see all of your faces at the same time. Everything has edges.</aac>

Aubrie knelt in front of his chair right there on the showroom carpet, taking both of his hands in hers as her eyes shone brightly through his crystal-clear lenses.

"Handsome *and* twenty-twenty," she whispered, pressing a kiss to his knuckles. "Welcome to high definition, J."

***

#### 4:30 PM — The Ride Home in High Definition

When the automatic glass doors of **LensWorks Optical** slid open and the nine friends stepped back out onto the sunny late-afternoon promenade of **Strickland Farm Shopping Center**, Jordan paused his wheelchair at the edge of the walkway and simply drank in the horizon.

Through his new gunmetal-and-tortoiseshell polycarbonate lenses and his calibrated behind-the-ear bridge hearing aids, the late-August afternoon in the New River Valley was so vivid it felt like stepping out of a dark monochrome room into wide-screen cinema.

Across the four-lane ribbon of **North Franklin Street (Business US-460)**, he could read every store banner along the facade of **New River Valley Mall** without squinting a muscle. Beyond the rooftops of the mall, he could trace the individual pine-covered ridges of the Blue Ridge Mountains rising against a deep cerulean sky. And through his hearing aids, the world had texture and geometry: he could hear the laughter of families walking down the **Strickland Farm** sidewalk, the crisp rustle of the LensWorks care-kit bag in Madison's hand, and the breeze moving through the parking-lot honey locust trees.

"Look at his face," Lauren whispered warmly to Hannah and Sarah, her artist's eyes crinkling with affection as she watched Jordan tilt his head back to trace the clouds against the mountain ridge. "He's looking at everything like he just landed on a brand-new planet."

"How is the sensory integration holding up with both visual and auditory inputs corrected simultaneously, J?" Zoë asked, stepping up beside his chair in her calm, analytical British cadence. "No headaches or vestibular lag?"

Jordan didn't have to cup his hand behind his ear, and he didn't have to hunch his nose down to two inches from his laptop screen. Sitting upright in his chair with effortless posture, he glanced down at the crisp, razor-sharp keys of his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro and typed into EchoType:

<aac>No headache at all. I can hear your voice clearly even with traffic on North Franklin Street, and I can read license plates all the way across the Strickland Farm parking lot.</aac>

"Wait until we get you back to Astronomy on Wednesday after Labor Day," Aubrie grinned, taking his hand and giving it an excited squeeze as they rolled down the accessible curb cut toward the North Franklin Street transit shelter. "Dr. Alistair's slides don't stand a chance now."

Down the boulevard toward downtown Christiansburg, a familiar, refined diesel hum approached—and this time, Jordan heard the distinct high-frequency turbocharger whistle above the low bass purr before the bus even crested the grade.

Gliding into the North Franklin Street stop in front of **Strickland Farm Shopping Center** was their northbound sixty-foot **Blue Ridge Transit** articulated coach. Three hours ago at Commonwealth Mall, the overhead sign had been an unreadable orange smear to Jordan's eyes. Now, from forty feet away on the sidewalk, he read every individual amber LED pixel on the front destination sign:

1 CPI
1 via S MAIN ST

As the front air suspension kneeled with a crisp pneumatic *pssshhh* and the yellow-edged aluminum low-floor ramp flipped smoothly onto the concrete pad, Mark and Jessica instinctively stepped half a pace behind Jordan's chair, ready to offer a steady hand on the incline.

Jordan glanced back at Mark and Jessica with a small, determined smile, then tapped a single line on his screen:

<aac>Let me try rolling up the ramp all the way by myself this time.</aac>

"All yours, captain," Mark beamed, stepping back with his hands raised in proud salute as Jessica gave Jordan an encouraging thumbs-up.

Holding his maroon-and-orange **CPI Poly Pass** in his fingers to show the driver, Jordan gripped his push-rims, leaned slightly forward, and drove his wheels up the textured aluminum ramp completely under his own power. His front casters glided effortlessly over the threshold, and he rolled smoothly down the wide front aisle straight into the open wheelchair bay, spinning his chair around in a clean, practiced 180-degree turn to back flush against the padded securement cushion.

"Look at that form!" the afternoon driver chuckled approvingly from the cab as Mark stepped in to click the four floor retractors onto the frame. "You ride this route like a seasoned pro, son."

As the sixty-foot coach pulled away from **Strickland Farm Shopping Center** and **New River Valley Mall**, heading north up **U.S. Route 460 Business** into Blacksburg, Jordan looked down the aisle of the bus first. Three hours ago, the fellow CPI students and townsfolk sharing the cabin had been comforting, friendly blurs. Now, in razor-sharp 20/20 focus, he could see the actual stitching on a fellow student's maroon *Forgers Engineering* sweatshirt, the tired, kindly smile of a retail clerk heading home from her shift with a paperback novel open in her lap, and a pair of upperclassmen nodding a casual, welcoming *"afternoon"* toward his wheelchair bay. Then he rested his elbows on his armrests and watched the valley unfold through the wide panoramic window in crystal-clear high definition: the green highway mile markers, the red-brick storefronts along South Main Street, the maroon-and-orange campus banners fluttering from the streetlights, and finally the soaring gray **Ironstone** collegiate-gothic towers of Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute rising against the golden late-afternoon sky.

Across the aisle and around his bay, his friends were chatting and laughing—debating what to grab for Friday night dinner at Kincaid Commons and planning out their three-day Labor Day weekend—and for the first time in his life, Jordan could follow every single voice in the group conversation without straining, guessing, or falling behind.

When the bus glided to a stop beneath **The Keystone Bridge** along **Commonwealth Mall** and the front ramp deployed onto the campus sidewalk, Jordan rolled smoothly off the bus into the warm sunlight.

Sitting on the campus pavement with his new glasses resting comfortably on the bridge of his nose, his hearing aids humming with the clear voices of the people who loved him, and his Poly Pass tucked safely in his pocket, Jordan looked back at the departing bus one more time.

This morning, he had been a boy who had never once traveled anywhere without his mother's car, looking out at a blurry, muffled world he had been taught to fear. Tonight, he could see, he could hear, and he knew he could go anywhere in the world.

### Part 9: Dinner with Isabel & Taking Out the Trash

**Date:** 2014-08-29 at 17:30 America/New_York

#### 5:30 PM — Dinner with Isabel

From the bus stop beneath **The Keystone Bridge**, the nine friends rolled together along the warm brick walkways of the academic quad toward **Kincaid Hall** for Friday night dinner.

Every few yards, Jordan found himself marveling at details he had passed all week without ever knowing they existed. Through his new rectangular polycarbonate lenses, the carved Gothic lettering above the limestone arches of Kincaid Hall was razor-sharp, and through his calibrated behind-the-ear bridge hearing aids, the bustling Friday-evening chatter of the student center didn't crash over him as a muddy, overwhelming roar. The directional microphones gently attenuated the background clatter of dishes and footsteps while keeping the voices of his friends right beside him crisp and effortless.

As Mark held the wide double doors of **Kincaid Commons** open and Jordan wheeled across the threshold toward the dining hall check-in podium, a familiar, warm voice called out from the beverage counter just ahead of them.

"Hey, Room 214 crew!"

Jordan looked up—and for the very first time in his life, he saw **Isabel Dawson**'s face from twenty feet away in crystal-clear 20/20 focus. Their second-floor Resident Advisor had her canvas messenger bag slung over one shoulder and a reusable travel mug in her hand, grabbing an early bite before her Friday evening seminar.

"Oh, hello, Isabel!" Aubrie beamed as the whole group lit up.

Setting her travel mug down on the edge of the counter, Isabel took two steps toward them—and then stopped in her tracks, her hazel-brown eyes widening in pure, delighted astonishment as she looked closely at Jordan's face.

Without a second of hesitation, Jordan rolled straight up to her, set his wheel locks, and opened both arms with a bright, unguarded grin.

"Oh, Jordan!" Isabel laughed softly, her voice catching with genuine emotion. Stepping smoothly to the side of his wheelchair, she bent down and wrapped her arm firmly around his shoulders in a warm, big-sisterly hug, giving his back two gentle, reassuring pats as Jordan hugged her back with all the gratitude in his heart.

When she straightened up and stepped back half a pace, Jordan tilted his chin slightly to the left and then the right—proudly showing off the sleek gunmetal-and-tortoiseshell frames resting on the bridge of his nose and the discreet matte-silver bridge hearing aids tucked neatly behind his ears. Tapping the keys of his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro on his lap, he triggered his EchoType output:

<aac>Well, what do you think?</aac>

Isabel brought a hand to her mouth, her eyes shining brightly as she took in the transformation. Just seven days ago, on Friday afternoon, she had knelt beside this exact wheelchair in Room 214 while a terrified, exhausted eighteen-year-old boy squinted with his nose two inches from a dim screen and cupped his hand behind his ear just to catch the sound of her voice. Now, he was sitting upright with effortless posture, looking straight into her eyes with clear, sparkling focus.

"Jordan, you look *incredible*!" Isabel said, her voice brimming with pride. "Those frames fit your face so well—and look at those hearing aids! Can you actually see and hear everything in here clearly right now?"

<aac>Everything,</aac> Jordan's "Sydney" voice replied, his grin widening. <aac>I can read the menu boards all the way across the dining hall without squinting, and I can hear every word you are saying without cupping my ear. Will you sit with us for dinner, Isabel?</aac>

"Please join us, Izzy!" Madison chimed in eagerly. "My class doesn't meet until Monday, and we've been celebrating all the way back from Christiansburg!"

Isabel glanced at her watch and smiled warmly. "My evening occupational-therapy seminar doesn't start until seven, so I have plenty of time. I would love to eat with you guys."

Ten minutes later, after loading up their trays at the grill and pasta stations—and after Zoë had secured her mandatory mug of 100-degree-Celsius black tea—the ten of them claimed a long wooden booth-and-table combination along the quieter perimeter wall of Kincaid Commons. Mark and Jessica slid two extra chairs out from the end of the table so Jordan could roll seamlessly into the head of the group right beside Aubrie and Isabel.

Before opening a new NeoEdit buffer to join the dinner conversation, Jordan reached into the side pocket of his backpack, pulled out his power adapter, and casually plugged it into the duplex wall outlet mounted along the wooden wainscoting beside the booth.

Sitting directly to his left, Isabel watched him plug the cord in—and then her gaze drifted quietly to the top-right corner of his Aura Glade desktop taskbar.

Her breath caught in a silent, observant realization.

On move-in Friday, the cheap, heavy plastic laptop his mother had sent him off with had possessed a completely dead battery; the moment its frayed cord was pulled from the wall, the screen had died and stripped him of his voice. Tonight, on this sleek matte-black Pinnacle Vanguard Pro that Zoë had set up for him, the battery telemetry icon in the corner of the Dark Aero panel read a solid **78% — Charging**.

Even after an entire afternoon out in Christiansburg—typing at the bus stops, communicating through two clinical exams at Montgomery Vision and Hearing Clinic, picking out his glasses at LensWorks Optical at Strickland Farm Shopping Center, and riding Route 1 all the way back to campus—the battery on this laptop didn't die on him. He wasn't tethered to the wall in fear of going mute anymore. He had only plugged it in simply to let it top off and charge because there happened to be an outlet right at the table.

Isabel didn't say a word aloud to embarrass him, but she took a slow sip of her water to hide the lump in her throat, silently thanking God for Zoë Brooks and the fierce, loving family sitting around this table.

For the next twenty minutes, between bites of warm pasta and garlic bread, Jordan happily recounted the milestones of his afternoon—typing rapidly in NeoEdit and triggering EchoType as he described how he had ridden a public bus for the very first time in his life without his mother driving him, how he had realized the fellow CPI students and Christiansburg townsfolk on Blue Ridge Transit weren't scary at all, and how he had wheeled himself up the bus ramp at Strickland Farm completely under his own power.

"Honestly, watching him roll up that ramp in Christiansburg like he owned the whole transit system was the highlight of my week," Sarah grinned in her thick Sydney cadence, raising her lemonade glass in a toast.

"And the optometrist at LensWorks said his prescription was ready in forty-two minutes flat," Lauren added warmly from across the table. "The moment he walked outside and looked across North Franklin Street at New River Valley Mall, you could tell his whole world had changed."

As the laughter around the table settled into a comfortable, contented hum and everyone finished their plates, Jordan's expression grew thoughtful. He glanced around the table at his eight friends—every single one of whom knew how controlling his mother was—and then looked over at Isabel.

Instead of triggering his synthesized voice across the dining room, Jordan switched to his silent NeoEdit terminal window, where his large neon-green text glowed clearly against the pitch-black background, and angled the screen toward Isabel and the table:

<aac>Isabel, can I ask you a serious question about university rules?</aac>

"Of course, Jordan," Isabel said gently, setting her fork down and giving him her full, undivided attention. "Ask me anything."

Jordan's fingers moved steadily across the tactile keys:

<aac>Today on the bus and at the clinic, I realized how much I want to stay here and build my own life. I know my mother only sent me to CPI because she expects me to fail and beg to come home. What would happen if I went to make an official statement with CPI Police—just to put it on record that I am eighteen, that I am safe here, and that if she ever calls them claiming I am missing or tries to take me back, I don't want to go with her?</aac>

Around the booth, Aubrie, Madison, Lauren, Zoë, Hannah, Mark, Sarah, and Jessica all quieted, listening intently. Aubrie reached under the table and gave Jordan's knee a warm, steady squeeze.

"First of all, Jordan, that is a really smart, proactive question to ask," Isabel said softly, keeping her voice low and reassuring for their table. "Because you are eighteen years old, you are a legal adult under Virginia and federal law. If you go over to the CPI Police Department on Southgate Drive to make a voluntary Adult Safe-Status and No-Contact Statement, the officers will take your statement seriously and log a permanent dispatch flag under your name and student ID. That way, if a parent ever calls Campus Police demanding a welfare check or trying to report you as a missing person, dispatch immediately sees on their screen that you already came in of your own free will, verified that you are safe, and stated that you do not wish to have contact."

Jordan nodded slowly, his green eyes behind his new glasses absorbing the procedural logic. Then his shoulders tensed just a fraction, and he typed the second half of his thought—the one piece of the puzzle that still scared him:

<aac>That makes sense. My only fear is that if I go to CPI Police and take my mother off my records, they will ask me to put down a new Emergency Contact. Right now, the only people in the whole world I trust are my friends sitting at this table. I don't have an adult authority figure outside of college that I know and trust yet. And I already read the Residence Life handbook, so I know that you, Kelsey, Henry, and any other university staff aren't allowed to be a student's personal emergency contact.</aac>

Isabel's heart ached with quiet empathy as she read the glowing green words. Even in the middle of reclaiming his independence, Jordan had already researched the policy himself so he wouldn't put her, Henry, or Kelsey in an impossible position.

"You're completely right about the university rule, Jordan," Isabel said gently, meeting his eyes with warm honesty. "Because Kelsey, Henry, and I are employed by CPI Housing and Residence Life—and the same goes for Ms. Higgins in Educational Accessibility or your professors—university conflict-of-interest and liability rules prohibit staff members from being listed as a student's personal emergency contact in the Registrar's system. If it were legal, I think half the staff in Bennett Hall would volunteer in a heartbeat."

She reached across the corner of the table and rested a brief, comforting hand beside his keyboard.

"Here is the good news, though," Isabel continued reassuringly. "You don't have to have everything figured out today. Making a statement with CPI Police or updating your emergency contact isn't a test with a deadline tomorrow morning. Right now, you are just finishing your very first week of classes. Take the next few weeks to breathe, enjoy your new glasses and hearing aids, and let your world grow naturally. As you get to know trusted adults outside the university—like your friends' families—you'll know in your heart when you have an adult authority figure you truly trust to hold that spot for you. And until the exact day you feel ready to make that change and walk into CPI Police, Henry, Kelsey, and I have your back every single day inside Bennett Hall."

Across the table, Zoë adjusted her glasses, a quiet, thoughtful glint in her analytical gray eyes as she exchanged a brief, unspoken glance with Aubrie—already filing away the exact logistical parameters of Jordan's need for trusted adult authority figures outside the university.

Jordan let out a long, steady breath, the tight knot in his chest dissolving completely. He tapped a final line onto his screen and smiled up at his RA:

<aac>Thank you, Isabel. That helps a lot. I'm really glad you're our RA.</aac>

"Being your RA is the best part of my junior year, Jordan," Isabel smiled back warmly.

***

#### 6:45 PM — Taking Out the Trash

At a quarter to seven, the ten of them bussed their trays at the conveyor window and stepped back out of **Kincaid Hall** into the golden, slanting light of the late-August evening.

Isabel walked alongside Jordan's wheelchair as the group strolled down the wide brick promenade toward the central campus crossroads, chatting with Hannah and Madison about the upcoming three-day Labor Day weekend. When they reached the stone walkway branching off toward **Callahan Hall**, where her Friday evening occupational-therapy seminar was held, Isabel paused and adjusted the strap of her messenger bag.

"Alright, guys, this is my turnoff," Isabel said warmly. "Have an amazing Friday night, and don't forget there are no classes on Monday for Labor Day."

Jordan rolled forward half a pace, set his wheel locks on the brick path, and looked up at Isabel with a grateful smile, opening his arms to give her a proper goodbye hug.

Isabel beamed, stepping right beside his chair and leaning down to wrap her arm securely around his shoulders in a warm, platonic side-hug. "I'm so proud of how far you've come this week, Jordan," she murmured, giving his shoulder an affectionate squeeze before stepping back and waving to the whole pack. "See you guys back on the second floor tonight!"

"Have a great class, Izzy!" Lauren and Aubrie called out as Isabel headed down the tree-lined path toward her lecture hall.

Releasing his wheel locks, Jordan fell back into formation with his eight friends as they turned onto the walkway leading toward **Washington Street SW** and **Bennett Hall**. With the sun dipping toward the western ridge of the Blue Ridge Mountains, the evening air was cool and pleasant, and Jordan was enjoying the simple thrill of watching the campus streetlights flicker to life in crisp, starburst-free 20/20 clarity.

Halfway along the walkway bordering the athletic practice fields, a group of four upperclassmen guys in reversible maroon-and-white **CPI Men's Lacrosse** practice pinnies and heavy equipment duffels came walking down the parallel path from the locker rooms, snickering loudly amongst themselves.

Normally, seeing lacrosse gear anywhere near Lauren and Sarah would have put the entire group on instant, protective alert. Mark and Jessica immediately shifted half a step closer to the two girls on instinct.

Except Tom Lawson wasn't with them—and through his newly calibrated behind-the-ear hearing aids, Jordan could hear every single word the four lacrosse players were saying as they passed within fifteen feet of the bench alcove.

"Wait, are you serious?" one of the taller defensemen laughed, shaking his head as he adjusted his stick bag over his shoulder. "He still hasn't shown his face at the athletic complex?"

"Bro, nobody's seen Tom on campus since Wednesday afternoon," the second player snorted, a stocky junior wearing a captain's band on his sleeve. "After Coach and the captains found out what went down at the Kincaid pool tables on Tuesday night—and then Housing sent over notice that he got himself officially barred from Bennett Hall for harassing two freshman girls—Coach called him into the office Wednesday morning and cut him from the roster on the spot. Told him to clean out his locker and hand in his playbook before noon."

All nine friends on the main walkway slowed their pace to a near-crawl, listening in stunned silence as the lacrosse players kept talking down the path.

"Good riddance, honestly," the third player said, zero sympathy in his voice. "Dude spent the whole first week bragging in the locker room like he was God's gift to campus, and the whole time he was two-timing two freshmen in the same dorm and acting like a creep. Coach said we don't keep guys like that in a Forgers jersey. The team took out the trash."

"My buddy in his Thursday morning business recitation said Tom didn't even show up to class yesterday or today," the first player added, snickering again as their voices trailed off toward the athletic parking lot. "And his roommate over in Westgate Hall said Tom threw two days of clothes into a duffel bag Wednesday afternoon and bolted without saying a word. Didn't officially drop his classes, didn't check out with Housing or move any of his stuff out of his dorm room—just pulled a total no-call, no-show because he's too embarrassed to show his face at CPI. Addition by subtraction, man. The guy was bad news—it's for the best that he's gone."

For three full seconds after the lacrosse players turned the corner toward the parking lots, nobody in Jordan's group made a sound.

Lauren and Sarah stood completely still on the brick path, staring at each other with wide, disbelieving eyes. Then, all at once, the invisible, suffocating tension that both women had been carrying in their shoulders since Tuesday night—the quiet dread of rounding a corner on the quad or walking into a lecture hall and seeing Tom's sneering face—simply vanished into the warm evening air.

"They kicked him off the team," Sarah breathed, a slow, astonished grin breaking across her face. "His own lacrosse team found out what a sleaze he was and threw him out on his ear!"

"And he hasn't even been on campus," Lauren whispered, her hand flying to her chest as she let out a shaky, incredulous laugh of pure relief.

They practically floated the rest of the way down the hill to the inner-campus entrance of **Bennett Hall**.

Instead of taking the upper Washington Street SW entrance straight onto the second floor, Mark tapped his **Poly Pass** at the **First-Floor Lower Entrance** at the bottom of the hill so the whole nine-person crew could come in together and ride the central elevator up.

Inside the warm, brightly lit **First-Floor Lobby**, working the Friday evening shift behind the curved oak **Front Desk**, was **Aaron Matthew Vance**—one of the **4th-Floor Male Resident Advisors** (Room 401, directly above Henry Walsh's room stack in the men's wing), a friendly senior in Civil Engineering wearing his maroon *CPI Residence Life* polo and a name badge reading **AARON V. — RA FLOOR 4**.

"Evening, Aaron!" Mark and Hannah called out cheerfully as the group rolled past the desk toward the elevator alcove.

Aaron glanced up from the desk duty logbook and flashed them a warm, easy grin, his eyes immediately catching Jordan's new frames. "Hey, guys! Happy Friday—and hey, Jordan, sharp glasses, man! Looking good!"

Jordan beamed, lifting a hand from his push-rim to give Aaron a proud wave before tapping a quick thank-you nod as the elevator doors chimed open.

Once all nine of them rode the elevator up to the second floor, rolled down the corridor past Isabel's whiteboard on Room 215, and filed into **Suite 214/216**—with the motorized arm pulling the heavy wooden door of Room 214 shut and locking it automatically after its ten-second timer—Madison spun around in the center of the rug with her hands on her hips and a massive grin on her face.

"So, interesting," Madison declared, looking around the circle of friends. "Tom is gone, huh? Kicked off the lacrosse team and hasn't even shown his face on campus in days. Great! One less thing to worry about!"

"Deadset," Sarah laughed, dropping onto the edge of Aubrie's lower bunk and letting her head fall back against the wooden frame in utter relief. "I didn't even realize how much I was bracing myself every time I walked past Kincaid Hall until those blokes walked by. Knowing even his own teammates realized he was trash and tossed him out? I feel like I can finally breathe."

"Me too," Lauren said softly, sitting down on the edge of Jordan's mattress (Bed A) right beside his wheelchair and resting her hand warmly over his forearm. Her brown eyes were bright and clear, completely unburdened for the first time all week. "It really feels like that chapter is completely over."

Aubrie looked at Lauren's relaxed smile, then glanced at Madison and Zoë, a warm, intuitive understanding passing effortlessly between them.

"Well," Aubrie said gently, smiling over at Lauren and Jordan, "after getting the best news of the week on the walk home, I think it's pretty obvious that tonight should be Lauren's turn to climb into bed with Jordan."

Lauren's cheeks warmed with a soft, grateful flush as she looked at Aubrie, and then turned to Jordan. "Would that be okay with you tonight, J? Just to celebrate having zero toxic ex-boyfriends left on this campus?"

Jordan didn't hesitate for a heartbeat. Smiling warmly at Lauren through his new glasses, he tapped his NeoEdit keyboard across his lap:

<aac>I would love that, Lauren. I am so happy you and Sarah don't have to worry about him anymore.</aac>

With the evening winding down after their big expedition to Christiansburg, the three members of the family who didn't live in Suite 214/216 began gathering their backpacks to head back to their own floors for the night.

"Alright, brother," Mark said, stepping up to Jordan's chair to clap a warm hand on his shoulder and bump knuckles with him before high-fiving him. "Get some rest tonight. Tomorrow we've got a whole three-day weekend ahead of us."

Sarah stepped up next, wrapping her arms around Jordan's neck in a fierce, affectionate hug and pressing a warm kiss to his cheek. "Night, J. And night, Lauren—sleep like a rock tonight, mate. We're free."

Finally, six-foot-three Jessica stepped forward, leaning down with a gentle, protective smile to give Jordan a warm, steady hug that practically enveloped his entire wheelchair frame. "Goodnight, Jordan. Proud of you today, mate."

Hannah gave Mark a lingering goodnight kiss at the door before pressing the square **PUSH TO OPEN** button on the interior wall. With a final chorus of goodnights, Mark headed toward the stairwell for Room 312 on the third floor while Sarah and Jessica headed upstairs toward Room 505 on the fifth floor, and the motorized door swung shut and clicked locked for the night.

### Part 10: Face to Face

**Date:** 2014-08-29 at 20:30 America/New_York

Once the hallway door clicked locked and Hannah, Lauren, and Zoë stepped through the connecting Jack-and-Jill bathroom into Room 216 to change into their pajamas, the quiet, comforting rhythm of bedtime settled over Room 214.

After a full Friday afternoon riding buses into Christiansburg, navigating two clinical exams, walking through Strickland Farm Shopping Center, and trekking back across campus from Kincaid Hall, Jordan needed to be cleaned up before heading to sleep.

"Come on, J," Aubrie smiled warmly, gathering a stack of clean bath towels, his soft cotton sleep shirt and flannel pajama pants, and their shower caddy while Madison grabbed her own towel and pajamas from the foot of her bunk. "Let's go get washed up."

Before they headed down the hall to the **Second-Floor Accessible Shower Room**, Jordan carefully removed his new prescription glasses and his behind-the-ear bridge hearing aids—tucking the hearing aids into their dehumidifying charging case on his nightstand so they would stay completely dry, though he kept his glasses on just until they reached the shower room so he could enjoy seeing the hallway on the way there.

When the heavy wooden door of the spacious, single-occupant accessible shower room clicked shut and locked behind the three of them, Jordan set his glasses safely inside their hard velvet-lined LensWorks case on the dry roll-under vanity counter right beside his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro.

Aubrie turned on the water in the wide, zero-threshold roll-in shower stall, adjusting the mixing valve until the tiles filled with rising, fragrant steam. Then, with the effortless, unhurried grace that had become part of their daily life, Aubrie and Madison helped Jordan out of his day clothes, slipped out of their own clothes without a trace of awkwardness or false modesty, and stepped under the warm spray together with him so all three of them could wash up.

With his glasses and hearing aids safely tucked away on the dry counter outside the stall, the world inside the shower softened back into gentle, warm shapes and the soothing, rhythmic hush of falling water—and yet, for Jordan, the sensation couldn't have been more different from the eighteen years that had come before.

Back in Virginia Beach—and on that final, suffocating night in the Merit Inn bathroom—being bathed by his mother had been an exercise in humiliation and rough, resentful control. Every scrub of a washcloth had been accompanied by a heavy, martyred sigh, a sharp complaint about his dead weight, or a reminder of what an exhausting burden he was on her life. And when he had first arrived at Bennett Hall, eighteen years of being opted out of every health class and shamed over his own biology had left him so terrified of the naked female body that the mere thought of being undressed around women had made his heart hammer in blind panic.

Now, sitting in the warm, cascading water as Aubrie gently lathered warm soap across his shoulders and back while Madison massaged shampoo through his hair with soft, affectionate fingers, there wasn't a single trace of fear in his chest. Since Tuesday night's gentle, clinical *Dimensions of Human Sexuality* study session—when Aubrie, Madison, and Zoë had patiently demystified the human body and replaced his mother's weaponized shame with tenderness and scientific clarity—the terror had completely vanished. In its place was pure, grounding warmth, gentle laughter in the steam, and the unmistakable feeling of being cherished.

When the water was turned off and Aubrie and Madison wrapped warm, dry cotton towels around his shoulders and dried off beside him before slipping into their pajamas and helping him dress in his clean sleep shirt and soft sweatpants, Jordan wheeled over to the roll-under vanity counter.

Putting his new glasses back on his nose and slipping his bridge hearing aids briefly behind his ears so he could hear their voices clearly, Jordan pulled his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro toward him on the dry counter. His heart was so full he couldn't wait until they got back to the room.

His fingers moved gently across the keys in NeoEdit, and he pressed execute on EchoType:

<aac>Thank you both for helping me wash up tonight. I am just so glad that you never think of me as a burden. And I am so glad that I am no longer terrified of the naked female body, so that the women in my life can bathe me without me being scared anymore.</aac>

In the warm, steam-softened glow of the accessible bathroom, both Aubrie and Madison stopped what they were doing.

Madison's bright blue eyes misted over instantly. Setting her hairbrush down on the counter, she stepped right up beside Jordan's chair, wrapped her arms tenderly around his neck, and pressed a warm, lingering kiss to the top of his clean, damp hair.

"Jordan, you will *never* be a burden to us," Madison whispered fiercely against his temple. "Not today, not tomorrow, not ever. Taking care of you is one of my favorite parts of the day."

Aubrie knelt down right in front of his wheelchair, taking both of his hands in hers and looking straight into his green eyes behind his glasses.

"Seeing you feel safe in your own skin—and safe with us—is the greatest gift in the world, J," Aubrie said softly, lifting his knuckles to press a tender kiss against them. "You never have to be scared with us again."

Five minutes later, the three of them rolled quietly back down the second-floor corridor and into **Room 214**.

Through the open connecting bathroom door, **Lauren** stepped in from Room 216, dressed in a soft oversized graphic-design t-shirt and plaid pajama shorts, her long reddish-brown hair brushed loose over her shoulders. Behind her, Hannah and Zoë poked their heads in to wish everyone goodnight and exchange their final bedtime hugs before closing the connecting door to turn in for the night.

In Room 214, Jordan rolled alongside the head of his accessible Twin XL bed (Bed A). He carefully took off his new glasses and bridge hearing aids, placing both neatly inside their protective cases on the nightstand within easy arm's reach, and executed a smooth, practiced pivot transfer onto the mattress.

Normally, whenever Aubrie, Madison, or Lauren shared his narrow Twin XL bed, Jordan slept **spooned**—curled on his side with his back pressed against whoever was holding him as the little spoon, or facing the wall while an arm draped protectively over his waist.

Tonight, as Lauren slid under the warm comforter beside him, something quietly, beautifully new happened.

Jordan shifted his shoulders back until his spine was pressed securely against the cool, solid cinderblock wall along the inside of Bed A—and instead of turning his back to be spooned, **he stayed facing outward toward Lauren**.

Lauren smiled softly in the dim amber glow of the campus streetlight filtering through the window blinds. Lying on her side facing him, she scooted right into the warm space against his chest, wrapping her arms around his torso as Jordan brought his arm tenderly around her shoulders.

For the first time, they were cuddled up **face to face**—their foreheads resting barely an inch apart on the shared pillow, breathing the same quiet air, able to look directly into each other's eyes with zero walls and zero fear between them.

"Goodnight, J," Lauren whispered softly, her fingers resting warmly over his collarbone as she closed her eyes with a peaceful sigh.

Across the small room, before Madison climbed the wooden ladder to Bed C and Aubrie pulled the comforter up over her shoulders in Bed B, the two roommates paused and looked over at the accessible bed along the wall—watching Jordan and Lauren cuddled up face to face in complete, serene contentment.

Aubrie and Madison looked at each other and shared a warm, glowing smile in the half-dark. There wasn't a flicker of envy or hesitation anywhere between them—only pure joy, because the no-jealousy pact they had built was working exactly as designed.

"Goodnight, everyone," Aubrie whispered softly as she clicked off the bedside lamp.

"Goodnight, suite family," Madison murmured from the top bunk.

With his back anchored against the wall and Lauren warm and safe in his arms, Jordan closed his eyes and drifted effortlessly to sleep.

## The Post-Census Verdict & The Nightly Pact

### Part 1: Strategic Analysis & The Main Event

**Date:** 2014-09-01 at 19:30 America/New_York

#### 7:30 PM — Strategic Analysis

Over the Labor Day weekend, a new, effortless rhythm had settled over Suite 214/216. With his new rectangular prescription glasses resting on the bridge of his nose and his calibrated bridge hearing aids bringing every voice and musical note into sharp relief, Jordan felt as though he had woken up from an eighteen-year coma.

And by Monday evening, the suite had established its newest sacred weekly tradition: wrestling night.

"Are you guys ready in there?!" Mark called out through the open suite doorway from Room 216, where he and Hannah were raiding the mini-fridge for sodas and grabbing bags of tortilla chips. "The pre-show countdown for **AWE Monday Night WAR** is starting in fifteen minutes!"

In Room 214, Jordan sat parked beside his desk with his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro resting on his lap, scrolling through the evening's match card and fan predictions with crystal-clear 20/20 vision. Lauren, who was sitting right on the edge of his bed with her legs tucked underneath her, leaned over to read his screen and pressed a warm, lingering kiss to his cheek.

"Don't get your hopes up, J," Lauren teased, her eyes crinkling with affection. "'Sly' Diego Chavez is definitely going to outsmart Preston Sinclair tonight. There is zero chance The Tycoon keeps that title belt clean."

Jordan grinned, his fingers flying across his NeoEdit terminal before he triggered his EchoType output.

<aac>Never underestimate how much Marcus Sterling cheats for his corporate favorites,</aac> his "Sydney" voice replied brightly. <aac>If Diego gets close to pinning him, Sterling will just send Avalanche down the ramp to wreck the ring.</aac>

"You're both looking at the wrong match!" Mark declared, walking into Room 214 with his arms loaded with chips and root beer before holding up a free hand to high-five Jordan. "Tonight is all about the main event—Jaxson 'The Outlaw' Vance versus 'The Blueprint' Silas Thorne! Plus, did you guys see the CPI Forgers season opener on Saturday? Total domination. I'm telling you, our defense is taking us all the way to the conference championship this year."

"You say that literally every September, babe," Hannah laughed, following him in with a stack of paper bowls as Sarah and Jessica stepped into the room from their fifth-floor trek downstairs.

"Are we heading down to the lobby, or am I going to have to listen to you two debate the biomechanical physics of a running lariat all night up here?" Madison teased, playfully ruffling Jordan's hair as she hopped down from her bunk.

Jordan's fingers danced across the keys at the exact same instant Mark opened his mouth.

<aac>It's not a debate, it's a strategic analysis!</aac> Jordan's terminal announced in near-perfect unison with Mark's voice, sending the entire room into a fit of laughter.

Even the women in the group who had never watched a single minute of **American Wrestling Entertainment** before meeting Mark and Jordan had come to love the Monday night ritual. They loved the over-the-top soap-opera theatrics, the absurd villainy, and most of all, the sheer, unguarded joy it brought to Jordan's face. Aubrie stood by the doorway watching Jordan laugh freely, her heart swelling with quiet pride. A week and a half ago, he had been a terrified, sensory-starved boy trembling in an empty room. Now, he was the warm, steady center of a loud, chaotic, loving family.

"Alright, troop, let's roll," Aubrie announced, stepping behind Jordan's chair with a bright smile. "I want to claim our couch cluster in the lobby before the third-floor engineering majors beat us to it."

***

#### 8:15 PM — The Main Event

The first-floor main lobby of Bennett Hall was buzzing with Labor Day evening energy, and the nine-person crew had arrived with ten minutes to spare—successfully claiming their favorite territory: a U-shaped cluster of deep, mismatched leather sofas arranged around the lobby's sixty-inch wall-mounted television.

On the screen, the pyrotechnics of **AWE Monday Night WAR** were in full swing. For the very first time in his life, Jordan wasn't watching a wrestling broadcast by squinting from two inches away at a grainy laptop stream with muffled audio. Through his new rectangular prescription glasses and calibrated behind-the-ear hearing aids, every detail on the sixty-inch screen across the rug was razor-sharp, and the roar of the television crowd blended effortlessly with the laughter of his friends around him.

Suddenly, the arena lights on the broadcast cut to a smug, corporate spotlight, and a crushing, downtuned arena-metal guitar riff and heavy stomping drumbeat blasted through the lobby speakers:

*"I'm in control! (I own the board, I own the ring!) I'm in control! (I pull the strings on everything!) Welcome to the bottom line, where every single cent is mine!"*

A chorus of theatrical groans and boos erupted from the couch cluster as AWE General Manager **Marcus Sterling** strutted out onto the television stage in an obnoxiously expensive three-piece suit, flashing his trademark patronizing smirk at the camera.

"Oh, somebody please put that bloke through an announce table!" Sarah shouted in her thick Sydney accent, tossing a single piece of popcorn at the screen while Jessica, sitting beside Madison on the left sofa, chuckled deeply.

For Jordan, the scene around him was a portrait of pure, unimaginable bliss. Rather than staying in his wheelchair at the edge of the rug, Mark and Aubrie had helped him transfer onto the center cushion of the main sofa, with his folded manual chair parked neatly beside the armrest and his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro resting on the coffee table in front of him.

His left arm was wrapped comfortably around Sarah, who was leaning warmly against his side. His right arm was draped around Lauren, who had her head resting contentedly on his shoulder. On the left sofa, Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, and Jessica were curled up under a fleece throw blanket, heckling Marcus Sterling on the broadcast. On the right sofa, Hannah and Mark were cuddled together over a giant bowl of popcorn.

Less than a week ago, both Lauren and Sarah had been walking on eggshells inside their own dorm, dreading the next manipulative text message or hallway ambush from a boy who treated relationships like secret territory to be hoarded and controlled. Now, with Tom gone from campus in disgrace, the two women sat side by side on the exact same couch with Jordan between them, more relaxed and unburdened than either of them had looked since arriving in Blacksburg.

Across the coffee table on the adjacent sofa, Aubrie was laughing, her head tilted back in pure delight at a one-liner Zoë had just deadpanned about Marcus Sterling's haircut.

Catching Jordan's eye across the rug, Aubrie didn't stiffen or feel a single flicker of territorial insecurity at seeing Lauren and Sarah tucked under his arms. Instead, she looked straight at Jordan, Lauren, and Sarah, and gave the three of them a radiant, loving smile and a subtle thumbs-up.

At that exact second, Lauren lifted her head from Jordan's shoulder and pressed a soft, affectionate kiss right to the corner of his jaw. On his left, Sarah let out a contented sigh and snuggled even deeper against his side, resting her hand warmly over his chest.

And Aubrie just beamed—her hazel eyes shining with pure, unselfish joy. There was no possessiveness. There was no competition. There was only blessing.

On the television screen, just as **Jaxson "The Outlaw" Vance** hoisted **"The Blueprint" Silas Thorne** up for his finishing slam in the center of the ring, Marcus Sterling frantically signaled toward the entrance ramp—sending the four-hundred-pound enforcer **Avalanche** charging down the aisle to smash the referee's count and trigger a chaotic disqualification.

"Called it!" Mark groaned, throwing his hands in the air as popcorn flew. "Jordan literally called that exact finish upstairs twenty minutes ago!"

On the center couch, Sarah grinned and tapped the edge of Jordan's Vanguard Pro on the coffee table so he could type.

Jordan didn't even need EchoType for the whole lobby. Leaning forward slightly with Lauren and Sarah still tucked warmly against his sides, he typed a single line in bright neon-green letters on his NeoEdit screen for the couch cluster to read:

<aac>Told you. Never bet against corporate interference on a Monday night.</aac>

### Part 2: Interlude: Mutiny at McConnell Transit Center

**Date:** 2014-09-08 at 07:35 America/New_York

At 07:35 AM on Monday, September 8, 2014, a damp late-summer river fog still hung low over the New River Valley as **Walter Hendricks**—General Manager of **Radford Transit**—stood in a high-visibility yellow safety vest on the brick-paved boarding island of the **McConnell Transit Center**, right outside McConnell Library in the heart of **Radford University**.

Standing beside Walter under the steel transit canopy were **Douglas Keaton**, City Manager for the independent **City of Radford**, and **Dr. Catherine Sterling**, Vice President for Student Affairs and Campus Administration at **Radford University**. Walter had personally asked both of them to meet him at the transit hub at 07:30 AM so they could witness with their own eyes what **Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute**'s unannounced freshman housing crisis was doing to their city.

"Look at the clock on the canopy, Doug," Walter said grimly, tapping his clipboard with a ballpoint pen while his Vanguard dispatch radio crackled on his belt. "For ten years, our local network has run like a Swiss watch because of the geography of this city. Radford is compact—it takes roughly fifteen minutes for a bus to run from here at McConnell Transit Center out to its far terminal, and fifteen minutes to come back. That allows us to run thirty-minute headways on every local city route—meeting here at :15 and :45 past the hour—using just a *single* thirty-foot bus per route."

"A system designed and funded for Radford residents and Radford University students," Dr. Sterling noted, folding her arms across her crimson Radford University blazer as dozens of RU nursing and education majors waited along the brick curb with their red student IDs in hand.

"Exactly," Walter nodded. "We only own thirty-foot low-floor buses, Catherine. Twenty-six seats, thirty-eight people absolute maximum if they're packed to the yellow standee line behind the driver's shoulder. And then in early August—after CPI over-enrolled their freshman class by nearly a thousand kids, filled every room at **The Hotel at Poly** on their own campus, and filled every highway hotel at Exit 118C in **Christiansburg**—CPI's Office of Housing and Residence Life quietly master-leased over a hundred hotel rooms along **West Main Street** and **Tyler Avenue** right here in the City of Radford without picking up the phone to warn a single one of us."

"Didn't CPI tell you last week that they were running their own direct hotel shuttles?" City Manager Keaton asked, frowning.

"They are—using buses CPI owns plus motorcoaches they chartered from private operators," Walter replied. "And every single one of those direct hotel buses fills to the doors under the hotel porte-cochères in three minutes flat! The other eighty or ninety CPI freshmen who can't squeeze onto CPI's morning hotel bus—or who have an eight o'clock lab or a nine o'clock quiz that doesn't line up with CPI's charter schedule—walk right out to the city sidewalk on West Main Street and Tyler Avenue holding their shiny new **CPI Poly Passes**, because their orientation packet told them a Poly Pass gets them free rides on Radford Transit and Blue Ridge Transit."

Right on cue, Walter's Vanguard radio squawked to life:

<pa>Dispatch from Unit 104, inbound on West Main. Come in, Base.</pa>

Walter keyed his lapel mic. "Unit 104, this is Hendricks at McConnell. Go ahead, Darrell."

<pa>Boss, I'm ten minutes into my inbound run from Jeffries Drive and I'm already at thirty-eight standees to the yellow line,</pa> the veteran driver's voice came back tight with frustration over the speaker. <pa>I pulled up to the West Main hotels at 7:31 and forty-five CPI freshmen in maroon hoodies rushed the front door with Poly Passes. I had to shut the door in seven kids' faces just to clear the stairwell. I've got the destination sign flipped to FULL BUS—I just had to pass up fourteen Radford University students at the Grove Avenue apartments and three seniors holding two quarters at Norwood Street. And with everybody wedged in the aisle with engineering tubes and backpacks, I'm running five minutes behind the 7:45 pulse.</pa>

Dr. Sterling's jaw tightened as a murmur of anger rippled through the Radford University students waiting at the McConnell shelter who overheard the radio call.

"Copy that, 104. Do the best you can and get here safely," Walter sighed into his mic. He lowered his hand and looked at Keaton and Dr. Sterling. "Do you see what that does to a single-bus route? Because there is only *one* bus running that thirty-minute cycle between McConnell Transit Center and Jeffries Drive, those fourteen Radford University students Darrell just had to pass up on West Main Street can't catch a follower bus in five minutes. They are stranded on the sidewalk for another *thirty minutes*—and when Darrell comes back inbound at 8:15, the next wave of CPI hotel kids at West Main will fill his bus to the windshield before he ever reaches the RU apartments again!"

At 07:50 AM—five minutes late, blowing the :45 pulse transfer window for the entire city—Unit 104 from West Main and Unit 107 from Tyler Avenue wheezed into the McConnell Transit Center turnaround, their air-suspension bellows groaning under the crush load.

When the folding front doors hissed open, a sea of **Forger Maroon** sweatshirts, freshman orientation lanyards, and overstuffed backpacks poured out onto the brick island in the middle of Radford University's campus—sixty-four CPI freshmen tumbling off the two thirty-foot buses and immediately looking around in confusion for a bus to Blacksburg.

"And here comes the second half of the trap," Walter said quietly, pointing toward the empty Bay 1 stall signed **RADFORD CONNECTOR — TO FAIRLAWN, PRICES FORK & CPI**. "Because our local city routes run every *thirty* minutes at :15 and :45, while the ***Radford Connector*** up to CPI only runs once every *sixty* minutes at :15 past the hour—heading out West Main Street across the New River Bridge onto US-11 through Fairlawn, up Peppers Ferry Road through Belview and Centerville, and across Prices Fork Road onto Stanger Street into Commonwealth Mall—the *Radford Connector* only meets the local bus lineups here at McConnell Transit Center *every other trip*."

Out on the brick island, a tall CPI freshman in a maroon jacket stared at the printed timetable bolted to the Bay 1 signpost and groaned aloud to a cluster of twenty other CPI freshmen who had already been sitting on the brick wall since 07:15 AM.

"Are you kidding me?!" the freshman shouted, throwing his hands up. "The 7:15 *Radford Connector* was already full and left us behind, and the local bus we just rode from the hotel dropped us off on the :45 lineup—so there isn't another *Radford Connector* until *8:15*?!"

At 07:55 AM, a **Blue Ridge Transit** bus rumbled into Bay 4 at the far end of the island, its destination sign flipping between **3 PEPPER PLAZA** and **via US-11**.

"Hey!" another CPI student yelled across the platform, pointing at the Blue Ridge Transit bus. "Don't wait twenty minutes for the 8:15 Connector! That's **Blue Ridge Transit Route 3**—it runs every thirty minutes down US-11 into Christiansburg! We can ride the 3 to **Pepper Plaza Transit Center** and transfer to **Blue Ridge Transit Route 1** going up Business 460 into Blacksburg!"

Like a dam breaking, forty-two CPI freshmen sprinted across the brick plaza toward Bay 4, crowding past eight Radford residents and Fairlawn commuters who had been waiting in an orderly line for Route 3. Within ninety seconds, the Blue Ridge Transit bus was packed to the front windshield and pulled away toward US-11 East, leaving twenty-two CPI freshmen still stranded at Bay 1 alongside the growing crowd of Radford University students.

Walter didn't even have to wait five minutes for the punchline. His radio clicked over on the regional inter-agency dispatch channel from Blue Ridge Transit's operations center in Christiansburg:

<pa>Blue Ridge Dispatch to Radford Base—Walter, if you've got CPI hotel kids at McConnell jumping on our Route 3 thinking they're going to catch Route 1 at Pepper Plaza, tell them to save their breath. The thirty CPI kids who rode our 7:25 Route 3 over US-11 just got dumped on the concrete island at Pepper Plaza next to the Courthouse, and they can't get on a single northbound Route 1 bus because every sixty-foot artic coming up from Christiansburg Transit Center is already stuffed to the gills with the CPI freshmen from the Christiansburg hotels!</pa>

City Manager Keaton rubbed his forehead in disbelief. "So whether a student is riding Radford Transit, Blue Ridge Transit, a CPI-owned shuttle, or a private charter coach from Radford or Christiansburg, every single bus in the New River Valley is packed to the roof."

"Wait until 8:15," Walter said grimly.

Over the next fifteen minutes, the :15 local pulse buses began converging on McConnell Transit Center from across the city—and with them came another fifty CPI hotel freshmen who had crowded onto the 8:00 AM inbound runs on West Main and Tyler Avenue, once again leaving Radford University students behind at neighborhood stops across town. By 08:12 AM, over **one hundred and ten CPI freshmen** were jammed shoulder-to-shoulder across the brick island of McConnell Transit Center, spilling off the curb into the active bus lane and blocking the main pedestrian crosswalk in front of Radford University's McConnell Library so that RU students walking to their 8:30 AM classes couldn't even cross Fairfax Street.

When Unit 101—the single **thirty-foot *Radford Connector* bus**—turned onto the plaza at 08:14 AM, the crowd surged forward before the bus had even come to a complete stop.

"Step back from the curb! Stay behind the yellow tactile strip!" Walter barked, blowing his safety whistle as two **Radford University Police Department** officers hurried across the plaza to keep the surging crowd of panicked eighteen-year-olds from pinning each other against the side of the thirty-foot bus.

When the front door opened, thirty-eight riders crammed inside in less than two minutes until a freshman girl's backpack was pressed flat against the inside of the windshield glass. Beside the front bumper, another CPI freshman girl in a maroon lanyard burst into tears when the driver held up his palm across the doorway.

"Please, I have an 8:50 General Chemistry lab check-in in Blacksburg!" she sobbed, holding up her blue CPI Poly Pass. "If you miss first-week lab safety, the department drops you from the course! I've been trying to get out of the West Main hotel since Quarter to Seven!"

"I'm sorry, sweetheart, I physically cannot close the doors if one more person steps on this bus," the driver said gently before pulling the lever to fold the doors shut.

As the single thirty-foot *Radford Connector* pulled out onto East Main Street at 08:18 AM, **seventy-four people** were left standing on the McConnell Transit Center island—including sixteen Radford University students who needed to reach internships at New River Valley Mall and dozens of RU students whose local connecting buses had just departed four minutes late without them because of the gridlock in the bus bays.

Dr. Catherine Sterling turned away from the curb, her face set like granite as she looked at City Manager Keaton and Walter Hendricks.

"Walter, you've called CPI Parking & Transportation and their Housing office four times over the past two weeks, haven't you?" Dr. Sterling asked sharply.

"Four times," Walter confirmed. "And every time, they told me to wait until their Post-Census Room-Freeze Day on Monday, September 8, and promised the numbers would sort themselves out."

"Well, it is Monday, September 8, and Radford University's campus transit hub just had to be policed like a riot zone because a university fifteen miles away decided to use our thirty-foot city buses as their unpaid overflow dorm shuttle," Dr. Sterling said coldly.

"Come up to my office at City Hall—both of you," City Manager Keaton said, gesturing toward his city vehicle parked at the end of the block. "No more phone calls to mid-level dispatchers. We are drafting an official joint complaint on City of Radford, Radford Transit, and Radford University letterhead right now, and we are sending it straight to CPI's Vice President for Administration and their Director of Housing before lunch."

### Part 3: Interlude: The Post-Census Verdict

**Date:** 2014-09-08 at 14:00 America/New_York

Stepping out of the lower-level lobby of **Eleanor Bennett Commonwealth Hall** onto the sunlit brick walkway of the inner-campus quad, **Kelsey Brennan** walked thirty paces east past the solid interior masonry firewall and pulled open the separate exterior glass door of the central **Office of Housing and Residence Life (Suite 110–120)**.

Compared to the frantic, all-hands triage center she had walked into on Move-In Saturday sixteen days earlier, the Central Housing annex on Monday, September 8 felt calm and orderly. Inside the conference room in **Suite 115**, **Dr. Alan Mercer** (Director of Housing and Residence Life), **David Thorne** (Associate Director of Housing Assignments & Operations), and **Ms. Patricia Higgins** (Director of the Office of Educational Accessibility) were already seated around the oval mahogany table.
