"Afternoon, Kelsey," Dr. Mercer greeted her, gesturing to the chair beside Patricia as Kelsey set her portfolio on the table and slid printed copies of **Isabel Dawson**'s and **Henry Walsh**'s fourteen-day evaluations across the polished wood. "We were just reviewing the final post-census campus occupancy numbers that David locked in with the Registrar at noon."

"How did the post-census numbers shake out?" Kelsey asked.

David Thorne turned his laptop screen toward her, showing the campus-wide housing and overflow hotel dashboard.

"It's still the tightest fall census in CPI history, Kelsey," David said, shaking his head as he pointed to the three-tier hotel tracker on his screen. "When the overflow crisis hit in July and August, we filled up every single room at **The Hotel at Poly** right next to campus first. When **The Hotel at Poly** hit one hundred percent capacity, we leased the highway hotel blocks down at Exit 118C in **Christiansburg**, and when Christiansburg filled up, we had to lease a third tier of overflow hotels all the way out in **Radford**."

"And I don't have to tell you what a commuter nightmare the off-campus hotels—especially Radford—have been for the last two weeks," Dr. Mercer remarked dryly, rubbing his temples as he tapped a formal letterhead memo sitting on the corner of the table. "At least the kids at **The Hotel at Poly** can walk across the street to their classes. If you're commuting in from a hotel in **Christiansburg** or **Radford**, it doesn't matter whether you're riding **Blue Ridge Transit**, **Radford Transit**, one of the direct shuttle buses **CPI** owns, or one of the motorcoaches we chartered from surrounding private operators—every single bus is stuffed to the brim, shoulder-to-shoulder standing room only, on every trip. The students trapped at the **Radford** hotels hate it the most: because the City of Radford is small enough that a single local bus can reach its outer terminal in fifteen minutes and run a thirty-minute pulse back to the **McConnell Transit Center**, while **Radford Transit's *Radford Connector*** only runs *once every sixty minutes* up to CPI, the *Radford Connector* only meets the local bus lineups at McConnell every *other* trip."

"And the ones who try to outsmart the schedule don't fare any better," David Thorne added with a grimace. "Half the kids at the Radford hotels figured out they could hop on **Blue Ridge Transit's Route 3** at the McConnell Transit Center and ride it east down **US-11** to **Pepper Plaza Transit Center** in Christiansburg to link up with **Route 1** heading up **Business 460** into Blacksburg—only to get off at Pepper Plaza and discover that **Route 1** is already stuffed to the gills with all the overflow students coming in from the Christiansburg hotels."

Dr. Mercer picked up the letterhead memo and gave a rueful shake of his head.

"To top it off, right before lunch the Vice President for Administration walked down here with this **Official Joint Administrative Complaint (RT-COR-RU-2014-0908)** signed by **Walter Hendricks** at **Radford Transit**, Radford City Manager **Douglas Keaton**, and **Dr. Catherine Sterling** at **Radford University**," Dr. Mercer continued. "And frankly, I can't even blame them. Radford Transit only has thirty-foot buses in their entire fleet. They never expected to suddenly become an emergency freshman shuttle service for a major land-grant university like CPI, and after over a hundred of our hotel freshmen swarmed the 8:15 AM *Radford Connector* at McConnell Transit Center this morning and left actual Radford University students and staff stranded on the curb, Radford gave us until five o'clock Thursday afternoon to start clearing those hotels and put dedicated relief coaches at McConnell—or they're cutting off Poly Pass boarding at the West Main and Tyler Avenue hotel stops."

"Parking & Transportation already dispatched two contracted forty-five-foot motorcoaches down to McConnell Transit Center for the afternoon :45 off-pulse lineups to satisfy the first half of their demand," David explained. "And on the housing side, between twenty-two incoming freshmen who failed to show up for the first two weeks of classes and fourteen early withdrawals during add/drop week, we finally freed up thirty-six beds on campus at noon today—including one very strange ghost vacancy over in **Westgate Hall**. Apparently a freshman Business major on the lacrosse team, **Tom Lawson**, got cut from the team roster during the first week of classes and simply vanished off the face of the earth. His roommates say he hasn't slept in his bed since Tuesday of week one, and his professors flagged him as a total no-call, no-show across all five of his courses, though he never bothered to file a withdrawal form with the Registrar or move his clothes out of his closet."

Kelsey kept her expression impeccably neutral, though she quietly filed that detail away—remembering all too well the Tuesday evening scene outside Kincaid Commons when Tom Lawson had tried to double-time Sarah Braithwaite (Room 505) and Lauren Barnes (Room 216) in front of six-foot-three Jessica Gallagher, and how Bennett Hall's front desk had permanently banned him from the building that same night.

"Every single one of those post-census vacancies is going straight toward rescuing freshmen out of the **Radford** hotels first so we can take the pressure off the *Radford Connector* and our CPI shuttle fleet," David continued, clicking over to the West Campus availability grid. "Which brings us directly to Bennett Hall, Suite 214/216. Strictly on paper, if Suite 214/216 had been a disaster over the last two weeks, we *could* hold back five scattered female beds from the post-census pool—three in **Bradshaw Hall** and two in **Thornton Hall**—and split the five women up across those two buildings today, though doing so would mean leaving five other freshmen stranded out in Radford on those packed buses."

Dr. Mercer picked up the two reports from **Isabel Dawson** and **Henry Walsh**, reading through both documents in silence while Patricia Higgins opened her OEA folder beside Kelsey.

For nearly two full minutes, the only sound in Suite 115 was the rustle of paper as the Director of Housing read every line of Isabel's account—from the clockwork bathroom and Room 212A roll-in shower schedule, to Zoë and Daniel Brooks upgrading Jordan's laptop on Move-In Night, to the group taking Jordan on the Blue Ridge Transit bus to Christiansburg for his first-ever glasses and hearing aids, to Jordan's private plea (<aac>This is the first place I have ever felt like I belong. Please do not make them leave.</aac>).

When Dr. Mercer finished reading Henry's report, he set both pages down on the mahogany table, took off his reading glasses, and looked at Patricia Higgins.

"Patricia, what does your office's two-week check-in show on the academic and accessibility side?" Dr. Mercer asked.

"I met with Jordan and his suitemates in Callahan Hall last week before his Christiansburg clinic appointment, and my staff processed his diagnostic paperwork from **Dr. Andrew Vance** and **Dr. Evelyn Harper** at the Montgomery Vision and Hearing Clinic on Friday evening," Patricia said, her voice carrying a rare warmth beneath her crisp professional cadence. "Alan, when that young man sat in my office on August 21 with his mother, she had kept him for eighteen years without a single pair of prescription glasses despite severe bilateral myopia, and without hearing aids despite moderate-to-severe sensorineural hearing loss. If he had been placed in a standard suite with roommates who ignored him—or if his suitemates had bailed on him after Move-In Day—he wouldn't have lasted three weeks at this university."

Patricia tapped the green OEA accommodation summary sheet in her folder.

"Instead," Patricia continued, "because of the five young women in Suite 214/216 and their friends on Floors 3 and 5, Jordan now has full prescription vision correction, digital behind-the-ear hearing aids paired with our classroom FM lapel-mic transmitter, a reliable Aura Glade communication laptop, and four dedicated peer note-takers covering every single one of his classes. I spoke with **Dr. Alistair** in Astronomy and **Dr. Gable** in History this morning—both of them told me Jordan is sitting in the front row, engaged, and performing at the very top of their freshman sections."

Dr. Mercer looked around the table—from Patricia's OEA summary, to Isabel and Henry's floor reports, to Kelsey.

"Sixteen days ago at this exact table," Dr. Mercer said slowly, "I said that none of us had a crystal ball. I said that a verbal agreement made in the middle of Move-In Day chaos didn't prove that one eighteen-year-old freshman man and five eighteen-year-old freshman women could actually live together in a forced-triple suite sharing one bathroom. I wanted them to prove it in the real world."

A genuine, unguarded smile creased the corners of the veteran director's eyes.

"Well, they proved it," Dr. Mercer said flatly. "In twenty-two years of higher education housing administration, I don't think I have ever read a two-week RA evaluation like the ones Isabel Dawson and Henry Walsh just turned in. Those six students didn't just 'make do' with a clerical error—they built the strongest, healthiest residential community in Bennett Hall. If this office walked upstairs today and broke up Suite 214/216 just to force their floor chart back into a traditional single-gender box now that five scattered beds opened up in Bradshaw and Thornton, we wouldn't be doing our jobs. We would be actively sabotaging six of our own students."

"Completely agreed," David Thorne said, nodding immediately as he clicked a checkbox on his West Campus assignment screen. "And locking Suite 214/216 as permanent means I can release those five female beds in Bradshaw and Thornton right now so all thirty-six post-census vacancies go straight into our formal remediation response to Radford Transit and the City of Radford at three o'clock."

"Kelsey," Dr. Mercer said, sliding a heavy, cream-colored sheet of university bond paper stamped with the Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute seal across the table toward her, "this is **Form HRL-2014-COED-PERM—the permanent Suite Arrangement Consent Form for the entirety of the 2014–2015 academic year**. Because the official post-census room-change freeze takes effect at five o'clock this afternoon, having all six residents sign this permanent form tonight locks Suite 214/216 in our master database through May 2015. Once all six signatures are on that page, nobody inside or outside the university administration can claim their arrangement was temporary or forced."

"I'll take it up to Room 214 right after they get back from dinner tonight," Kelsey said, carefully placing the bond-paper form and her blue fountain pen into her portfolio.

As Kelsey closed her binder, Dr. Mercer leaned back in his chair, looking thoughtfully at David and Patricia.

"You know," Dr. Mercer mused quietly, "when we fixed the spreadsheet bug two weeks ago so unisex names couldn't trigger an accidental co-ed assignment again, we treated Suite 214/216 purely as a one-off emergency anomaly. But looking at what Isabel and Patricia just documented—how a disabled student's trusted peer-support and care circle naturally crossed gender lines—maybe we ought to pay closer attention to how Suite 214/216 does over the rest of this academic year."

"You're thinking about the **Opt-In Gender-Inclusive Housing** proposals that came up at the state housing directors' conference in Richmond last spring?" David Thorne asked with sudden interest.

"I am," Dr. Mercer nodded. "Obviously, we would *never* place students into a co-ed suite at random—what happened on August 23 was a clerical fluke that happened to land on six extraordinary kids. Again, no crystal ball for the rest of the year: let's see how they handle midterms, winter weather, and spring semester. But if Suite 214/216 finishes May 2015 with zero behavioral incidents and the kind of academic and personal thriving they've shown in these first two weeks... with their permission, their suite might just be the founding case study we take to the Vice President of Student Affairs to launch an official **Opt-In Gender-Inclusive Housing Pilot** next fall."

### Part 4: Interlude: Relief at the :45 Pulse

**Date:** 2014-09-08 at 16:40 America/New_York

At 04:40 PM, the late-afternoon sun slanted across the brick plaza of **McConnell Transit Center** outside McConnell Library as Radford University classes let out for the afternoon.

Standing beside Bay 1 with **Gregory Donovan**—who had driven down from Blacksburg in a maroon **CPI Fleet Services** supervisor SUV twenty minutes earlier to shake Walter's hand and apologize in person—Walter watched as Radford Transit's thirty-foot local buses pulled in for the **04:45 PM off-pulse lineup**.

Seconds later, right on cue at 04:43 PM, a gleaming **forty-foot low-floor transit bus** painted in **Forger Maroon and Burnished Forge Gold** turned smoothly onto Fairfax Street and glided into Bay 1, its amber LED destination sign alternating cleanly between:

<led>RADFORD CONNECTOR RELIEF / TO CPI via PRICES FORK</led>

Right behind it on East Main Street, two fifty-six-passenger **forty-five-foot highway motorcoaches** with **CPI HOTEL EXPRESS — WEST MAIN & TYLER AVE** placards in their windshields rolled past on their fifteen-minute loop straight to the hotel porte-cochères, carrying returning CPI freshmen directly to their hotel lobby doors without a single one of them needing to board Radford Transit's thirty-foot Unit 104 on West Main Street.

At Bay 1, the twenty-eight CPI and cross-enrolled students who stepped off the :45 local pulse walked straight onto the forty-foot maroon **CPI Fleet Services** relief bus instead of piling up on the brick sidewalk for thirty minutes or running across the island to crowd onto **Blue Ridge Transit's Route 3**. And over at Bay 2 and Bay 3, Radford University students in crimson-and-blue hoodies stepped onto Unit 104 and Unit 107 with plenty of open seats to spare.

Walter keyed his lapel mic as Unit 104 pulled out right on schedule at 04:46 PM.

"Base to Unit 104—how's your load looking heading out West Main, Darrell?"

<pa>Twenty-one seated, zero standees, and right on the money, Boss,</pa> Darrell's voice came back cheerfully over the radio. <pa>Those big maroon coaches just scooped up every CPI kid at the West Main hotels before I even got to the light. Looks like we got our city back.</pa>

### Part 5: The Suite Arrangement Consent Form & One Hundred and Five Percent

**Date:** 2014-09-08 at 18:30 America/New_York

#### September 8, 2014 • 6:30 PM — The Suite Arrangement Consent Form

Monday, September 8 marked the end of the two-week post-census trial window that **Dr. Alan Mercer** had established on Move-In Day.

For the six residents of Suite 214/216, those sixteen days had flown by in a whirlwind of firsts: their first full week of college lectures, their first bus trip together down to Christiansburg to pick up Jordan's prescription eyeglasses and digital behind-the-ear hearing aids, and their first Monday night watching ***AWE Monday Night WAR*** together in the first-floor lobby lounge. When **Isabel Dawson** and **Henry Walsh** had checked in privately with each of the six suitemates over the past week to remind them of Dr. Mercer's confidential "no-fault opt-out" guarantee, all six of them had given the exact same answer: nobody wanted to leave.

At 6:30 that Monday evening, just after the suite had returned from dinner at Kincaid Commons and settled into Room 214 to go over their Tuesday reading assignments, a familiar, cheerful knock sounded on the hallway door.

Hannah stepped over and pressed the square stainless-steel **PUSH TO OPEN** handicap button on the interior wall to unlock and swing the heavy oak door open. Standing on the threshold was their Hall Director, **Kelsey Brennan**, holding a brushed-aluminum clipboard and a blue ballpoint pen, with **Isabel Dawson** (Room 215) and **Henry Walsh** (Room 201) smiling warmly right behind her in the hallway before the ten-second dormitory hold-open timer counted down.

"Hi, everyone—happy Monday," Kelsey said, stepping inside while Isabel and Henry lingered just inside the open doorway with matching grins. "Sorry to interrupt your evening study hour, but since five o'clock today officially marked the university's **Post-Census Room-Change Freeze**—and the end of your fourteen-day provisional agreement from Move-In Day—I wanted to bring you the news from my afternoon meeting with **Dr. Alan Mercer** in the central **Office of Housing and Residence Life**."

Around the small cinderblock room, five pairs of eyes—and Jordan's behind the crystal-clear polycarbonate lenses of his new glasses—locked onto Kelsey at once.

Sitting in his wheelchair beside his desk with his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro open on his lap, Jordan realized with a quiet start just how different this moment felt compared to sixteen days ago.

On Move-In Saturday (August 23), when Kelsey and Dr. Mercer had walked through that exact doorway with a clipboard, anything past arm's length had been a blurry smear of light and shadow, spoken voices across the room had sounded like a muffled underwater hum unless he cupped his hand behind his ear, and the mere thought of an adult authority figure asking for his opinion had made his hands shake with eighteen years of conditioned terror.

Tonight, through his new glasses, he could read the tiny gold lettering on Kelsey's CPI Residence Life lapel pin from eight feet away. Through his new digital behind-the-ear hearing aids, every syllable of Kelsey's warm voice came through in crisp, effortless high definition. And with **Aubrie** sitting right on the edge of the lower bunk beside his wheel, **Madison** perched on the desk chair, and **Zoë**, **Lauren**, and **Hannah** standing shoulder-to-shoulder by the connecting doorway, Jordan didn't shrink back an inch.

"First of all," Kelsey said, her eyes crinkling with warmth as she looked around the circle, "in the spirit of total transparency: when David Thorne ran the final post-census numbers at noon today after two weeks of campus-wide add/drop and no-shows, thirty-six beds finally opened up on campus—which Central Housing is using first to rescue the poor freshmen who have been trapped out in the **Radford** overflow hotels dealing with connecting buses to the McConnell Transit Center, the once-hourly **Radford Connector**, and the packed-to-the-brim CPI and chartered shuttle buses every morning, while **The Hotel at Poly** and the **Christiansburg** hotels are still full. Technically, five of those post-census vacancies were scattered female beds across West Campus in Bradshaw Hall and Thornton Hall."

Madison's jaw set instantly, and Lauren took half a step closer to Jordan's chair as if ready to barricade the door with her own body. "Kelsey, we already told Izzy and Henry—"

"Hold on, Madison—let me finish," Kelsey laughed, holding up a reassuring hand while Isabel grinned from the doorway. "Because when Dr. Mercer sat down with me and Ms. Higgins from Educational Accessibility at two o'clock today, he read the fourteen-day evaluation reports that **Izzy** and **Henry** wrote about your suite."

Jordan glanced over at Isabel and Henry by the door. Isabel gave him a warm wink, and Henry offered a proud thumbs-up.

"Izzy and Henry told Dr. Mercer the truth about what the six of you have built in here over the last two weeks," Kelsey continued, her voice softening with genuine pride. "They reported that while standard single-gender suites on this floor have already needed roommate mediations over thermostats and noise, Suite 214/216 has operated with zero complaints, total mutual respect, and clockwork coordination. They reported how the five of you—along with your friends on Floors 3 and 5—have stood by Jordan as his peer note-takers, campus navigators, and family. And Dr. Mercer said that on Move-In Day, none of us had a crystal ball—he wanted the six of you to prove in the real world that this arrangement could work. Today, he said that breaking up the strongest, most supportive suite in Bennett Hall just to fill five scattered beds across campus would be a disservice to all six of you."

A collective cheer erupted across Room 214. Madison pumped both fists in the air, Lauren threw her arms around Hannah and Zoë's shoulders, and Aubrie reached over to squeeze Jordan's hand with a radiant grin that made Jordan's chest swell with warmth.

Kelsey held up the brushed-aluminum clipboard, which held a single crisp sheet of heavyweight cream bond paper stamped at the top with the embossed seal of **Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute**.

"Because your suite's co-ed configuration began as an emergency exception, the fourteen-day temporary form expires tonight," Kelsey explained, handing the clipboard and blue ballpoint pen to Hannah. "To lock your suite in permanently through May 2015, Dr. Mercer has already pre-signed the administrative approval block at the bottom of this page. All he needs for the university's permanent audit vault is one final, written confirmation signed by all six residents."

Across the top of the heavyweight bond paper, in bold serif type that Jordan could read effortlessly from his chair without squinting, was the heading:

**OFFICE OF HOUSING AND RESIDENCE LIFE — 2014–2015 SUITE ARRANGEMENT CONSENT FORM (FORM HRL-2014-COED-PERM)**

Beneath the header, a concise paragraph stated in clear institutional language that having completed the fourteen-day post-census evaluation period with distinction, all six eighteen-year-old adult residents of **Suite 214/216 in Eleanor Bennett Commonwealth Hall** were fully aware of the co-ed nature of their living assignment, that each resident consented to the arrangement of their own free will without coercion, and that all six requested that the assignment be made **permanent for the entirety of the 2014–2015 academic year**.

"This is for your protection just as much as the university's," Kelsey added gently. "Once all six of your signatures are on this bond paper, nobody—inside or outside the administration—can ever claim your living arrangement was forced or temporary."

To Jordan, looking at the heavy cream bond paper as it passed from hand to hand around the room, it felt less like a housing form and more like a constitutional treaty. It was the permanent legal charter of their chosen family.

One by one, the five women read the paragraph and signed their full names in blue ink beside their printed student ID numbers and bed codes:

- **Madison Elizabeth Scott** (Room 214, Bed C)
- **Zoë Wren Brooks** (Room 216, Bed A)
- **Hannah Ashlee Parker** (Room 216, Bed C)
- **Lauren Nicole Barnes** (Room 216, Bed B)
- **Aubrie Jean Kelly** (Room 214, Bed B)

Aubrie handed the clipboard and blue pen to Jordan last.

Unlike Move-In Day, when his fingers had trembled with fear that having a voice would get him punished, Jordan's hand was completely steady. Resting the brushed-aluminum clipboard against the flat matte-black lid of his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro, Jordan looked clearly through his glasses at the top signature line (Room 214, Bed A) and signed his name in bold, clean blue ink:

**Jordan Fuller (Aubrey Jordan Fuller)**

Then he flipped open his laptop lid, typed a single line into EchoType, and hit play so his chosen "Sydney" voice spoke for the whole room and for his two RAs standing by the door:

<aac>Thank you, Kelsey, Izzy, and Henry. And thank you to my suitemates for keeping me.</aac>

"Always, J," Aubrie murmured softly, resting her hand over his shoulder. "You're stuck with us for the whole year now."

"Thank you all," Kelsey said warmly, taking the clipboard back and inspecting the six signatures with a satisfied nod. "This goes straight into Dr. Mercer's locked vault across the firewall first thing tomorrow morning. Have a wonderful week, Suite 214/216."

***

#### September 19, 2014 • 3:30 PM — Transforming Jordan into a Forger

By the third Friday of September, the first crisp, cool breeze of Appalachian autumn had arrived in Blacksburg, and the energy across campus was electric. Homecoming Week was just days away, and the walkways around **Commonwealth Green** were already a vibrant sea of Foundry Maroon and Molten Orange.

After their Friday afternoon classes wrapped up, the entire nine-person crew—Jordan, Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Mark, Sarah, and Jessica—walked over to **The Foundry**, the **CPI Campus Bookstore** at the edge of the academic district, to pick up supplies.

The moment Jordan rolled through the automatic glass doors of the rotunda-shaped building, he was hit by a wave of pure, unfiltered collegiate spirit. Through the crisp lenses of his new glasses, the store looked like a cathedral dedicated to an identity he desperately wanted to belong to. Towering racks overflowed with heavy-cotton **CPI Forgers** hoodies, burnt-orange jerseys, pennants, and embroidered baseball caps.

"Okay, I officially need this for the Homecoming game," Madison announced, holding up a fitted maroon t-shirt with metallic gold and orange *FORGERS* lettering across the chest.

"Solid choice," Mark grinned, trying on a burnt-orange CPI cap with the classic anvil-and-hammer crest. "Gotta represent in The Anvil."

Jordan wheeled himself quietly down the center aisle, reaching out to brush his fingers against the thick, fleece-lined sleeve of a heavy maroon CPI Forgers hoodie. He had never owned a single piece of school-spirit clothing in his life. Back in Virginia Beach, his mother had only ever bought him the cheapest, plainest clothes from discount racks, insisting that anything with a logo was a "frivolous waste of money" on someone who didn't participate in school activities. He imagined pulling this maroon hoodie over his shoulders and rolling into **The Crucible** next Saturday alongside sixty-five thousand screaming fans—not as an outsider looking in, but as a Forger.

Then he flipped over the cardboard price tag hanging from the cuff.

Fifty-four dollars.

Jordan's stomach dropped. His mother had left him with barely enough cash in his checking account to cover his lab fees and required textbooks, and she monitored every bank transaction online like a hawk. He let the soft maroon sleeve slip from his fingers, locked his jaw, and quietly began to turn his wheelchair away from the rack.

Aubrie, who had been watching him from the end of the aisle, stepped gently in front of his chair.

"You're not getting it, J?" she asked softly.

Jordan's cheeks flushed warm. He looked down at his Vanguard Pro resting on his lap and typed a quiet line into NeoEdit, angling the screen just toward her so he wouldn't embarrass himself in front of the whole store.

<aac>I can't afford it. My mother only left enough in my account for books, and she checks the statements.</aac>

Over by the t-shirt wall, the playful chatter among Madison, Mark, Hannah, Lauren, Zoë, Sarah, and Jessica stopped instantly. Without a word, all seven of them walked over, closing ranks around Jordan's chair as their expressions shifted from carefree to fiercely protective.

"Oh, no, mate, that is not how this works," Sarah said firmly, crossing her arms.

"Dude, Homecoming Week starts Monday," Mark added, stepping up beside Aubrie. "You can't roll into The Crucible without Forger gear. It's practically in the CPI student constitution."

Jordan shook his head, his fingers typing rapidly on his terminal before he triggered EchoType.

<aac>I can't pay you guys back.</aac>

"This isn't a loan, Jordan," Hannah said, her warm, steady "big sister" voice carrying absolute authority. "This is your initiation. You're part of our family now, which means you're part of this school, too. All eight of us are pitching in—and if your mother checks your bank statement, she won't see a single cent missing."

Before Jordan could type another protest, his chosen family sprang into coordinated action.

"We're getting the heavyweight maroon hoodie," Aubrie declared, pulling a size medium off the rack and laying it across his lap.

"And this heather-grey **CPI FORGERS** crew-neck t-shirt for everyday wear, plus the *'Beat VDU!'* shirt for Saturday," Madison insisted, snatching both from the display table and placing them on top of the hoodie.

"And the cap to top it off," Mark finished with a grin, setting the burnt-orange CPI anvil-crest baseball cap right on top of the pile.

Jordan looked down at the stack of maroon, heather-grey, and orange fabric resting on his knees, then up through his glasses at the eight smiling, expectant faces surrounding him—from six-foot-three Jessica beaming down at him to Lauren and Zoë nodding in quiet solidarity. They weren't pitying him. They were claiming him.

A sharp, overwhelming prickle of emotion stung behind his eyes—not a meltdown of fear, but a surge of pure, unadulterated gratitude. His fingers tapped two simple words into his terminal:

<aac>Thank you.</aac>

Ten minutes later, after the group split the tab at the register, Aubrie and Madison helped Jordan slip the new maroon CPI Forgers hoodie over his head right outside **The Foundry**. It was thick, fleece-warm, and smelled like new cotton.

When the nine of them rolled back into **Suite 214/216** in **Bennett Hall** twenty minutes later, Jordan wheeled into the connecting jack-and-jill accessible bathroom to wash his hands and paused in front of the tilted mirror mounted above the roll-under sink.

Through the crisp polycarbonate lenses of his new glasses, he stared at his reflection. With his new glasses, his subtle behind-the-ear hearing aids, and the heavyweight maroon **CPI Forgers** hoodie draped over his shoulders, he almost looked like a real college freshman—except for the patchy, uneven eighteen-year-old facial fuzz along his jaw and upper lip.

In eighteen years in Virginia Beach, Jordan had **never once been clean-shaven**. His mother had flatly refused to let him near a safety razor, insisting that his Cerebral Palsy fine-motor spasticity would cause him to slice his own face open, and she had never bothered to teach him how to groom himself. Whenever she had wanted him to look "presentable" for company, she had simply cornered him in the bathroom and scraped a cheap, dry electric hair trimmer roughly across his chin without guards or lotion, leaving his skin raw and stinging while complaining about having to groom a grown teenager.

Unconsciously, Jordan lifted his right hand and touched the patchy stubble on his chin, his shoulders sagging half an inch.

Standing in the open doorway of Room 214, **Mark** caught the look in the mirror immediately.

"Hey, J," Mark said casually, leaning against the doorframe with a warm, easy grin. "Since we're officially transforming you into a full-fledged CPI Forger before Homecoming Week... you want a hand getting a real clean shave?"

Jordan blinked, looking up at Mark in the mirror. Turning to his Vanguard Pro on his lap tray, he typed honestly:

<aac>I've never actually had a clean shave before. My mother never let me near a razor because of my hands.</aac>

Mark's expression softened with quiet, brotherly understanding, though he kept his voice upbeat and completely matter-of-fact so Jordan wouldn't feel self-conscious for a second.

"Well, we're fixing that right now, brother," Mark said, grabbing his dopp kit from his backpack in Room 214 and stepping into the bathroom. "Every guy deserves to know what a proper hot-towel shave feels like. And tomorrow when we're out, we'll pick you up an ergonomic rotary foil shaver with a wide rubber grip so you can do touch-ups yourself whenever you want without ever worrying about a blade."

Mark ran the tap until the water was steaming hot, soaked a clean white hand towel, wrung it out, and gently draped the warm cloth across the lower half of Jordan's face for thirty seconds to soften the bristles. Jordan closed his eyes behind his glasses, letting out a long, slow breath at the soothing warmth.

Then Mark lathered up a palmful of rich, cedar-scented shaving cream, spread it evenly across Jordan's jaw, cheeks, and upper lip, and held up a fresh, multi-blade safety razor.

"Alright, man—just tilt your chin up about ten degrees and relax your jaw," Mark coached calmly, resting his left hand steadily on Jordan's shoulder as a grounding anchor so Jordan knew every movement before it happened. "Short, smooth strokes with the grain. I've got the angle completely locked."

With unhurried, practiced precision, Mark drew the razor cleanly down Jordan's cheek, rinsing the blade under the warm faucet between each gentle pass. Nobody rushed him. Nobody scraped his skin dry or sighed about how long it took. Standing by the open doorway of Room 214, **Aubrie Jean** and **Hannah** watched with quiet, misty-eyed smiles as Mark chatted easily with Jordan about Saturday's football matchup, treating the ritual like the most natural brotherly hangout in the world.

Two minutes later, Mark wiped away the last trace of foam with a warm, damp washcloth and patted a splash of soothing, alcohol-free balm onto Jordan's skin.

"There you go," Mark grinned, stepping back and clapping Jordan warmly on the shoulder. "Take a look, Mr. Fuller."

Jordan looked into the lowered mirror above the sink.

Staring back at him was a clean-shaven nineteen-year-old young man in dark-framed rectangular glasses and a maroon **CPI Forgers** hoodie, his jawline smooth and clear for the very first time in his life. As he ran his fingertips lightly across his smooth chin, a huge, luminous smile broke across his face. He didn't look like the neglected boy locked in a back room in Virginia Beach anymore. Inside and out, he looked like a CPI Forger.

#### September 19, 2014 • 7:30 PM — One Hundred and Five Percent

Friday evening in Suite 214/216 had begun as a quiet, triumphant celebration.

It was the tail end of CPI's beginning-of-semester **Health and Safety Week**—the mandatory campus-wide compliance week held near the start and end of every semester. All week long, Environmental Health & Safety (EHS) had been running its annual once-a-year daytime fire drills across every academic building on campus. By sheer luck of the schedule, every single academic-building drill that week had gone off while Jordan was somewhere else: Walton Hall had been evacuated on Tuesday morning twenty minutes before his afternoon Astrophysics lecture; Colonial Hall's alarm had sounded on Wednesday while he was across campus eating lunch at Kincaid Hall; and Commonwealth Hall had run its drill on Thursday afternoon right after his Calculus section let out.

In Bennett Hall, the only sign of Health and Safety Week that Suite 214/216 had noticed was a bright yellow Residence Life checklist pinned to the corkboard outside **Isabel Dawson**'s door in Room 215 reminding residents not to daisy-chain extension cords, overload surge protectors, or hang laundry from the sprinkler pipes. Yesterday afternoon, **Zoë** had dutifully inspected every power strip in both rooms, declared Suite 214/216 one hundred percent compliant with the Virginia Statewide Fire Prevention Code, and checked the item off her mental list.

None of them gave Health and Safety Week a second thought tonight—because tonight, Suite 214/216 had something far bigger to celebrate.

At seven-thirty that evening, **Dr. Alistair** had posted the grades on Canvas for their first college **ASTR 101: Introduction to Astronomy & Astrophysics** exam.

Sitting in his wheelchair at his desk in his brand-new maroon **CPI Forgers** hoodie, Jordan had clicked open the gradebook tab on his Pinnacle Vanguard Pro while **Aubrie Jean** leaned over his shoulder—and for three full seconds, Jordan had simply stared at the screen through his new glasses in stunned disbelief.

He hadn't just passed his first college exam.

He had scored a perfect **100%**, plus all five bonus points on Dr. Alistair's brutal orbital-mechanics extra-credit derivation, for a total score of **105%**.

"A hundred and five percent!!" Aubrie Jean had shrieked with pure joy, throwing both arms around Jordan's shoulders and kissing his cheek while **Madison**, **Zoë**, **Hannah**, and **Lauren** crowded around his desk to read the glowing numbers for themselves.

"Look at Dr. Alistair's comment in the rubric margin!" Zoë had pointed out, her analytical gray eyes shining with pride. *"'Flawless Keplerian transfer derivation—cleanest vector notation in the lecture hall.'"*

For a young man who had spent eighteen years being told by his mother that his mind was broken and that going to college was a pointless fantasy, seeing **105 / 100** stamped across a university astrophysics gradebook felt like watching the sun rise for the first time.

By a quarter to eight, the initial burst of cheering had settled into a warm, peaceful Friday night glow. Sitting at his desk in his fleece-lined Forgers hoodie, Jordan was happily reviewing his next chapter of astrophysics notes while basking in the quiet pride of his suitemates. Across Room 214, Aubrie Jean was curled up on the lower bunk in her reading glasses, reading under a soft fleece blanket, Madison was lounging on the top bunk scrolling through her mPhone, and Zoë, Hannah, and Lauren were chatting casually through the open connecting bathroom doorway in Room 216 as the digital clock on Jordan's desk ticked toward 8:00 PM.

### Part 6: Fire Alarm in the Dormitory

**Date:** 2014-09-19 at 20:00 America/New_York

![Inside Bennett Hall Room 214 with the corridor door swung open inward and the Simplex fire alarm strobe flashing, Isabel Dawson—wearing a neon-yellow high-visibility vest over her sweater and blue jeans—crouches at eye level holding open the official CPI EHS log folder to promise a tearful Jordan he is safe as he begins loosening his grip on his desk, while Madison supports an upset Aubrie near the doorway.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e001/c012/s003/fire-drill.jpg)

The clock hit 8:00 PM.

Without a single second of warning, a piercing, metallic, 100-decibel shriek ripped through the cinderblock walls of Suite 214/216, accompanied by the blinding, rhythmic white flash of the wall-mounted ADA emergency strobe lights and the heavy *thud* of the hallway's electromagnetic smoke-barrier doors automatically releasing and slamming shut.

***BZZZZT! BZZZZT! BZZZZT!***

"Oh, you have *got* to be kidding me!" Madison groaned from the top bunk, clapping her hands over her ears. Across the connecting doorway in Room 216, Hannah and Lauren winced in unison.

For the four women in the suite without severe sensory sensitivities, the unannounced 8:00 PM klaxon was a loud, obnoxious inconvenience.

For Aubrie and Jordan, the sudden sensory and psychological detonation was catastrophic.

On the lower bunk, Aubrie let out a sharp, strangled cry, dropping her book and clamping both palms violently over her ears as she curled into a tight ball on her side, sobbing openly against the acoustic assault.

At his desk, Jordan's entire body jolted so hard his wheelchair frame rattled against the linoleum. Through his new digital behind-the-ear hearing aids, the 100-decibel klaxon tore straight into his skull like a circular saw, while the high-intensity white strobe flashes reflecting off the cinderblock walls sliced across the crisp polycarbonate lenses of his new glasses. Tears spilled instantly down his cheeks as a ragged, wordless cry tore from his throat.

"Fire alarm—we need to evacuate the building," Zoë called out over the shriek, her crisis-management instincts snapping into gear as she strode into Room 214, reached into her desk drawer for Aubrie's emergency noise-reducing earmuffs, and tossed them to Madison before stepping to the entry wall. Zoë pressed her palm firmly against the square stainless-steel **PUSH TO OPEN** handicap button beside the doorframe. With an electronic click and the whir of the overhead motor, the lock released and the heavy wooden door of Room 214 swung wide open into the strobing corridor, starting its ten-second dormitory hold-open timer.

Madison scrambled down the bunk ladder in two seconds flat, fitting the padded earmuffs snugly over Aubrie's ears and wrapping the fleece blanket tightly around her shoulders.

"I've got you, Aubs—I know the noise is awful," Madison murmured against her temple, guiding a weeping Aubrie up to her feet with a firm, steady arm around her waist. "We're going straight out the Washington Street doors where it's quiet."

Even with tears streaming down her face from the overwhelming noise, Aubrie leaned into Madison's side and willingly began shuffling toward the open hallway door to escape the sound.

Everyone in the room naturally assumed Jordan was crying for the exact same reason—that the piercing 100-decibel horn and flashing strobes had simply overloaded his ears and eyes.

They had no way of knowing the sheer, suffocating nightmare exploding inside Jordan's mind, and because Jordan was completely non-verbal, he had no words to tell them.

Jordan had never attended a college orientation session on residential fire procedures, and because he had lucked out and missed every daytime academic-building fire drill during **Health and Safety Week**, after eighteen years of being kept isolated inside his mother's house in Virginia Beach, he had no concept that universities ran routine, unannounced evening fire drills in the dorms. In his mind, Room 214's heavy, automatically locking door was the only barrier on earth standing between him and Aubrie Sinclair. Nobody in the outside world could get through that locked door from the hallway without an authorized Poly Pass.

And now the alarm was screaming, and Zoë had just unlocked and opened the door.

To Jordan, there was only one terrifying explanation: *his mother was outside Bennett Hall, and she had pulled the fire alarm on purpose to flush him out of his locked room so she could grab him in the chaos and drag him back to Virginia Beach.*

"I've got Jordan's laptop!" Hannah shouted over the horn, unplugging his Vanguard Pro and tucking it safely into his backpack so he wouldn't be left without his voice outside, while Lauren stepped behind his wheelchair and reached for the push-handles to gently guide him toward the open door behind Aubrie and Madison. "Come on, J, let's get you outside away from the noise!"

The instant Lauren eased his chair half an inch backward toward the open doorway, Jordan snapped.

A raw, guttural scream of pure, animal terror ripped from his throat. Lunging forward in his seat, Jordan locked both hands onto the thick wooden edge of his desk in a white-knuckled death grip. His sneakers kicked wildly against his footplates, his torso thrashing as he shook his head frantically from side to side, tears blinding his glasses as he fought with every ounce of strength in his upper body to keep his wheelchair from being rolled toward the hallway.

Lauren and Hannah froze in shock, immediately letting go of the push-handles so they wouldn't hurt his arms or wrench his shoulders.

"Jordan?!" Lauren gasped, kneeling beside his wheel while Hannah crouched on his other side, both of them trying gently to coax his trembling forearms as the door's ten-second timer expired and the heavy wooden door began to swing shut. "Hey, sweetie, it's okay, it's just us! We have to go outside—the alarm is way louder in here!"

Zoë hit the square **PUSH TO OPEN** button a second time to swing the door back open for evacuation, her gray eyes widening as she looked from Aubrie—who was standing right at the threshold with Madison, ready to leave despite how badly the noise hurt her ears—to Jordan, who was still clinging to his desk and screaming in sheer, wordless horror every time his eyes darted toward the open hallway.

Across the room, Madison, Aubrie, Zoë, Hannah, and Lauren all exchanged a stunned, chilling look.

This wasn't just Jordan being overwhelmed by the noise of the fire alarm. If it were the sound hurting his ears, he would have wanted to get out of the cinderblock echo chamber just like Aubrie did, or he would have clamped his hands over his hearing aids. He wasn't covering his ears at all. He was sacrificing his hands to hold onto the desk because he was terrified of *leaving the locked room*.

Just as the realization hit his found family like cold water, rapid, authoritative footsteps pounded down the strobing second-floor corridor.

**Isabel Dawson** rounded the corner. Because the 8:00 PM Friday drill was unannounced, she wasn't in her CPI Residence Life uniform polo and khakis; instead, she had thrown a neon-yellow **CPI Residence Life** high-visibility vest over her casual sweater and blue jeans, carrying a black two-way radio in one hand and an official **CPI Environmental Health & Safety (EHS)** log folder in the other as she conducted her mandatory room-by-room floor sweep.

"Second floor, evacuate toward the Washington Street doors—do not use the elevators!" Isabel called out down the hall—and then she stopped dead in her tracks outside the open doorway of Room 214.

Through the open door, Isabel saw Madison supporting a tearful Aubrie by the threshold—upset by the 100-decibel klaxon, yet understanding it was a fire drill and struggling bravely to execute the evacuation protocol—while Lauren and Hannah knelt beside Jordan's wheelchair, trying gently to get him out of the room as Jordan clung to the edge of his desk with white knuckles, screaming in terror and refusing to budge.

One look at Jordan's terrified eyes fixed on the open doorway—and the stunned, helpless expressions on his suitemates' faces—told Isabel that something far deeper than alarm noise was happening here.

Isabel didn't bark an evacuation order, and she didn't reach for his chair. Instead, as the ten-second dorm door timer began to close the door again, she stepped straight into Room 214, pressed the **PUSH TO OPEN** button with her elbow to reset the ten-second timer, and dropped to both knees directly in front of Jordan's wheelchair so she was completely below his eye level.

"Jordan! Hey—Jordan, look at me!" Isabel said clearly, pitching her voice right into the midrange frequency where she knew his hearing aids picked up speech best.

Still clutching the desk as if his life depended on it, Jordan's tear-streaked eyes darted down to her face.

Deliberately, slowly, Isabel tapped the reflective silver stripe on her neon **CPI Residence Life** vest, held up her black two-way radio, and then opened the official **CPI Environmental Health & Safety (EHS)** log folder right in front of his glasses for him to inspect, pointing a steady finger at the bold printed header and table at the top of the sheet:

**COMMONWEALTH POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE — ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH & SAFETY (EHS)**
**SCHEDULED RESIDENTIAL FIRE DRILL LOG — FALL SEMESTER (DRILL 1 OF 2 — HEALTH & SAFETY WEEK)**

"Look at the paper, Jordan—read the heading," Isabel said, her voice steady, warm, and unshakeable beneath the wail of the horn. "Nobody pulled the alarm to trick you or hurt you, and nobody is waiting outside for you. This is an official, scheduled university fire drill for Health and Safety Week. Environmental Health and Safety runs two of them in every dorm every single semester—one right now at the beginning of the semester, and one toward the end of the semester. That's all this is."

Jordan stared at the printed university seal and the typed schedule table inside her EHS log folder, his chest heaving with ragged, hitching sobs as the words registered through the fog of panic.

"All ten RAs in Bennett Hall—a guy and a girl on every single residential floor, Floors 2 through 6—are in these yellow vests sweeping the building right now," Isabel continued gently, keeping her eyes locked on his. "Henry is standing right at our second-floor Washington Street doors holding them open for us, and Kelsey is right outside on the sidewalk with the Environmental Health and Safety fire marshals and Housing staff timing the drill with a stopwatch. You are completely safe. Nobody is going to touch you, and nobody is taking you anywhere. We are going to roll out to the grass together for five minutes while Kelsey and the EHS officers sign our floor sheets, and then we are coming right back inside to your room. Okay?"

For three heartbeats, nobody in Room 214 breathed.

Slowly, as the truth of the printed EHS log sank in—that there was no ambush waiting on the sidewalk, and that his mother wasn't outside—the raw, suffocating terror in Jordan's green eyes broke into a wave of exhausted, shuddering relief. One finger at a time, his trembling hands uncurled from the wooden edge of his desk, though tears still spilled freely down his cheeks.

He looked at Isabel, then at Lauren, Hannah, Zoë, Madison, and Aubrie, and gave a shaky nod.

"That's it—you've got this," Lauren whispered thickly, wiping a tear of her own from her cheek as she stepped behind his chair, while Zoë pressed the square **PUSH TO OPEN** button one final time so the motorized arm held the heavy door wide open.

Moving as a tight, protective diamond—Lauren pushing Jordan's wheelchair, Madison supporting Aubrie under the blanket, Isabel walking right at Jordan's left armrest in her neon vest, and Zoë and Hannah clearing a lane through the strobing second-floor corridor—they rolled straight out the ground-level hillside doors onto the **Washington Street** sidewalk at the top of the slope. **Henry** was already holding the heavy exterior crash-bar door wide open to keep the threshold clear, while out along the curb and lawn, **Kelsey Brennan**, two **CPI Environmental Health & Safety (EHS)** officers in reflective jackets with clipboards and stopwatches, a **Housing & Residence Life Area Coordinator**, and the other eight Bennett Hall RAs in their neon-yellow vests were guiding streams of students from all five residential floors fifty yards across the grass away from the fire lane.

Outside in the cool night air, with fifty yards of open lawn buffering them from the building's exterior horns, the brutal 100-decibel shriek dropped to a distant background ring.

Madison sat with Aubrie on a low stone retaining wall under the trees, rubbing her back while Zoë, Hannah, and Lauren stood shoulder-to-shoulder around Jordan's chair—still deeply shaken by what they had just witnessed inside Room 214. None of them pressed Jordan about it out here on the crowded lawn while he sat hunched in his hoodie, his shoulders still trembling with quiet aftershocks and hitching sniffles, but an unspoken certainty hung heavily between them: *something terrible had happened to Jordan before he came to CPI to make him that terrified of stepping outside a locked door.*

A few minutes later, after the final upper-floor stairwells emptied and all ten RAs checked in with Kelsey and the EHS fire safety officers to confirm all six floors of the building were clear, the flashing white strobes inside Bennett Hall's windows clicked off, the horns fell silent, and **Kelsey Brennan** gave the official all-clear over the staff two-way radios.

Before heading back to the doors, Isabel walked straight back over to Suite 214/216's spot on the Washington Street sidewalk in front of **The Addition**—the three-story 1980s wing of Bennett Hall extending beside the five-story-above-grade 1964 **Tower**—her EHS log folder tucked under her arm, and crouched down beside Jordan's wheelchair again so she didn't tower over him.

"Hey," Isabel said gently, her voice warm in the sudden quiet of the September night. "How are you holding up, Jordan? Are you okay?"

Jordan looked down at his RA through watery lenses—his cheeks crusted with dried tear tracks, fresh tears still slipping slowly down his face as quiet, involuntary sniffles hitched in his chest. In his eighteen years, he had kept a very tiny, fiercely guarded mental list of people who would never hurt him, mock him, or use his helplessness against him: Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Hannah, Mark, Sarah, and Jessica.

Now, looking at Isabel crouching beside his wheelchair in her neon vest over her sweater and blue jeans, something permanent clicked into place inside his chest. She hadn't laughed at him for screaming and clinging to his desk. She hadn't barked at him or treated him like a problem for holding up her floor sweep. In the middle of a building-wide alarm, she had knelt on the floor and given him the exact proof he needed to feel safe.

Right then and there, Jordan added **Isabel Dawson** to his list of **Safe People**.

He didn't reach for his backpack to pull out his laptop. Instead, with a shaky, hitching sniffle and a fresh tear rolling down his cheek, Jordan leaned forward in his wheelchair and pulled Isabel into a hug.

Isabel wasn't expecting it, and for a split second she froze—momentarily caught off guard as his trembling arms wrapped around her neck. Yet almost immediately, her wide eyes softened with deep, quiet understanding. She recognized the unspoken weight of a trauma survivor behind how terrified he had been of leaving that locked room, and she knew that this sudden embrace was Jordan's wordless way of telling her that he was adding her to his small circle of trusted people. Setting her EHS log folder and two-way radio down beside her knee, she wrapped her arms around Jordan's shoulders in a warm, steady, protective hug, holding him patiently while a few more quiet sobs shuddered through his frame and began to subside.

![Outside the three-story 1980s Bennett Hall Addition on the Washington Street sidewalk after the fire drill all-clear, Jordan leans forward from his manual wheelchair and pulls a momentarily surprised, deeply moved Isabel Dawson—crouching in her high-visibility vest over her sweater and blue jeans—into a grateful hug as he adds her to his circle of Safe People.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e001/c012/s003/jordan-hugs-isabel-outside.jpg#fullwidth)

"You're safe here, Jordan," Isabel murmured softly, rubbing his back gently until his breathing steadied a fraction before easing back with a warm smile. "Always. Anytime something feels scary or overwhelming in this building, Henry and I have your back."

Settling back against his seat cushion, Jordan rubbed the sleeve of his hoodie across his wet eyes and gave another small, hitching sniffle as his crying slowly tried to subside. Even though he was still visibly shaken up and trembling from head to toe, a stubborn spark in his chest wanted his newest Safe Person to see what he had accomplished right before the alarm had shattered his night. With a shaking hand, he reached into the pocket of his CPI Forgers hoodie, pulled out his mPhone, unlocked the screen, and turned it toward her.

Glowing on the display was the CPI Canvas gradebook page for **ASTR 101: Introduction to Astronomy & Astrophysics**:

**Exam 1 Score: 105 / 100 (100% + 5 pts Extra Credit)**

Isabel leaned in to read the screen, and her eyes went wide.

"Shut up!" Isabel gasped, a huge, radiant grin breaking across her face as she read the line twice. "A hundred and five percent?! On Dr. Alistair's first Astrophysics exam?! Jordan, half the sophomores in the Engineering wing barely survive that class with a C!"

Beside her, Lauren, Hannah, Madison, Zoë, and even Aubrie—who had slid her earmuffs down around her neck—smiled warmly around him as a tiny, watery smile broke through the drying tears and sniffles on Jordan's pale face.

"Henry! Get over here!" Isabel called out as Henry walked up the sidewalk from the crosswalk in his own high-visibility vest. "Our guy in 214 just dropped a hundred and five percent on his first college Astrophysics exam!"

"No way—one-oh-five?!" Henry grinned, walking right over and softening his tone gently when he saw Jordan's red, tear-streaked eyes. He held out a steady, low-pressure fist. "Man, you are officially tutoring the entire second floor before midterms. That is legendary."

Jordan bumped his trembling knuckles lightly against Henry's fist, letting out another quiet sniffle as they turned to head back inside.

As they rolled back through the ground-level Washington Street doors and down the second-floor corridor to Room 214—where Jordan tapped his OEA-encoded Poly Pass to the reader to unlock the latch and trigger the ten-second dorm door opener—he was still visibly shaken up, with dried tears staining his cheeks, a few lingering tears still clinging to his lashes, and soft sniffles hitching in his chest as the crying slowly tried to subside. Yet as he glanced back at Isabel giving him a warm, watchful nod from the doorway of Room 215 right across the hall before his own door swung shut and clicked locked, he knew he had one more person standing guard over his home.

### Part 7: The Nightly Pact & The First Night of the Pact

**Date:** 2014-09-19 at 21:00 America/New_York

#### 9:00 PM — The Nightly Pact

Back inside the quiet warmth of Suite 214/216 after the all-clear was given, the lingering adrenaline from the fire alarm was only slowly beginning to ebb away. Jordan was still visibly shaken up from the sheer terror of the evacuation; even wrapped in a soft fleece blanket in his wheelchair, dried tear tracks still marked his cheeks beneath his glasses, a few fresh tears still welled at the corners of his eyes, and his chest hitched every few seconds with the quiet, involuntary sniffles of hard crying that was trying to subside. All six suitemates were huddled together in Room 214, cradling steaming mugs of hot chocolate with mini-marshmallows that Madison had insisted on warming up to help him and Aubrie settle.

Jordan had turned his hearing aids back down to their comfortable indoor profile now that the hallways were silent, his Vanguard Pro open on his lap as he took a shaky sip from his mug and let out another soft sniffle.

"I still cannot believe they subject legal adults to unannounced 100-decibel acoustic assaults at eight o'clock on a Friday night," Lauren said, shaking her head as she blew across the top of her mug. "It's genuinely barbaric."

"What matters is that our emergency response protocol functioned with zero casualties," Zoë observed from the foot of the bunk, her gray eyes resting warmly on Jordan and Aubrie. "Your sensory and cognitive freeze responses were completely understandable, but your immediate willingness to trust our manual override was the decisive variable."

"And it's a good thing we all have each other," Madison added softly, glancing around the circle of blankets. "Especially so nobody has to be alone... you know. After a crash like that."

A quiet, meaningful stillness settled over the room. Everyone knew what Madison was referring to—the nights Aubrie had held Jordan after his move-in meltdown and his 2:00 AM nightmare, and the night Jordan had held Lauren after Tom's betrayal had shattered her world.

As always, it was Aubrie who gave gentle, fearless voice to the thought forming in everyone's mind.

"It shouldn't only take an emergency or a heartbreak for us to have that," Aubrie said softly, looking first at Jordan with a tender smile before turning her gaze to Madison, Zoë, Lauren, and Hannah. "That feeling of waking up safe... of knowing you aren't alone in the dark... all of us deserve that. And after eighteen years of nightmares, Jordan deserves that every single night."

Lauren nodded wholeheartedly, hugging her knees to her chest. "That Tuesday night after everything with Tom came out... sleeping next to Jordan was the only reason I didn't fall apart in the dark. Just feeling someone kind breathing beside me fixed something in my head."

"Then we should formalize the protocol," Zoë said, her pragmatic, systematic mind immediately seeking structure so no one would ever feel uncertain or hesitant. "Establishing a clear, explicit nightly arrangement ensures equity and eliminates any potential for social ambiguity."

"It doesn't have to be a laminated spreadsheet on the bathroom door, Zo," Madison laughed gently, her cheeks warming slightly. "But yeah. If we're all really doing this—no jealousy, no weirdness—then it should be an open invitation. Whenever one of us needs comfort, or just wants to be close to him at night, we rotate."

Every pair of eyes in the room turned toward Jordan. They were offering him their hearts, their trust, and their nights, but none of them would take a single step unless it was truly what *he* wanted.

Jordan set his hot cocoa mug on his desk and placed his hands on the keyboard of his Vanguard Pro. Looking around at the women who had rescued him from the storm of his old life, he typed carefully into EchoType and pressed execute:

<aac>I want that more than anything. Knowing one of you is right there beside me is the only reason the nightmares stopped. I trust all of you completely.</aac>

Hannah smiled warmly from her spot near the connecting door, taking a sip of her cocoa. "You guys already know I think what you have is the most beautiful, healing thing in the world, and my daytime hugs are on call twenty-four-seven," she said with gentle affection. "And you know that at night, Mark and I have our own bed and our own relationship in 216."

"Of course," Aubrie said immediately, reaching out to squeeze Hannah's hand. "You and Mark are our bedrock, Hannah. And for the rest of us—me, Madison, Zoë, and Lauren..." Aubrie's eyes brightened with an inclusive thought. "And for Sarah, too, whenever she stays down here with us and needs a safe harbor. The invitation is open to all five of us."

Jordan sat quietly in his wheelchair for a moment, letting out another small, lingering sniffle from the fire drill as his mind traced the constellation of people who made him feel safe in this building. Less than an hour ago, when he had been screaming and clinging to his desk in blind terror, **Isabel Dawson** had knelt down on the linoleum right in front of his wheelchair, shown him her clipboard, and rescued him from the panic. Outside on the lawn, he had hugged her and added her to his inner list of **Safe People**.

In Jordan's sheltered, earnest mind—having never navigated college social structures or staff hierarchies before—the equation felt completely simple: *Safe People who protect me are the people who can hold me at night.* And honestly, after how gentle and warm Isabel had been when he hugged her on Washington Street, he wanted Isabel on that list too.

His fingers returned to the keyboard of his Vanguard Pro. Completely sincere, he typed out a question and pressed execute:

<aac>What about Isabel? After how she helped me during the fire drill tonight, I added her to my list of Safe People. Can we add Isabel to the list of people who are allowed into my bed with me too? I would really like her to be part of it.</aac>

For a fraction of a second, the warm, easy atmosphere in Room 214 froze solid.

Aubrie, Madison, Lauren, Zoë, and Hannah all exchanged a quick, wide-eyed glance. There wasn't a single trace of jealousy in the room—none of them begrudged his affection for their RA for even a heartbeat. Instead, every single one of them felt a sudden spike of protective alarm for Jordan's fragile emotional state.

He was still visibly shaken up from the fire drill, his cheeks still streaked with dried tears, his nervous system raw and depleted after a massive panic response. And now they were going to have to tell him *no* about someone he had just trusted with his whole heart.

Silently, operating on pure instinct, the five women prepared themselves for Jordan to go into a second meltdown. Aubrie shifted half an inch closer to his wheelchair on the edge of Bed B; Lauren and Madison subtly set their hot chocolate mugs down on the floor so their hands would be free to hold and ground him if the rejection triggered a sensory crash; Hannah and Zoë softened their posture, bracing for the storm.

"Jordan, sweetheart," Aubrie began, her voice impossibly gentle and warm as she reached over to rest a steady hand on his forearm. "First of all, I love that you added Isabel to your list of Safe People. She completely earned that tonight, and she cares about you so much."

"She really does," Lauren agreed softly, leaning forward with warm, reassuring eyes. "What she did for you during the drill was incredible. You can trust her with anything, J."

"However," Zoë stepped in, keeping her voice deliberately calm, measured, and gentle so it wouldn't sound like a reprimand, "while Isabel is unequivocally one of your Safe People, she cannot be included in the Nightly Bed Pact."

Aubrie held her breath, her thumb rubbing a slow, soothing circle against Jordan's wrist while Madison and Lauren tensed slightly, ready to wrap their arms around him the second his breathing hitched.

"It's not because she doesn't care about you, Jordan, and it's not because you asked anything wrong," Aubrie explained softly, looking straight into his green eyes behind his glasses. "It's because of what a Resident Advisor is. Us five—and Mark, Hannah, and Sarah—we're all freshmen. We're your peers and your equals. But Isabel is a junior employed by the university. As our RA, she's in an official position of authority and power over everyone who lives on this floor."

"Precisely," Zoë added gently. "University housing regulations establish a strict institutional boundary between Residence Life staff and the students under their supervision. Because Isabel holds a position of power—enforcing rules, conducting safety sweeps, and filing official reports—sharing a bed with a resident on her floor would be considered highly inappropriate by the university. Even with the purest intentions, it would send the wrong message to the rest of the floor regarding favoritism and staff boundaries, and if anyone ever found out, the university would fire her immediately and take away her room across the hall."

"We want to keep Isabel safe too," Madison said tenderly, offering him a soft, sympathetic smile. "And keeping her safe as our RA means she stays our protector right across the hall in 215, while the bed pact stays just the five of us."

The five suitemates went quiet, every muscle poised for the emotional crash they were sure was coming.

**Except the meltdown never came.**

Jordan didn't tense up. His breathing didn't accelerate, his hands didn't ball into fists, and no fresh tears spilled over his lashes. Instead, he sat very still in his wheelchair, his head tilting slightly as his sharp, analytical mind processed the architecture of what they had just explained.

For eighteen years in Virginia Beach, Jordan had lived under someone who wielded absolute, unchecked power over him without a single boundary or rule to protect him. Now that Aubrie and Zoë had mapped out the social and institutional mechanics of a Resident Advisor, the logic clicked into place in his mind with crystal clarity. Isabel wasn't just an older friend who lived in Room 215; she held a position of authority and power over Floor 2. If a staff member in a position of power climbed into a resident's bed, it would cross a line that existed to protect everyone—it would be highly inappropriate, it would send the completely wrong message, and worst of all, it could cost Isabel the job she was so good at.

Jordan gave a slow, steady nod. Reaching up with the corner of his blanket to wipe away the last lingering sniffle from the fire drill, he placed his fingers calmly back on the keyboard of his Vanguard Pro and typed:

<aac>I understand. Because Isabel is our Resident Advisor, she is in a position of power, so being in the bed pact would be inappropriate and would send the wrong message. And I never want to do anything that would get Isabel in trouble. She can stay on my Safe People list as my RA across the hall, and the bed pact is just for us.</aac>

Around the room, five simultaneously held breaths released in a wave of pure, astonished relief.

Madison's shoulders dropped two inches as a radiant, proud smile broke across her face, and Lauren let out a soft, watery laugh, reaching over to squeeze Jordan's knee. Aubrie's eyes shone with quiet pride as she leaned in and pressed a warm kiss to his cheek.

"You are amazing, Jordan," Aubrie whispered.

There it was: the **Nightly Pact**, spoken aloud and agreed upon without a single trace of fear, possessiveness, or misunderstanding. Mark and Hannah had their devoted partnership, Isabel and Henry stood watch as his trusted RAs across the hall, and around Jordan stood a five-star constellation—Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, and Sarah—bound together by an intuitive, zero-jealousy promise that none of them would ever have to face the dark alone again.

Zoë nodded once, a rare, radiant smile softening her face. "The parameters are clear, ethically sound, and mutually ratified."

Madison picked her mug back up off the rug and raised it in a toast. "Best. Suite. Ever."

***

#### 10:30 PM — The First Night of the Pact

As the last of the hot chocolate disappeared and the mugs were rinsed in the suite sink, a heavy, peaceful drowsiness settled over the six suitemates. The spike of adrenaline from the 8:00 PM fire alarm had completely burned off, leaving their muscles ready for sleep.

"Alright," Zoë said, standing up from the rug and stretching her arms overhead. "As productive as tonight's constitutional ratification has been, my circadian rhythm requires sleep."

"So..." Madison began, her usually exuberant voice dropping to a soft, almost shy register as she looked first at Jordan, and then over at Aubrie. "Whose turn is it tonight?"

The simple question hung warmly in the quiet room—the very first real-world invocation of the pact they had just made.

Sitting on the edge of Bed B, Aubrie didn't hesitate for a millisecond. She looked up at Madison and offered a serene, encouraging smile, giving a small nod toward Jordan's bed. The message was unmistakable: *Go ahead. You've earned your turn.*

"I'd really like to take tonight," Madison said, her bright blue eyes filled with a gentle sincerity as she looked back at Jordan. "If that's okay with you, J?"

Jordan looked at Madison, then glanced at Aubrie, whose warm, unclouded smile confirmed that the safety of their constellation was 100% real. He tapped a quick, quiet response on his NeoEdit screen and angled it toward Madison:

<aac>I would really like that, Maddie.</aac>

With that, the suite flowed through its bedtime routine. Hannah, Lauren, and Zoë said their goodnights, gave Jordan their evening hugs, and stepped through the connecting bathroom into Room 216. In Room 214, after helping Jordan change into his soft cotton sleep shirt and sweatpants, Aubrie curled up under the covers of her own lower bunk across the room, letting out a long, contented sigh. There was no tension in the air—only the deep peace of a sanctuary she had helped build.

Jordan carefully removed his new glasses, setting them in their protective case beside his bridge hearing aids on the nightstand, and executed his pivot transfer from his wheelchair onto his accessible Twin XL mattress.

A moment later, the overhead light clicked off, and Madison—dressed in her soft flannel pajama pants and an oversized t-shirt—padded quietly across the rug instead of climbing the wooden ladder to Bed C.

The Twin XL mattress was narrow, built for one college student, which meant sharing it required zero distance between them.

"Scooch over, Forger," Madison whispered playfully in the dim glow of the campus streetlight outside the window.

Jordan smiled and shifted toward the wall, making room. Madison slid under the comforter right behind him, the immediate, radiating warmth of her body chasing away the September chill. She settled in as the big spoon, wrapping her arm securely around his waist and pulling his back flush against her chest, her chin resting lightly against his shoulder.

It was a mirror of the grounding deep pressure Aubrie and Lauren had given him, yet distinctly Madison—warm, lively, and unconditionally affectionate, declaring without words that he was cherished and safe.

Lying there in the quiet dark, held closely by one of his best friends while his girlfriend slept peacefully just six feet away, Jordan felt his heart rate slow into a steady, rhythmic calm. After eighteen years of isolation and terror in the dark, his nights were now guarded by a rotating constellation of people who loved him simply for who he was. He closed his eyes and drifted effortlessly into a dreamless sleep.

## Homecoming & The Safe Harbor

### Part 1: The Door Decorating Contest & Game Day

**Date:** 2014-09-26 at 13:30 America/New_York

#### September 26, 2014 • 1:30 PM — The Door Decorating Contest

By Friday, September 26th, 2014, the entire Blacksburg campus was humming with the kinetic energy of Homecoming Weekend. Jordan had been at Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute for just over a month, and for the first time in his eighteen years, he wasn't merely surviving—he was thriving. With his new glasses bringing the lecture halls into razor-sharp focus, his behind-the-ear hearing aids filtering the classroom acoustics, and his chosen family anchoring every day, he finally felt like he belonged.

Shortly after their Friday classes wrapped up for the weekend, Madison Scott burst through the door of Room 214, her arms overflowing with rolls of Foundry Maroon and Molten Orange butcher paper, crêpe streamers, tempera paint bottles, and a brightly printed Residence Life flyer.

"Okay, team, listen up!" she announced, her voice brimming with her trademark bubbly energy. "The Bennett Hall Homecoming door decorating contest is officially underway, and judging is at five o'clock. We are going to win."

Zoë looked up from her desk in Room 216 through the open connecting doorway and pushed her glasses up the bridge of her nose. "Statistically, Madison, the odds of winning a subjective aesthetic contest against seventy other residential doors in this building are low."

"Not if we have a professional artistic edge," Lauren chimed in, walking out of Room 216 alongside Hannah. As a Graphic Design major, her warm brown eyes were already sparkling at the sight of the heavy butcher paper. "I am completely in. What's the vision?"

"I'm glad you asked," Madison grinned. "We don't just decorate one door. We do both. A coordinated, two-door suite masterpiece."

Zoë's eyebrow arched with sudden interest. "A linked diptych across adjoining hallway portals. That maximizes our visual surface area and doubles our structural impact for the judges. Acceptable. I'm in. What is the conceptual design?"

Sitting in his wheelchair near his desk with his Vanguard Pro resting on his lap tray, Jordan felt an unfamiliar, buoyant flutter of excitement in his chest. His mother had always dismissed school spirit as loud, vulgar, and beneath them, but here in Suite 214/216, it felt like joy. His fingers tapped swiftly across his keyboard, and the warm Australian female cadence of EchoType spoke for him.

<aac>What about our mascot?</aac> Jordan's laptop synthesized. <aac>The Forgers?</aac>

"Yes!" Aubrie said, lighting up as she immediately latched onto his idea. "We can have our Forger mascot on one door..."

"...and on the other door," Lauren picked up, her hands already framing the proportions in the air, "we draw the VDU Admiral mascot getting completely crushed!"

"Crush Norfolk!" Mark cheered, poking his head into the open doorway as he, Sarah, and Jessica arrived from across campus to join the afternoon festivities. "I love it. The Forger's Hammer!"

For the next two hours, the second-floor hallway outside Rooms 214 and 216 transformed into a happy, chaotic art studio of butcher paper, acrylic paint, and maroon-and-orange streamers. Lauren took command as lead illustrator, sketching a towering, muscular CPI Forger wielding a glowing blacksmith's hammer in rich Foundry Maroon and Molten Orange for the door of Room 216. For the door of Room 214, she drew a comically bewildered VDU Admiral in Chesapeake Teal and Harbor Gold—representing "Norfolk"—cowering beneath the descending anvil of the Forger's hammer, complete with a cracked golden anchor and bicorne hat.

To Jordan's surprise and delight, Lauren handed him a wide flat brush and put him in charge of the banner lettering along the lower half of the butcher paper before it went up on the doors. Seated in his wheelchair with the paper taped flat across two pushed-together desks, his careful, methodical strokes proved ideal for the bold block typography: **GO FORGERS!** across the Room 216 banner, and **BEAT NORFOLK!** across the Room 214 banner.

Just as Mark and Hannah finished taping the two giant murals flush against the heavy oak hallway doors, footsteps approached down the corridor. **Isabel Dawson** rounded the corner wearing her CPI Residence Life lanyard and holding a judging rubric on her clipboard, accompanied by **Henry**, who was carrying a lukewarm travel mug of coffee and a bag of pretzel rods.

Both of them stopped dead in their tracks in front of Rooms 214 and 216.

"Whoa," Henry breathed, tilting his head back to take in the full two-door panorama. "Okay, pack it in, Izzy. Contest is over. Nobody on the third floor is beating a two-door comic strip."

Isabel's face broke into a wide, delighted smile as she stepped closer to inspect the crisp block lettering on Room 214's door, then looked down at Jordan's maroon-and-orange paint-stained knuckles.

"Did you do the typography on these banners, Jordan?" Isabel asked warmly.

Jordan's cheeks warmed with quiet pride as he gave a shy nod and tapped a quick key on his lap tray.

<aac>Lauren sketched the outlines. I painted the block letters,</aac> EchoType replied.

"The kerning is cleaner than half the posters our student government prints," Isabel laughed, jotting a string of tens across her clipboard rubric. "Seriously, you guys—turning both suite doors into a single connected scene is brilliant. Kelsey is going to lose her mind when she comes up to do the final walkthrough."

"We aim to please," Madison beamed, wiping a smudge of orange paint off her cheek.

As Isabel and Henry continued down the hall toward the stairwell, Jordan looked back up at the two towering doors, his fingers still speckled with dried maroon paint, surrounded by his friends laughing in the corridor. He wasn't an outsider watching college life happen through a window anymore. This was his home, and this was his team.

***

#### September 26, 2014 • 3:30 PM — Chalk the Walk

Later that afternoon, the Group of 8—joined by Jessica—headed down the hillside elevator of Bennett Hall and out onto the sun-drenched concrete walkways bordering **The Commonwealth Green** for "Chalk the Walk," one of CPI's oldest Homecoming traditions. All along the wide perimeter of the central quad, student organizations, academic clubs, and residence hall teams had claimed numbered squares of pavement to create vibrant sidewalk chalk murals before the evening festivities began.

Lauren, thoroughly in her element as their resident Graphic Design major, knelt beside their assigned six-by-six-foot square of concrete with a spiral sketchpad in hand.

"Okay, we're adapting the suite door diptych for a single square," Lauren announced, rapidly sketching out a grid with a stick of white chalk. "The Student Activities guidelines say we have to keep it 'tasteful,' so we can't make it look like a crime scene, but we can definitely make a statement."
