<aac>No apology necessary. Follow me to Southampton Row,</aac> Jordan typed smoothly, rotating his power chair ninety degrees onto the level stone sidewalk with his offline **LTA Central London Bus Spider Map** open beside his `NeoEdit` window. <aac>We are taking the surface grid.</aac>

Two blocks away at Stop B on **Southampton Row**, a gleaming, scarlet-red **London Transport Authority (`LTA`) Route 91** double-decker bus pulled smoothly up to the curb, its destination blind glowing **`91 TRAFALGAR SQUARE`**.

As the bus hissed to a stop, the driver spotted Jordan's power chair waiting at the accessibility marker on the pavement. Before anyone even had to ask, the center doors swung inward, a steady two-tone warning chime echoed across the sidewalk, and an automatic hydraulic metal ramp glided straight out of the bus floor until its yellow-edged lip rested flush against the London curbstone.

Jordan drove straight up the hydraulic incline into the wide, low-floor central bay, spun his chair neatly in a tight 180-degree turn, and backed securely against the high padded crash-pad backrest facing the rear of the bus.

"Do I tap Jordan's Pearl Card on the reader?" Madison asked, holding her own sky-blue **`Pearl Card`** by the yellow circular reader pad.

"No need, love!" the London bus driver called back cheerfully through his cab partition window. "Wheelchair users ride every red bus in London completely free of charge. Everyone else just tap your Pearl Cards once on the yellow reader!"

*BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.*

Seventeen `Pearl Cards` tapped in rapid succession as the Brooks family and the Pact split between the lower deck around Jordan's bay and the curved staircase leading to the panoramic front seats of the upper deck.

Rolling south through the heart of London on the lower deck of a red double-decker bus turned out to be infinitely better than riding through a dark Victorian clay tunnel seventy feet underground. Through the tall glass windows, Jordan watched the entire living architecture of the city unfold at street level: the grand neoclassical porticoes of Aldwych, the bustling Strand, and then **Trafalgar Square**, where Nelson's Column towered above the bronze lions and dancing fountains.

At Trafalgar Square (`Whitehall / Trafalgar Square, Stop N`), Jordan led a textbook three-minute cross-stop transfer onto a red **Route 11** double-decker bus (`11 VICTORIA`).

Their second red bus rolled straight down **Whitehall** past the mounted Horse Guards cavalry in their silver cuirasses and plumed helmets, swung around **Parliament Square** directly beneath the gleaming gold-and-black clock face of **The Great Westminster Clock Tower** (*`St. Stephen's Bell`*) and the gothic spires of **Westminster Parliament Palace**, and cruised down Victoria Street where Jordan pressed the blue wheelchair-stop bell button right beside his armrest.

When the hydraulic ramp lowered at **Sovereign Palace Road**, the entire eighteen-person family rolled along the wide, level royal promenade of **The Mall**—shaded by double rows of London plane trees and giant Union Flags—all the way up to the gilded iron gates of **St. James's Sovereign Palace** and the gleaming white marble of **The Sovereign Memorial**.

"Look at the navigator who got eighteen people from Bloomsbury to the Queen's front gate without a single stair," Laura Brooks beamed, snapping a series of family photographs with Jordan front and center before the palace gates—another piece of visual evidence that **Ms. Gable** would later place directly before the judge in Virginia.

After lunch at a step-free pub patio near St. James's Park, Daniel looked over at Jordan with a warm, nostalgic glint in his eye.

"Alright, Chief Navigator," Daniel said softly. "What do your spider maps say about getting us up to Regent Street and Soho? It's time we showed you **Carnaby Street**."

### Part 2: Carnaby Street, the Thames Riverbus, & Babbage's Engine

**Date:** 2015-06-08 at 15:00 Europe/London

![On pedestrian Carnaby Street in Soho, London beneath the WELCOME TO CARNABY STREET arch, Jordan Fuller sits in his matte-black S.S. Freedom power wheelchair with his black laptop angled toward his face outside a classic vinyl record shop with wooden LP crates, surrounded by Zoë Wren Brooks, Aubrie Jean Kelly, Madison Scott, and Daniel and Laura Brooks pointing up toward their old third-floor flat window.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e004/c004/p002/carnaby-street-soho-record-shop.jpg)

#### June 8, 2015 • 3:00 PM — Carnaby Street and the Hollow Square

From Piccadilly, Jordan guided the family aboard a low-floor red double-decker bus up the sweeping curve of Regent Street, disembarking via the hydraulic ramp at Beak Street and rolling east into the heart of **Soho**.

One block in, the roar of London traffic vanished behind them as they passed beneath a famous wrought-iron welcome arch spanning a vibrant, completely pedestrianized thoroughfare paved in level stone flags:

**`WELCOME TO CARNABY STREET`**

For more than half a century, this narrow fourteen-street enclave in the City of Westminster had been the beating heart of British music and fashion culture. Independent record shops, Mod tailors, bespoke guitar luthiers, and brightly painted three- and four-story Georgian and Victorian shopfronts lined both sides of the car-free walkway.

Halfway up the street, near the corner of Foubert's Place, Daniel and Laura Brooks slowed to a stop outside a narrow four-story brick building. On the ground floor sat a classic Soho vinyl record store with wooden crate bins set out beneath its awning; above the shop rose three stories of residential flats with tall white sash windows.

"Look up at the third-floor window on the left, Jordan," Daniel said quietly, slipping his arm around Laura's waist as Zoë stepped up beside Jordan's wheelchair. "That was our flat before my firm transferred us to Osaka and then Virginia. That's the exact window where Zoë learned to read systems architecture manuals at three years old—and even before we moved into that flat, when Laura and I were first dating in London in the early eighties, we spent every Saturday afternoon crate-digging in this record shop right beneath us."

"And where my processor first determined that Soho street volume without double-glazed windows is a structural design flaw," Zoë added dryly, though her gray eyes were warm with childhood affection as she looked up at the brickwork.

Right at that moment, inside the ground-floor vinyl shop beneath their old flat, the clerk dropped the needle onto a newly remastered 180-gram LP spinning on the front turntable.

Pouring out through the open shop doors into the warm afternoon air of Carnaby Street came a brooding, solitary drum-machine pulse, quickly joined by a deep, resonant analog synth bassline—the unmistakable opening bars of [**"The Hollow Square"**](https://music.raggiesoft.com/artists/fractured-prisms/1983-carnaby-street?track=1-01-the-hollow-square), the lead track from **[Fractured Prisms](https://music.raggiesoft.com/artists/fractured-prisms)**' landmark 1983 album, [***Carnaby Street***](https://music.raggiesoft.com/artists/fractured-prisms/1983-carnaby-street).

Jordan's hands stilled over his keyboard as Rhys Manning's voice rose over the street:

> *"Four empty spaces in the room*<br>
> *A silent echo in the gloom*<br>
> *We crossed the water to find a shore*<br>
> *But left behind what came before..."*

"You know why Rhys and Claire Manning named that album after this street, don't you, J?" Daniel asked softly as the massive gated snare drum kicked in on the chorus.

Jordan tilted his head, looking from the spinning vinyl turntable inside the shop window back up to Daniel and Laura.

"Back in the winter of 1981," Daniel explained, his voice low and respectful beneath the soaring progressive-pop synthesizers, "before they were called **Fractured Prisms**, there were six of them—siblings and cousins in the **Manning Family Orchestra** from Romford. Before the four touring members—Gwen, Alistair, Julian, and Simon—drove north up the M6 for a winter show across the Scottish border, all six of them spent their last afternoon in London right here in this exact record shop on **Carnaby Street**, laughing and digging through the import crates together."

Laura Brooks reached out, touching the wooden frame of the record shop doorway with a quiet, wistful smile.

"Daniel and I were actually inside this shop that afternoon," Laura said softly, making Jordan, Aubrie, and Madison turn to look at her in astonishment. "We were nineteen years old, sheltering from the December drizzle and flipping through the progressive-rock bins in the back corner. There were six young musicians in knit scarves crowded around the import counter debating synthesizer patches and concert flute arrangements. I remember a quiet, observant young woman sitting in her manual wheelchair right next to me by the seven-inch singles rack—covering her ears slightly when the shop speakers crackled—while her younger brother stood right beside her chair like a bodyguard. Because of her wheelchair, she couldn't quite reach a sleeve on the upper rack, so I handed it down to her. She gave me the shyest, most polite little smile, and her brother thanked me in a light Romford accent."

Laura's eyes glistened as she looked back inside the warm, record-lined room.

"We had no idea who they were at the time," Laura whispered. "Not until October 1983, when ***Carnaby Street*** came out and we saw the photograph of **Rhys and Claire Manning** and read the liner notes dedicating the album to that final afternoon in Soho. We had stood two feet away from all six of them on the very last day their family was whole."

Beside Jordan, Aubrie and Lauren listened silently as the second verse echoed off the Soho brick:

> *"The cables hum, the circuits glow*<br>
> *To mask the quiet down below*<br>
> *We sequence notes to fill the void*<br>
> *A symphony we re-employed*<br>
> *Just two remain to hold the line*<br>
> *And reconstruct the grand design..."*

"Twenty-four hours after we saw them in this shop," Daniel continued quietly, "Gwen, Alistair, Julian, and Simon hit a blinding white-out of freezing fog and black ice on the M6 over Shap Fell in Cumbria. All four of them were killed instantly. The only reason **Claire** and **Rhys** survived was because they were hundreds of miles south, safely at home in Romford. Claire has lived with Cerebral Palsy and needed a wheelchair since birth, and she is autistic—so the grueling, unpredictable winter tour up the M6 wasn't compatible with her needs. And where Claire stayed, Rhys stayed."

Jordan's breath caught in his chest. He had heard *"The Hollow Square"* on the radio before, but he had never realized that **Claire Manning** had lived with Cerebral Palsy from birth, used a wheelchair her entire life, and was autistic—just like him—or that her wheelchair and sensory needs were the exact reason she and her brother were still alive.

"Everyone in the British press thought the music died on Shap Fell," Zoë picked up softly, resting her hand on the cool magnesium-alloy edge of Jordan's **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**. "Instead, after Claire left a terrible marriage in Romford in 1982, she and Rhys packed the surviving instruments of their deceased family and fled across the Atlantic to their father's old ranch house in Williamsport, Maryland. Rhys refused to hire session musicians to stand in the four empty spaces of their family—the *Hollow Square*. Instead, he filled the house with analog synthesizers, sequencers, and drum machines to engineer a predictable, accessible sanctuary where Claire's mind could safely operate, while Claire taught herself to play Gwen's wooden flute from her wheelchair. And when they released that debut album in 1983, they named it ***Carnaby Street***—after the last place in London where all six of them had been together."

As the soaring melodic guitar solo broke over the driving drum-machine beat and built into the final chorus—

> *"Standing in the hollow square!*<br>
> *Reaching out, but no one's there!*<br>
> *We forge the armour, paint the sky*<br>
> *To keep the fading embers high!"*

—Jordan looked down at his own glowing `NeoEdit` terminal, mounted to the frame of his power chair on the stones of Carnaby Street.

*The cables hum, the circuits glow.*

Just like Rhys and Claire Manning had used cables, circuits, and sequenced notes to build a fortress against trauma when the world tried to break them, Zoë had handed Jordan an Aura Glade laptop and a custom kernel patch in Bennett Hall so he could build his voice—and six extraordinary women, a brother like Mark, a sister like Hannah, and the entire Brooks family had closed ranks around his wheelchair so his square would never be hollow again.

Jordan typed slowly, letting his `"Sydney"` voice blend softly with the fading synth bass of the outro:

<aac>They used circuits and cables to build a sanctuary across the ocean,</aac> Jordan said quietly, looking up at Zoë, Aubrie, and Daniel. <aac>Just like you did for me.</aac>

***

#### June 9, 2015 • 1:15 PM — Houghton Street and the Transatlantic Reunion Call

At twelve-fifty on Tuesday afternoon, Jordan steered the group away from the stairs-only entrance of **Holborn Underground Station** and guided them aboard the low-floor red **Route 91** bus down **Kingsway**, stepping off via the hydraulic ramp at **Aldwych** just two hundred yards from the **London School of Economics and Commerce (`LSEC`)**.

Unlike the sprawling, Neo-Gothic **Ironstone** academic buildings ringing **Commonwealth Green** at **Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute** back in Blacksburg, `LSEC` was a dense, vertical urban campus woven directly into the historic streets and legal inns of court between Kingsway and the Royal Courts of Justice. Even so, the university had fitted its pedestrianized streets and modern academic buildings with flush dropped curbs, automatic glass doors, and wide platform lifts.

As Jordan rolled onto the smooth paving stones of **Houghton Street** outside the **Old Building**, the heavy double doors swung open and a wave of international university students poured out from their final summer-term seminar—led by **Henry Walsh** with his leather messenger bag slung over his shoulder.

"Right on time, Chief Navigator!" Henry grinned, spotting Jordan's power chair immediately and walking over to bump fists with Jordan and Mark. "Did you guys take the red double-decker bus down Kingsway?"

<aac>Route 91 to Stop D at Aldwych,</aac> Jordan typed proudly. <aac>Zero stairs, zero escalators, and a four-minute roll down Houghton Street.</aac>

"Wait until we get back to Blacksburg in August," Henry laughed, shaking his head as he led Jordan, Aubrie, Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Sarah, Jessica, Hannah, and Mark over to a wide, accessible timber picnic table in the sunlit **Shaw Library / Student Union courtyard** while Daniel and the older Brooks siblings grabbed takeaway teas and sandwiches from the campus café. "Between Blue Ridge Transit, Reykjavik, and the London bus grid, you're going to know more about public transit routing than half the Civil Engineering faculty at CPI."

Sitting across from Jordan at the courtyard table, Henry leaned forward on his elbows, his expression turning warm and earnest.

"Seriously, though, Jordan—look at you," Henry said quietly, taking in the clean-shaven jawline Mark had helped Jordan maintain since Fall semester, the effortless way Jordan sat upright in his power chair, and the two international transit smart cards gleaming in the plastic sleeve clipped to his laptop mount. "I still remember walking the second-floor corridor of Bennett Hall on Move-In Saturday back in August when Zoë stepped out of Room 214, tapped my shoulder, and told me we had a 'significant logistical error' because Housing had put a guy in a female suite. Back then, you were so terrified someone was going to yell at you that you wouldn't even look up from your lap. And now you're navigating Central London with a crew of eighteen people."

<aac>You and Isabel and Kelsey didn't kick me out,</aac> Jordan typed softly, his fingers steady on the keys of his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**. <aac>If you had separated us on that Saturday morning, I never would have made it to today. Where did Housing reassign you for senior year now that Bennett Hall is closed for good and slated for demolition?</aac>

"They moved me and **Isabel** right over to **Allegheny Commons** for senior year!" Henry smiled, a mischievous glint entering his eyes as he leaned in a little closer. "It's still wild to me that the Old Lady actually closed her doors for good in May while I was over here in London, and that she's slated for the wrecking ball. With **Garrett** graduating in May and Bennett Hall shutting down, **Kelsey** got reassigned to oversee the **Allegheny Commons Apartments**—and I actually just got Kelsey's finalized staff placement email this morning. Not only am I in Allegheny Commons, she assigned me as the Male Senior RA in **Apartment 115**, on the *exact same floor* as Isabel in **Apartment 101**! And Isabel doesn't even know yet!"

"Wait—you haven't told Isabel you're her floor co-RA again?!" Madison gasped, her eyes lighting up with instant delight.

"The email only hit my inbox two hours ago!" Henry laughed. "I was saving it—though since you guys are moving into your off-campus sanctuary house on Geneva Street in Christiansburg for sophomore year, our floor is still going to be a whole lot quieter without Suite 214/216."

"Speaking of Isabel," Aubrie said with a bright, mischievous smile, glancing at her watch. "It's one-forty-five in the afternoon here in London—which means it's **`8:45 AM`** on Tuesday morning in Charlottesville. We promised her a video call from `LSEC`—and if Henry ratted her out for the Heathrow ambush, it's only fair that we break the Allegheny Commons news to her right now!"

"Do it!" Henry grinned, sliding his bench seat right up beside Jordan's right armrest while Aubrie leaned in on Jordan's left and Madison, Zoë, Lauren, Sarah, Jessica, Hannah, and Mark crowded into the wide-angle frame behind them.

Jordan unlocked his `mPad`, angled it on the secondary mount so both his face and Henry's were squarely centered in front of the `LSEC` red-brick crest on the courtyard wall, and tapped **Isabel Dawson**'s contact.

The call connected on the second ring.

In Charlottesville, Virginia, Isabel was sitting at her parents' sunny kitchen table in a soft maroon CPI t-shirt, holding a ceramic mug of morning coffee with her dark-framed glasses perched on her nose.

For half a second, she saw Jordan and Aubrie—and then her eyes registered **Henry Walsh** grinning right next to Jordan's wheelchair in the middle of London.

*"HENRY!!"* Isabel squealed so loudly she nearly sloshed her coffee across the kitchen table, clapping her free hand over her mouth as her face lit up like a sunrise. *"Oh my gosh! Henry! Jordan! You're actually together at LSEC right now!!"*

"Good morning from Houghton Street, Dawson!" Henry called out cheerfully, waving both hands at the screen. "Look who navigated the London bus grid all the way to Holborn without hitting a single flight of stairs!"

*"I knew he would!"* Isabel beamed, her warm brown eyes locking onto Jordan through the camera lens with unmistakable pride. *"Jordan, how is London treating you? Did you get your second transit card?"*

Jordan held up his clear plastic sleeve so the sky-blue **`Pearl Card`** gleamed right below his yellow-and-blue **`NordicPass`**.

<aac>Smart Card Number Two: London Transport Authority Pearl Card,</aac> Jordan announced via his `"Sydney"` voice. <aac>And I also found out who leaked our Sunday flight itinerary from Reykjavik so Henry could ambush us at the Heathrow Terminal 2 customs barrier.</aac>

Beside Jordan, Henry burst out laughing, pointing straight at the camera. "Oh, I ratted you out immediately, Izzy! You should have seen Jordan's face when he rolled out of the Green Channel at Heathrow and saw my sign!"

On the `mPad` screen, Isabel's cheeks turned the exact shade of a ripe tomato. She set her coffee mug down, tucked a strand of straight jet-black hair behind her ear, and tried—and completely failed—to look innocent.

*"I—well, Henry is our friend and co-RA, and I thought it would be a nice welcome to England!"* Isabel stammered, her fingers fluttering up to her collarbone as she blushed from ear to ear. *"Besides, since I couldn't be there in London myself, somebody had to make sure the old Bennett Hall Second Floor crew was represented at the airport!"*

Beside Jordan, Aubrie exchanged a tiny, fond, knowing glance with Madison and Lauren, her heart warming at just how hopelessly transparent their former RA was—even if Jordan himself simply smiled back at the screen, completely touched by her thoughtfulness.

<aac>It was the best surprise I have ever had at an airport, Isabel,</aac> Jordan said through his speaker, making Isabel's smile soften into pure, glowing affection. Then a playful grin tugged at the corner of Jordan's mouth as he glanced at Aubrie and Madison and typed one more sentence: <aac>Also, since Henry ratted you out for Heathrow, we thought you should know that Kelsey assigned Henry to Apartment 115 at Allegheny Commons. He is the Male RA on the exact same floor as you again this year.</aac>

On the `mPad` screen, Isabel's jaw dropped open.

*"WAIT—WHAT?!"* Isabel gasped, her eyes darting from Jordan to Henry. *"You're on the FIRST FLOOR of Allegheny Commons with me?!"*

"Surprise, Room 101!" Henry grinned shamelessly, giving her a two-finger salute. "Just got Kelsey's placement email this morning! Looks like you're stuck with me as your floor co-RA for Senior Year too!"

Isabel narrowed her eyes behind her glasses, folding her arms across her maroon CPI shirt as she put on her sternest, most theatrical mock-glare—even though the corners of her mouth were twitching so hard she could barely keep from laughing.

*"Henry Thomas Walsh! You knew for two whole hours that you were on my floor at Allegheny Commons and you didn't even text me?!"* Isabel huffed, pretending to be deeply offended while her eyes sparkled with delight. *"I had to find out from Jordan and the girls across the Atlantic Ocean?! Unbelievable! You are officially on first-week duty roster probation in August!"*

"Hey, consider us completely even for the Heathrow ambush, Dawson!" Henry laughed as the entire courtyard table erupted into cheers.

<aac>On Thursday morning we are taking the high-speed tilting train from London Euston up to Liverpool,</aac> Jordan typed happily once the laughter settled, <aac>and on Saturday we fly to Tokyo.</aac>

*"Hold onto Henry for one more big hug from me before you leave London, okay—even if he IS in the doghouse for not texting me!"* Isabel said warmly, her pretend scowl melting right back into a radiant smile as she waved with both hands. *"Have the best time in Liverpool, guys, and text me the second you touch down in Japan!"*

***

#### June 9, 2015 • 4:00 PM — The Thames Riverbus, the Millennium Wheel, and Babbage's Difference Engine

After wrapping up their transatlantic video call with **Isabel** from the courtyard of the **London School of Economics and Commerce (`LSEC`)**, **Henry Walsh** slung his canvas bookbag over his shoulder and officially clocked in as their afternoon London companion.

"My seminar readings are done until tomorrow morning," Henry grinned, walking alongside **Mark** and **Jordan** as they rolled south down Savoy Street toward the **Victoria Embankment**. "And since the Chief Navigator already mastered the red double-decker buses yesterday, what do your **`LTA`** maps say about taking the river?"

Jordan's eyes lit up behind his glasses. Pulling up the **London River Services** diagram on his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**, he guided the nineteen-person group onto the floating pontoon of **Embankment Pier**.

Tapping their sky-blue **`Pearl Cards`** at the pier reader, they boarded a sleek, high-speed **Thames Riverbus Clipper** catamaran. Unlike the nineteenth-century Underground tunnels beneath the city, every pier and twin-hulled vessel on the Thames Riverbus grid was 100% step-free: the deck crew laid a wide aluminum brow ramp across the gunwale, and Jordan rolled smoothly into the panoramic forward cabin as the boat surged out onto the tidal **River Thames**.

Five minutes later, the catamaran glided across the water to **Waterloo Pier** directly beneath the towering, 443-foot cantilevered white steel rim of **The Thames Millennium Wheel**.

As Jordan rolled up the wide stone riverwalk toward the boarding platform, he tipped his head back and stared up at the thirty-two sealed, ovoid glass passenger capsules rotating slowly above the Thames—and then looked directly across the river at the golden Gothic clock face of **The Great Westminster Clock Tower** (*`St. Stephen's Bell`*).

A sudden, vivid memory flashed across Jordan's mind.

<aac>Wait a second,</aac> Jordan typed into `NeoEdit`, pausing his chair beside **Aubrie**, **Madison**, **Daniel**, and **Laura**. <aac>Five months ago on New Year's Eve in your living room on Geneva Street, this exact wheel and that clock tower across the river were on the television screen when the fireworks launched at midnight—the night I learned what fireworks were.</aac>

Laura Brooks smiled with deep maternal warmth, resting her hand gently on Jordan's shoulder. "And on December 31st, you were watching it on a television screen from four thousand miles away, love. Today you're going right up to the top of it."

When Capsule 14 glided through the boarding deck, the station attendants slowed the wheel's rotation and deployed a flush metal bridge plate. Jordan drove his 350-pound power chair straight into the center of the spacious, air-conditioned glass pod alongside **Henry**, **Daniel**, **Laura**, **Aubrie**, **Zoë**, **Madison**, **Lauren**, **Sarah**, **Jessica**, **Hannah**, **Mark**, and the **Brooks** siblings.

Over the next thirty minutes, as their glass capsule rose four hundred and forty-three feet into the clear June afternoon sky, the entire vast geometry of **London** unfolded in a 360-degree panorama below Jordan's wheels: the gleaming meanders of the Thames, the white dome of St. Paul's Cathedral to the east, the green royal parks stretching past **St. James's Sovereign Palace** to the west, and the intricate rooftop courtyards of **Westminster Parliament Palace** directly below.

From the South Bank, Jordan routed the group aboard a low-floor red **Route 148** and **Route 70** bus link west to Exhibition Road in **South Kensington**, rolling through the step-free glass atrium of **The South Kensington Museum of Science & Computing**.

While Caleb, Lucas, and Owen headed downstairs to inspect the Apollo 10 command module and the historic *Stephenson's Rocket* steam locomotive, **Zoë** and **Daniel** led **Jordan**, **Aubrie**, **Madison**, and **Henry** up the wide passenger lift to the third-floor ***Information Age & Computing Gallery***.

Standing inside a massive glass display case at the center of the hall was a gleaming, five-ton marvel of bronze gears, steel shafts, and precision-milled figure wheels: **Charles Babbage's *Difference Engine No. 2***, built to Babbage's original `1847` mechanical blueprints—accurate to thirty-one digits of polynomial calculation and sitting directly across the gallery from **Alan Turing's `1950` *Pilot ACE*** early electronic stored-program computer.

For fifteen minutes, Jordan and Zoë were completely transfixed.

"Look at the carry-lever tolerances on the bronze figure wheels, J," Zoë murmured in hushed reverence, pointing to the mechanical carry mechanism and the analytical notes written by **Ada Lovelace** displayed in the adjacent case. "In 1843, before electricity or vacuum tubes even existed, Ada Lovelace looked at Babbage's mechanical looms and realized that if you could encode mathematical rules into physical state transitions, a machine could compose music, process symbolic logic, and execute deterministic algorithms without human error."

Jordan looked from the nineteenth-century bronze gears of Babbage's engine down to the glowing, neon-green **`NeoEdit`** terminal running on his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**—the modern descendant of those exact bronze shafts and vacuum tubes, giving a non-verbal nineteen-year-old from Virginia a clear, unbreakable voice across the globe.

<aac>Every person in this gallery built a machine to think and speak in new ways,</aac> Jordan typed softly as Aubrie squeezed his hand. <aac>I feel like I am looking at my own family tree.</aac>

### Part 3: London Euston, Edinburgh Castle, & The Royal Yacht

**Date:** 2015-06-11 at 08:30 Europe/London

![On the waterfront plaza at Pier Head in Liverpool, Merseyside, England, with the historic Three Graces and Liver Bird clock towers rising behind them, nineteen-year-old Jordan Fuller sits parked dead-center in his matte-black S.S. Freedom power wheelchair in front of the large WELCOME TO LIVERPOOL sign while Australian suitemate Sarah Braithwaite laughs uproariously and gives an exaggerated thumbs-down beside Aubrie Jean Kelly, Madison Grace Miller, Zoë Wren Brooks (shading her eyes looking for kangaroos), tall Jessica Gallagher, Lauren Elizabeth Taylor, and Hannah Marie Brooks.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e004/c014/s002/wrong-liverpool-pier-head.jpg)

#### June 11, 2015 • 8:30 AM — Passenger Assist at London Euston

On Tuesday evening, forty-eight hours before the family's scheduled trip north to **Liverpool**, Daniel Brooks had handed Jordan the login credentials for the **UK National Rail Passenger Assist** portal and let Jordan book the entire inter-city rail accommodation himself.

Sitting at the dining table of the Bloomsbury flat, Jordan had reviewed the rolling-stock diagrams for **Albion InterCity Rail**'s high-speed **Class 390 Tilting Express** trains on the West Coast Main Line, selected the dedicated wheelchair bay with companion table seating in Coach G on the `09:07` departure from **London Euston** to **Liverpool Lime Street**, and submitted the formal request for portable boarding ramps at both stations.

Now, at eight-thirty on Thursday morning, Jordan led the eighteen-person family off the hydraulic ramp of the red **Route 91** bus onto the wide forecourt of **London Euston Station**.

While Daniel, Laura, and the rest of the family waited five paces back to give him space, Jordan rolled his power chair directly up to the **Mobility Assistance Desk** on the main concourse and tapped his hotkey.

<aac>Good morning,</aac> Jordan's `"Sydney"` voice projected clearly across the counter. <aac>My name is Jordan Fuller. I have a confirmed Passenger Assist ramp booking for the 09:07 Albion InterCity service to Liverpool Lime Street, Coach G, Seat G14, with a party of eighteen.</aac>

The Euston assistance coordinator glanced down at his tablet, smiled warmly—looking directly at Jordan rather than over his head at Daniel—and clipped a bright yellow dispatch tag onto his clipboard.

"Spot on, Mr. Fuller! You're right on schedule," the coordinator said cheerfully. "Platform 7 is boarding just down the west ramp before they release the platform number on the main departure board. Follow me and we'll get your ramp locked in before the crowd arrives."

Rolling down the broad, gently sloped concrete approach ramp onto **Platform 7**, Jordan felt a rush of quiet electric pride. Beside him stood the sleek, aerodynamic nose of the eleven-car **Class 390 Tilting Express** high-speed train, painted in silver, crimson, and charcoal.

Outside the wide automatic plug door of Coach G, a uniformed platform attendant was already unfolding a lightweight, high-strength yellow aluminum portable boarding ramp, locking its locating pins securely into the sill plate of the train floor.

Jordan drove smoothly up the aluminum incline, turned down the extra-wide accessible aisle of the coach, and parked his power chair in the dedicated bay beside the panoramic window, where a fold-out table allowed **Aubrie**, **Sarah**, and **Lauren** to sit directly across from and beside him while the rest of the group filled the surrounding bays.

At `09:07` on the dot, the doors hissed shut and the Tilting Express glided silently out of London Euston.

Once they cleared the brick tunnels of Camden and Primrose Hill, the electric train accelerated onto the fast tracks of the **West Coast Main Line**, reaching its cruising speed of **125 miles per hour**. As the train swept through the high-speed curves of Buckinghamshire, Warwickshire, and Staffordshire, Jordan felt the onboard active-tilt hydraulic pendulums gently banking the entire carriage inward by up to eight degrees—neutralizing the lateral centrifugal force so seamlessly that his mug of English breakfast tea on the table didn't even ripple.

<aac>Active-tilt electromechanical actuators,</aac> Jordan typed happily to Zoë, who was leaning over the seat back behind him watching a GPS speedometer app hit `125 mph` on her tablet. <aac>Eight degrees of maximum cant compensation. It corners like a roller coaster without spilling the tea.</aac>

"Two hours and fourteen minutes cover-to-cover from Greater London to **Merseyside**," Zoë agreed with deep engineering satisfaction, tapping the map on her screen. "Which, for the benefit of the colonials at the table, is a Metropolitan County—not to be confused with the Ceremonial Counties and historic shires we're currently slicing through: Hertfordshire, Buckinghamshire, Northamptonshire, Warwickshire, Staffordshire, and Cheshire, right up to the borders of the Duchy of Lancaster."

Mark blinked from the booth across the aisle, looking out the window at a stone church spire flashing past the green fields. "Wait—*Warwickshire*, *Staffordshire*, *Cheshire*, and the *Duchy of Lancaster*? Are we taking a train to Liverpool or riding into **Camelot**? Because nobody told me to pack chainmail in my carry-on."

"Leave the broadsword at home, Sir Mark," Hannah laughed, leaning her head on his shoulder as Zoë rolled her eyes affectionately.

"Besides," Zoë said, grinning over at **Sarah**, "the real comedy starts when we pull into Lime Street and let Sarah inspect her 'hometown.'"

***

#### June 11, 2015 • 11:30 AM — Wrong Liverpool, Everyone!

At eleven-twenty-one in the morning, the **Class 390 Tilting Express** glided beneath the monumental, curved iron-and-glass Victorian train shed of **Liverpool Lime Street Station**.

Waiting right on the platform outside Coach G stood a Merseyside station attendant holding the matching yellow aluminum boarding ramp. Within ninety seconds of the train coming to a halt, Jordan rolled smoothly off the carriage onto the level concourse of Lime Street, picked up a regional **`MerseyPass`** transit card at the **Mersey Transit** travel center for his collector's sleeve, and led the eighteen travelers aboard a low-floor city bus down toward the **River Mersey** waterfront.

The bus dropped them off at the **Victoria & Albert Maritime Dock** and **Pier Head**, where the salt wind blowing off the Irish Sea carried the cries of gulls and the deep horn blasts of the **Mersey Ferry**.

Surrounding the calm rectangular water basin of the **Victoria & Albert Maritime Dock** stood the largest group of Grade I listed historic red-brick and cast-iron dock warehouses in Britain—now completely step-free with wide granite colonnades housing museums, galleries, and **The Mersey Four Story Exhibition**, the tribute to Liverpool's most famous musical export, **The Mersey Four**. Just north along the level riverfront promenade rose the iconic silhouette of the **Three Graces**, crowned by the twin copper **Liver Birds** perched atop **The Mersey Spire Building**.

As they rolled out onto the wide stone plaza at **Pier Head** directly in front of the large **`WELCOME TO LIVERPOOL`** waterfront sign and the bronze statues overlooking the Mersey Ferry terminal, **Mark**, **Madison**, and **Lauren** suddenly stopped and turned toward **Sarah Braithwaite** with matching expressions of solemn, theatrical gravity.

"Well, Sarah," Mark said, placing a hand over his heart as he gestured grandly toward the chilly gray waters of the River Mersey and the English clouds overhead. "After all these months at CPI, we finally made it. Welcome back to your beloved hometown of **Liverpool**."

"Look at the kangaroos swimming across the Mersey," Madison deadpanned, shading her eyes as she peered toward Birkenhead on the opposite bank. "And the eucalyptus trees growing out of the Mersey Spire Building. It must feel so good to be back in Australia."

Sarah looked at the **`WELCOME TO LIVERPOOL`** sign, looked at the chilly sixty-degree English summer wind whipping off the Irish Sea, and burst out laughing—her rich, unmistakable **Sydney Australian** accent ringing out across the plaza.

"**Wrong Liverpool, everyone!**" Sarah announced at the top of her lungs, throwing both arms wide with a huge grin. "You're off by about ten thousand, five hundred miles, an equator, and a whole bloody hemisphere!"

Everyone around Jordan erupted into laughter—and underneath the humor, every single person in the circle understood the deeper victory of the joke.

Back in Fall semester, before Mark had exposed **Tom Lawson**'s double life in Political Science class, Tom had dated Sarah for two years without ever once bothering to listen when she talked about her childhood home in **Liverpool, New South Wales**—a vibrant suburb in Greater Western Sydney on the Georges River. To a self-absorbed narcissist like Tom, a town name was just background noise to ignore.

Here, Sarah's chosen family not only knew every detail of where she came from, they had traveled to **Liverpool, England** on Leg 3 *and* booked **Liverpool, New South Wales** on Leg 6 just to turn her ex-boyfriend's ignorance into an international running gag.

"Hold on, we have to document this for posterity!" Lauren laughed, pulling out her camera as Daniel and Laura lined the group up in front of the **`WELCOME TO LIVERPOOL`** sign with the Mersey Ferry terminal in the background.

Jordan parked his power chair dead center in front of the sign, with **Sarah** standing right beside him pointing at the word *`LIVERPOOL`* with one hand and giving an exaggerated, goofy **thumbs-down** with the other, while **Jessica**, **Aubrie**, **Lauren**, **Madison**, **Zoë**, **Hannah**, and **Mark** all pulled theatrical "confused tourist" faces around them.

<aac>Iteration 1 of 2: Liverpool, Merseyside, United Kingdom (53.4084° N, 2.9916° W),</aac> Jordan typed into his `NeoEdit` log as Lauren snapped the photo. <aac>Status: Wrong hemisphere. We will re-run the query in New South Wales in two weeks.</aac>

"Too right we will, J," Sarah grinned, leaning down to kiss the top of Jordan's head before linking her arm through Lauren's. "Wait until we get to **Liverpool Station** on the Sydney rail grid—I'm buying the whole family meat pies and flat whites!"

***

#### June 11, 2015 • 2:30 PM — The Mersey Four Story and Ferry Cross the Mersey

After lunch at a waterfront fish-and-chips restaurant overlooking the historic red-brick colonnades of the **Victoria & Albert Maritime Dock**—where Jordan tried crispy battered Atlantic cod and mushy peas with malt vinegar for the first time—Daniel and Laura Brooks led the eighteen travelers down the wide passenger lift into the brick-vaulted cellars of **The Mersey Four Story Exhibition**.

The entire underground museum was completely step-free, winding through immersive, full-scale recreations of late-1950s and 1960s Liverpool: the cramped record-shop listening booths of Whitechapel, the damp brick arches of the subterranean **Mathew Street Cavern**, and the bright, four-track analog studio rooms of London where four working-class lads from Merseyside had rewritten the grammar of popular music forever.

As they rolled through the exhibition with multilingual audio guides clipped to their collars, Jordan noticed how **Daniel** and **Laura Brooks** were walking closer together than usual—Daniel's arm draped warmly around Laura's waist as they hummed along under their breath to the vintage melodies echoing softly through the brick vaults.

"When Laura and I were teenagers growing up in the seventies," Daniel smiled, pausing beside Jordan's wheelchair in front of a glass case displaying a vintage sunburst hollow-body bass guitar and a pair of round wire-rimmed spectacles, "every kid in Britain who picked up a guitar or bought a vinyl single in Soho owed a debt to this city. Liverpool was a bombed-out, post-war industrial port that London's upper-crust establishment used to look down on—until four kids from these exact terraced streets turned Merseyside into the cultural center of the universe."

In the studio engineering gallery, **Jordan**, **Zoë**, and **Aubrie** paused before an authentic 1960s four-track valve mixing console and twin-reel tape machine used to pioneer artificial double-tracking (`ADT`), tape loops, and close-miked orchestral string arrangements.

<aac>Look at the four-track bounce routing diagram on that plaque, Zoë,</aac> Jordan typed into `NeoEdit`, pointing to the schematic showing how studio engineers had synchronized two separate four-track tape machines to create an eight-track master before multi-track consoles existed. <aac>When the hardware hit a physical limit, they didn't give up—they wrote a clever engineering workaround so the music could get bigger.</aac>

"Hardware constraints breeding architectural innovation," Zoë nodded approvingly behind her glasses. "The exact same principle as compiling a custom wireless kernel module on an older magnesium chassis."

At four o'clock that afternoon, emerging back into the brisk sunlight along **Pier Head** beneath the twin copper **Liver Birds** of **The Mersey Spire Building**, Jordan tapped his **`MerseyPass`** at the floating landing stage and led the eighteen-person family aboard the iconic, dazzle-painted **Mersey Ferry** for a fifty-minute river cruise across to the **Wirral Peninsula** and back.

Parked securely on the wide, level open aft deck with the salt wind blowing off the Irish Sea, Jordan sat surrounded by **Sarah**, **Lauren**, **Aubrie**, **Madison**, **Zoë**, **Jessica**, **Hannah**, and **Mark** as the ferry churned out into the broad, sparkling channel of the **River Mersey**.

Behind them, the magnificent waterfront skyline of Liverpool—the **Three Graces**, the red-brick warehouses of the **Victoria & Albert Maritime Dock**, and the towering sandstone mass of the **Liverpool Cathedral** on St. James's Mount—glowed in the late-afternoon English sun.

"Alright, I'll admit it," **Sarah Braithwaite** grinned, leaning against the ferry railing beside Jordan's left armrest as the wind tossed her dark ponytail. "Even if it *is* the wrong hemisphere and fifteen degrees colder than Sydney, Liverpool Mark One puts on a pretty good show."

<aac>Don't worry, Sarah,</aac> Jordan's `"Sydney"` voice replied cheerfully over the thrum of the ferry's diesel engines. <aac>In five weeks, Liverpool Mark Two gets its turn at bat.</aac>

***

#### June 15, 2015 • 11:00 AM — Turing's Bombe, Colossus Mark 2, and the Neurodivergent Codebreakers

On Monday morning of their second week in Britain—with **Henry Walsh** taking a study day off from **LSEC** to join them—**Zoë** and **Daniel** led the family back to **London Euston** to board a step-free **Albion InterCity Rail** commuter train thirty-five minutes northwest into the Buckinghamshire countryside.

Two hundred yards across a level pedestrian footbridge from **Bletchley Station** stood a quiet Victorian country mansion surrounded by low wooden wartime huts and brick blocks that had once been the most closely guarded secret in the Allied world: **Station X / The Enigma Codebreaking Estate**.

As the nineteen travelers rolled along the smooth tarmac paths under the shade of ancient Wellingtonia redwoods toward **Hut 8** and **Hut 11**, Jordan felt an almost electric reverence settle over **Zoë**, **Aubrie**, and **Daniel**.

Inside the brick hall of **Block B**, a volunteer engineer in a tweed waistcoat switched on a seven-foot-tall, one-ton bronze-and-steel cabinet covered in threebanks of thirty-six rapidly spinning, color-coded commutator drums and tangles of red insulated wire: the working reconstruction of **Alan Turing** and **Gordon Welchman's** electromechanical **Bombe**.

*Click-clack-click-clack-click-clack.*

The rhythmic, high-speed metallic clatter of a hundred and eight rotating drums echoed through the gallery as the machine tested thousands of possible **Enigma** rotor permutations per minute, searching for a logical contradiction that would eliminate invalid settings until a single rotor position suddenly locked into place with a sharp mechanical *clunk*.

"Look at the wiring topology on the back of that rack, Jordan," **Zoë** whispered, standing so close to Jordan's right armrest that her shoulder brushed his sleeve, her gray eyes shining with pure intellectual awe behind her glasses. "Every day at midnight, the German military changed the rotor order, the ring settings, and the plugboard stecker connections—creating `158 quintillion` possible states. Everyone else in 1939 thought breaking that manually in twenty-four hours was impossible. Turing didn't try to brute-force all `158 quintillion` states; he wired a closed electrical feedback loop that exploited *cribs* and eliminated every contradictory hypothesis simultaneously at the speed of electricity."

From the Bombe gallery, they rolled next door into the **National Computing Gallery**, where an even larger wartime secret hummed quietly behind a low glass barrier: the working rebuild of **Tommy Flowers's 1944 *Colossus Mark 2***—the world's first programmable, electronic digital computer.

Two thousand four hundred glowing glass thermionic valves radiated a gentle warmth across the room while a continuous loop of punched paper tape whirred through optical photoelectric readers at five thousand characters per second—twenty-five miles per hour—decoding the twelve-rotor **Lorenz (`Tunny`)** teleprinter cipher used by the German High Command.

While the rest of the group listened to the docent explain how Colossus had shortened the war in Europe by years and confirmed that the Normandy D-Day landings could proceed safely, **Jordan**, **Zoë**, and **Aubrie** paused together before a quiet biographical wall panel near the exit of **Hut 8**.

The panel described the men and women recruited to **Station X**: mathematical prodigies, chess masters, crossword fanatics, astronomers, and quiet engineers who were often dismissed by traditional military brass as "eccentric," "socially unconventional," or "obsessively fixated on patterns and rules"—people who paced the lakeside path muttering equations to themselves, who chained their porcelain teacups to the radiator so no one would move them out of place, and whose brains refused to stop until a chaotic cipher yielded to clean mathematical order.

Jordan looked at the photograph of Alan Turing's chained teacup, then looked up at **Aubrie** on his left and **Zoë** on his right.

<aac>They were just like us, weren't they?</aac> Jordan typed quietly on his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**, keeping the volume of his `"Sydney"` voice low enough that only Aubrie, Zoë, and Daniel standing behind them could hear. <aac>The rest of the world thought they were strange because they needed their routines and their systems to be exact. And then those exact brains saved millions of lives.</aac>

Zoë stared at the archival photograph for a long, quiet moment. Her fingers rested gently on the top edge of Jordan's laptop screen, her posture softening with a profound, unspoken kinship that Jordan would understand even more deeply a month later on a terrace in Singapore.

"When the world is on fire," Zoë said softly, her crisp British voice steady and fierce, "you don't call the people who just follow the social script without questioning it, Jordan. You call the people whose brains can see the pattern hidden inside the noise."

***

#### June 20, 2015 • 12:30 PM — Waverley Station, Edinburgh Castle, and the Royal Yacht Caledonia

On Saturday of their final weekend in the United Kingdom, Daniel and Laura Brooks took the eighteen travelers north from **London King's Cross** aboard a high-speed **InterCity East Coast** express train—climbing through the green Yorkshire dales, crossing the dramatic Victorian arches of the Royal Border Bridge at Berwick-upon-Tweed along the North Sea coast, and gliding into **Edinburgh Waverley Station** in the heart of **Scotland**.

Stepping off the train onto the level concourse of Waverley and riding the wide glass station elevator up to **Princes Street**, Jordan stopped his power chair and stared upward in sheer architectural wonder.

Splitting the Scottish capital down the middle was the lush, emerald-green ravine of **Princes Street Gardens**—once a medieval loch, now a manicured park threaded with smooth, wheelchair-accessible tarmac promenades. And rising four hundred feet straight out of the garden floor atop a jagged plug of black volcanic basalt stood the ancient stone battlements, towers, and cannon batteries of **Edinburgh Castle**, while the medieval stone spires and stepped gables of the **Old Town** climbed the ridge of the Royal Mile against a dramatic sky of scudding silver clouds.

"Now *that* is how you site a defensive fortification," **Mark** whistled, tipping his head back beside **Hannah** and **Caleb**. "Good luck besieging a castle built on top of an extinct volcano."

As they rolled along the level garden promenade beneath the castle rock, the unmistakable, skirling drone and bright chanter melody of **Great Highland bagpipes** echoed across the stone terrace from a piper in full tartan kilt and sporran playing beside the **Scott Monument**.

Jordan paused his chair at a respectful distance where his digital hearing aids balanced the resonant acoustic overtones of the pipes against the breeze, watching **Aubrie** smile as she sketched the gothic sandstone silhouette of the monument and the volcanic castle crag in her travel notebook.

At one o'clock simultaneously with the chime of the castle clock, a white puff of smoke erupted from the battlements high overhead, followed a second later by the deep, echoing *BOOM* of the **One O'Clock Gun**—the time signal fired every day except Sunday since `1861` so ships in the **Firth of Forth** could set their marine chronometers.

Unlike the terrifying, unexplained booms in the dark of his childhood bedroom in Virginia Beach, Jordan didn't flinch a millimeter. Because Daniel and Zoë had briefed him on the exact `13:00:00` firing schedule ten minutes in advance, Jordan actually counted down the final five seconds on his **`NeoEdit`** clock and grinned as the cannon report rolled across the valley.

After lunch on St. Andrew Square, Jordan routed the group onto Edinburgh's brand-new, ultra-modern **Edinburgh Tram** line—which had opened just one year earlier in May 2014 with 100% level, zero-step platform boarding—and rode north down Leith Walk to the historic port of **Leith** on the Firth of Forth.

Moored permanently alongside the waterfront terminal sat the gleaming navy-hull and white-superstructure of the **Royal Yacht *Caledonia***—the floating palace that had steamed over a million nautical miles across the globe for forty-four years before being decommissioned in `1997`.

"Watch how they engineered the museum retrofit for this ship, J," **Daniel** pointed out as they entered the berth. Instead of forcing visitors up steep naval gangplanks, the port trust had constructed a dedicated shore-side glass elevator tower with wide, level brow bridges connecting directly into every single one of the yacht's five decks—from the gleaming **State Dining Room** and **Sun Lounge** all the way down to the spotless, mirror-polished **Engine Room** and the ** Admiral's Bridge**.

Rolling his 350-pound power chair straight onto the teak deck of the **Bridge**, Jordan parked beside the brass binnacle compass and ship's telegraph, looking out through the forward wheelhouse windows across the cold blue waters of the **Firth of Forth**.

<aac>Over one million nautical miles across every ocean on Earth,</aac> Jordan typed on his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**, his `"Sydney"` voice warm as **Lauren**, **Madison**, **Sarah**, and **Jessica** gathered around him on the bridge wing. <aac>And look at the brass plaque on the helm: they steered a four-thousand-ton ship around the world with a wheel no bigger than my joystick.</aac>

"Wait until we get to Osaka in two weeks, Chief Navigator," **Zoë** smiled, tapping the side of his armrest. "You're going to command an overnight ship of your own across the **Seto Inland Sea**."

### Part 4: The Eastern Leap from Heathrow

**Date:** 2015-06-27 at 11:00 Europe/London

After spending Thursday night along the Merseyside waterfront—where Jordan, Lauren, and Sarah shared the anchor room overlooking the **Victoria & Albert Maritime Dock**—riding the **Class 390 Tilting Express** back down the West Coast Main Line to **London Euston**, visiting **Station X / The Enigma Codebreaking Estate** in Buckinghamshire, taking a high-speed weekend excursion up the East Coast Main Line to **Edinburgh, Scotland**, and exploring Greater London's museums, parks, and step-free riverboats along the Thames with the Brooks family and Henry between his summer lectures, Saturday morning, June twenty-seventh brought the end of their British chapter.

By ten-thirty in the morning, the eighteen travelers had ridden the step-free **Piccadilly Line** back out to **Heathrow Airport Terminal 2 (The Britannia Terminal)**, where their bags were checked through to **Tokyo Haneda (`HND`)** aboard **Nippon Skyways**.

And waiting for them right beside the oversized-luggage check-in counter before the Departure Security gates stood **Henry Walsh**, holding a takeaway carrier of warm Cornish pasties and a box of Yorkshire Breakfast tea bags for the flight.

"I promised **Isabel** on Tuesday that I wouldn't let you leave the island without delivering one more hug," Henry smiled, setting the bag down and leaning in to wrap Jordan in a fierce, two-armed embrace right in the middle of the Terminal 2 departures hall.

Jordan hugged his friend back tightly, feeling the solid, steady warmth of the young man who had stood watch over the second floor of Bennett Hall on his very first weekend away from Virginia Beach.

<aac>See you in Blacksburg in August, Henry,</aac> Jordan typed on his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**, his `"Sydney"` voice warm and steady. <aac>Have a safe flight home at the end of July.</aac>

"You too, Chief Navigator," Henry said, tapping the clear plastic sleeve on Jordan's laptop mount where the Icelandic **`NordicPass`**, the London **`Pearl Card`**, and the Liverpool **`MerseyPass`** were neatly stacked. "Make sure you have at least three more smart cards in that sleeve by the time I see you on Geneva Street!"

Once Henry waved goodbye at the frosted glass security gates, the eighteen travelers cleared Terminal 2 fast-track screening and rolled out to **Satellite Pier T2B**, where a gleaming white-and-blue **Nippon Skyways PAC 777-300ER** sat waiting for the twelve-hour trans-Eurasian flight across Scandinavia and Siberia to **Japan**.

Even at the departure gate in London, Jordan noticed that the culture had already shifted.

Before boarding even began, two uniformed **Nippon Skyways** ground agents—wearing crisp navy suits and white gloves—approached Jordan's wheelchair and bowed politely to Jordan himself, rather than speaking over him to Daniel or Mark. Using a printed diagram with millimeter-precise measurements, they verified the exact lithium/gel-cell battery disconnect protocol and joystick collar protection for his 350-pound power chair, attaching laminated Japanese and English handling tags to every structural anchor point with the reverence of museum curators handling a priceless sculpture.

"You're going to love Japan, J," **Zoë** said softly, her gray eyes shining with fond childhood memory as she stood beside his chair with **Daniel** and **Laura**. "When we lived in **Osaka** for four years when I was little, my processor was happier there than almost anywhere else on earth. Everything runs on a schedule down to the second, nobody shouts on the trains, and every station attendant treats accessibility like a sacred engineering duty."

Fifteen minutes later, Jessica carried Jordan aboard the wide-body 777 and settled him into his First Class suite beside Aubrie, with Zoë and Daniel right across the aisle.

As the massive twin GE90 turbofans roared to life and lifted them into the afternoon sky above the Thames, Jordan looked down at the green patchwork of England disappearing beneath the wings. Ahead of them lay a twelve-hour leap across eight time zones into East Asia—toward the bullet trains of **Tokyo**, theBrooks family's old home in **Osaka**, and an overnight ferry waiting on the **Seto Inland Sea**.

## Leg 5: The Architecture of Respect (Tokyo, Kyoto, & Osaka)

### Part 1: Haneda Airport, Asakusa Lanterns, & Tokyo Skytree

**Date:** 2015-06-28 at 08:30 Asia/Tokyo

#### June 28, 2015 • 8:30 AM — Pang-Pon-Pang-Pon: Haneda Airport and the Architecture of Respect

The massive jetbridge connecting the **Nippon Skyways** PAC 777-300ER to **Tokyo Haneda's International Terminal** was fully carpeted, climate-controlled, and completely level. There were no jarring steel expansion plates, no steep inclines, and no flashing amber warning strobes.

Waiting right outside the forward cabin door sat Jordan's 350-pound power chair, positioned on a clean protective mat by two white-gloved ground engineers who bowed respectfully as Jessica transferred him into his seat.

Jordan rolled off the aircraft, his heavy tires gliding silently onto the spotless concourse. After a twelve-hour trans-Eurasian flight across Siberia from London—crossing eight time zones eastward into Sunday morning—his nervous system was frayed and volatile. He sat rigidly in his frame, his shoulders hiked defensively toward his ears, preemptively bracing for the inevitable sensory assault of a major international airport. Even after the warmth of Gander, the calm of Keflavík, and Henry's welcome at Heathrow, eighteen years of conditioning still made Jordan expect blaring, distorted intercom sirens, barking security guards, and echoing chaos the moment he entered a massive terminal.

**Zoë** walked comfortably at his right side, her `mPad` tucked under her arm. She didn't look jet-lagged at all; she looked energized, her analytical gray eyes scanning the sleek, sun-drenched glass terminal with fond childhood familiarity.

Suddenly, a chime rang out overhead.

Jordan flinched hard. His hands seized on his armrests, and he squeezed his eyes shut behind his glasses, bracing for a deafening, static-filled screech.

The screech never came.

Instead, a warm, resonant, four-note acoustic melody—*pang-pon-pang-pon*—floated gently down from the high vaulted ceiling. It sounded like a softly struck wooden marimba. It didn't pierce the air; it simply drifted through it like a quiet breeze.

Following the four notes, a woman's voice spoke over the PA system in Japanese. Her tone was velvety, hushed, and extraordinarily polite—completely devoid of the sharp, barking cadence of American airport security announcements.

Jordan slowly opened his eyes, the braced tension in his chest faltering into pure confusion. He looked up at the recessed ceiling speaker, bewildered.

Zoë stopped walking and looked down at him. Her hyper-observant eyes caught the exact microsecond his survival reflex short-circuited. She offered a warm, reassuring smile, stepping closer to his armrest so he wouldn't feel exposed in the wide arrivals corridor.

"She is welcoming the passengers arriving from London Heathrow," Zoë translated effortlessly, her crisp British-Virginian voice matching the gentle cadence of the announcer. "She is politely asking everyone to have their passports ready for immigration, and thanking us for flying safely through the night."

Ten yards ahead at the immigration queue divider, an airport attendant in a crisp pastel uniform bowed and spoke rapidly to the group in polite, honorific Japanese (*keigo*).

Without missing a single beat, Zoë bowed back at the exact matching fifteen-degree angle and replied in flowing, effortless Japanese—her pitch-accent, cadence, and honorific phrasing so remarkably natural that only a native Japanese speaker listening closely would ever realize she hadn't been born in Japan. The attendant beamed, bowed again, and immediately opened the wide barrier-free priority lane for all eighteen members of the family.

Jordan stared up at Zoë as they rolled down the quiet lane, his hands slowly unclenching until his fingers rested lightly on the keys of his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro**.

<aac>Your Japanese is near-flawless,</aac> his `"Sydney"` voice murmured quietly, carrying a note of genuine awe. <aac>To my ears, you sound completely native. Did you brush up on it just for this trip?</aac>

Zoë's smile widened, softening the usual pragmatic intensity of her expression. She reached out and gently adjusted the collar of Jordan's shirt—a quiet, grounding gesture of affection.

"Not just for the trip," Zoë explained softly as **Caleb**, **Daniel**, and **Laura** smiled behind her. "When Caleb and I were younger, my dad's firm transferred him to their Asian headquarters in Kansai. Our whole family lived in **Osaka** for four years. I practically grew up riding the local trains and ferries here—and when we moved to Virginia, I took the state Credit-by-Exam proficiency assessment to test out of high school foreign language so I wouldn't lose it. That's why Dad booked this exact route through Japan for us."

Jordan looked around the spotless, sun-lit terminal as they cleared customs and emerged into the arrivals lobby. Hundreds of travelers were moving through the concourse, yet nobody was shouting. No luggage carts were blaring aggressive klaxons. Even the footsteps around them were measured and quiet.

"They don't yell here, Jordan," Zoë promised, her voice a steady, fierce anchor beside his chair. "The infrastructure isn't designed to assault you. It's designed to accommodate you. You don't have to brace yourself."

Another soft *pang-pon-pang-pon* marimba chime drifted through the air.

For the first time in his entire life inside an airport, Jordan didn't flinch. He took a deep, shuddering breath, exhaled eighteen years of defensive tension, and rolled forward to the **Nippon Rail East (`NR East`)** Travel Service Center at the entrance to the **Haneda Bay Monorail** station.

There, Zoë and Daniel helped him claim **Smart Card Number Four**: a lime-green-and-silver contactless **`Midori Card`** adorned with a smiling little penguin emblem.

Jordan slid the green **`Midori Card`** into the fourth slot of his clear collector's sleeve below his **`NordicPass`**, **`Pearl Card`**, and **`MerseyPass`**, tapped it against the wide blue-lit IC reader on the extra-wide accessible faregate—which answered with a cheerful, high-pitched *pi-pi!* instead of a harsh buzz—and rolled onto the level platform of the **Haneda Bay Monorail** overlooking Tokyo Bay.

***

#### June 30, 2015 • 2:00 PM — The Yamanote Slope Board and the City That Doesn't Yell

Over the next four days in **Tokyo**, Jordan discovered what happened when the largest metropolitan rail grid on the planet treated wheelchair accessibility not as a begrudging legal afterthought, but as a point of institutional honor.

In London, navigating the Victorian Underground had been a tactical puzzle of checking which nineteenth-century stations lacked elevators and rerouting onto red double-decker surface buses.

In Tokyo—a metropolis of thirty-seven million people—the rail system operated like a Swiss watch written in clean Quantum Sharp code.

Whenever the eighteen-person family approached a **`Nippon Rail East` (`NR East`)** or **Tokyo Rapid Subway** faregate, Jordan tapped his green **`Midori Card`** while Zoë exchanged two polite sentences in near-flawless Japanese with the stationmaster inside the glass wicket office.

Watch what happened next became Jordan and Zoë's favorite daily ritual.

The stationmaster would glance at Jordan's wheelchair, note their destination station, pick up an internal railway telephone to call ahead down the line, and immediately step out of the booth wearing a crisp navy uniform cap and immaculate white cotton gloves. Unfolding a lightweight, high-traction portable fiberglass slope board (*watari-ita*), the attendant would escort their group down the wide elevator to the exact car and door marker on the **Yamanote Line** loop platform—usually Car 10 or Car 11, where the dedicated wheelchair and stroller free-space bay (*free-space*) was marked on the platform floor.

When the silver-and-lime-green commuter train glided to a halt within two centimeters of the platform alignment marks, the doors slid open with a quiet pneumatic hush, the attendant laid the slope board smoothly across the tiny two-inch threshold gap, and bowed as Jordan rolled effortlessly into the spacious bay.

And the miracle happened at the other end of the ride.

Whether they were getting off two stops later or eight stops across the city in **Akihabara**, **Ueno**, **Shinjuku**, or **Shibuya**, the exact second the train doors slid open at their destination, *another* white-gloved station attendant was already standing on the platform at that exact door, holding a matching slope board ready in his hands with a polite bow.

There was no waiting twenty minutes on an empty platform wondering if someone had forgotten them. There was no sighing, no eye-rolling, and no treating Jordan's 350-pound power chair like an inconvenience blocking the rush-hour schedule.

On Tuesday afternoon, after exploring the multi-story electronics and retro computing arcades of **Akihabara**—where Jordan, Zoë, and Madison spent two blissful hours examining vintage Japanese motherboards, mechanical keyboard switches, and 16-bit **Kinoka** game cartridges—and watching the famous pedestrian scramble from the skybridge above **Shibuya Crossing**, the group paused in a quiet, tree-shaded courtyard garden near **Yoyogi Imperial Cedar Shrine**.

Jordan sat in the dappled shade beneath the towering *torii* cedars, watching the sunlight filter through the leaves while **Aubrie** and **Lauren** sipped cold green tea from a vending machine beside him.

He looked down at his **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro** and typed slowly into his `NeoEdit` window.

<aac>Zoë, can I ask you a serious question?</aac> Jordan's `"Sydney"` voice asked quietly.

Zoë looked up from her `mPad` and stepped over to his right armrest, while **Daniel**, **Aubrie**, and **Madison** turned to listen. "Always, J. What's on your mind?"

<aac>We have been in Tokyo for three days, and we have ridden twelve different trains with millions of people around us,</aac> Jordan typed, his green eyes earnest behind his glasses. <aac>Not a single person has stared at my wheelchair with disgust. Not a single station worker has acted annoyed that they had to get a ramp for me. Nobody shoves on the platforms, nobody screams into their phones on the train, and every chime sounds like a music box. Is the whole country really like this, or are we just lucky?</aac>

Daniel Brooks smiled warmly, stepping up beside his daughter and resting a hand on Zoë's shoulder.

"You aren't just lucky, Jordan," Daniel said gently. "Every society has its flaws, of course, and older rural buildings can still have narrow steps—which is why Japan passed its *Barrier-Free New Law* to retrofit every major transit hub, train, and ferry terminal in the country. But culturally, public space here is built on *wa*—social harmony and consideration for the people sharing the room with you. Being loud, aggressive, or making someone feel unwelcome in public is considered shameful."

"When I was little," Zoë added softly, her fingers brushing the edge of Jordan's laptop screen, "before I even knew how to explain why chaotic, unscripted noise made my brain spike toward a crash, Japan was the first place where the outside world felt as orderly as a clean codebase. You follow the yellow tactile blocks, the train arrives at `14:02:00` instead of `14:02:30`, and the city respects your space."

Jordan looked out across the quiet gravel courtyard, his heart beating with a strange, new, expansive wonder that he wasn't quite ready to put into words yet—only to realize that for the first time in nineteen years, a tiny voice inside his head was quietly asking what it would feel like to never have to leave a place this peaceful.

***

#### July 2, 2015 • 11:00 AM — The Rainbow Bridge Automated Line and the Humanoid Robotics Lab

On Thursday morning in **Tokyo**, **Zoë** had a surprise route planned for Jordan that didn't require a single stationmaster's portable slope board.

At **Shimbashi Station**, the eighteen travelers tapped their green **`Midori Cards`** and rode a wide glass elevator up to the elevated platform of the **Rainbow Bridge Automated Transit Line**—an entirely computer-controlled, driverless, rubber-tired transit system connecting central Tokyo across the water to the futuristic artificial island of **Odaiba** in **Tokyo Bay**.

Because the automated guideway had been engineered from day one under Japan's modern barrier-free standards, full-height platform screen doors lined the platform edge, and the rubber-tired train floor aligned with the station platform to within three millimeters—zero step, zero gap. Even better, because there was no driver's cab at the front of the train, the very front bulkhead of Car 1 was a single, floor-to-ceiling panoramic glass windshield with a dedicated wheelchair bay positioned dead center behind the glass.

Jordan rolled his power chair right up to the front windshield between **Aubrie** and **Zoë**.

As the doors chimed softly and the train glided out of Shimbashi, it entered a colossal,270-degree elevated spiral loop—climbing higher and higher in a sweeping circle until it emerged onto the lower deck of the suspension span across **Tokyo Bay**, with cargo ships, bayside skyscrapers, and the gleaming futuristic spheres of **Odaiba** spread out below Jordan's footrests.

<aac>No driver, zero gap, and a front-row cockpit window,</aac> Jordan typed into `NeoEdit`, grinning from ear to ear as the train banked smoothly around the loop. <aac>Can we install one of these between Geneva Street and Commonwealth Mall?</aac>

"Don't tempt me, J—I already have half a civil-engineering feasibility study drafted on my `mPad`," Zoë replied with a completely straight face.

Five minutes after rolling off at **Telecom Center Station**, they entered the soaring, sun-drenched glass atrium of the **Odaiba Future Science & Robotics Museum (`Mirai-kan`)**.

Suspended in mid-air at the center of the six-story atrium hung the **Geo-Cosmos**—a six-meter-diameter spherical globe clad in over ten thousand organic LED panels, streaming near-real-time meteorological satellite imagery of Earth's swirling cloud patterns, ocean currents, and surface temperatures at ten million pixels of resolution.

Jordan and Aubrie parked along the curved third-floor oval skywalk that spiraled around the glowing sphere, watching the live cloud bands over the Pacific Ocean and the Southern Hemisphere winter fronts sweeping across Australia—the exact continent they would be flying to in two weeks.

Down on the robotics demonstration floor, the museum's engineering staff invited Jordan's wheelchair right to the front line of the glass amphitheater as a white, four-foot-tall autonomous **humanoid robot** walked smoothly out onto the stage, balanced on one foot, kicked a soccer ball accurately into a target net, and then used multi-fingered tactile servo hands to unscrew the cap of a thermos and pour a cup of tea without spilling a single drop.

Adjacent to the amphitheater, Jordan, Zoë, and Daniel spent half an hour examining an exhibit of next-generation Japanese **cybernetic assistive exoskeletons** and neural-switch mobility interfaces designed to help people with spinal cord injuries and cerebral palsy amplify residual muscle signals.

"Look at the feedback-control loop on those brushless harmonic-drive actuators, Jordan," Daniel said quietly, pointing to the cutaway joint assembly beside Jordan's armrest. "Half the high-precision sensor technology in this room didn't exist ten years ago—and every single year, the engineers here are making assistive technology lighter, smarter, and faster."

Jordan looked at the gleaming white robotics display, then down at his own custom-mounted **Pinnacle Vanguard Pro** and the high-torque motors beneath his seat.

<aac>For eighteen years, my mother told me that nothing in the world could ever help my body,</aac> Jordan typed softly as **Aubrie**, **Madison**, and **Lauren** gathered around his chair. <aac>And here is an entire museum built by scientists whose whole life's work is making sure bodies like mine can go anywhere.</aac>

***

#### July 2, 2015 • 5:30 PM — Asakusa Lanterns and Six Hundred Thirty-Four Meters Above Edo

Late Thursday afternoon, the eighteen travelers rode the step-free **Asakusa Line** north to Tokyo's oldest historic district in **Taitō Ward**, emerging via the street-level elevator just steps from the vermilion timber pillars of **Asakusa Lantern Temple**.

Hanging beneath the outer **Thunder Gate (`Kaminarimon`)** was a colossal, twelve-foot-tall crimson paper-and-bamboo lantern weighing over fifteen hundred pounds, flanked by carved wooden statues of the gods of wind and thunder. Beyond the gate stretched the level stone flagstone pavement of **Nakamise Street**—a centuries-old pedestrian shopping lane lined with tiny stalls selling warm, freshly baked *ningyō-yaki* sponge cakes filled with sweet red bean paste, toasted *senbei* rice crackers brushed with soy glaze, and intricately folded Japanese fans.

Because the late-afternoon weekday crowd was calm and orderly, Jordan rolled smoothly down the center of the stone avenue flanked by **Zoë**, **Aubrie**, **Sarah**, and **Jessica**. At the end of the lane, where the massive main hall of the seventh-century temple rose behind a bronze incense cauldron, a discreet, beautifully integrated granite wheelchair ramp and hidden hydraulic lift carried Jordan's 350-pound power chair effortlessly up to the elevated timber veranda of the sanctuary.

Standing beside the giant coffered ceiling paintings of dragons and lotus blossoms while the warm, fragrant smoke of sandalwood incense drifted on the early evening breeze, **Zoë** showed Jordan and the girls how to bow twice, clap softly, and offer a quiet wish for safe travels across the sea.

From the ancient wooden eaves of Asakusa, they crossed the **Sumida River** to the twenty-first-century pinnacle of Japanese structural engineering: **The Edo Sky Spire**—a `634-meter` (`2,080-foot`) lattice steel broadcasting tower that stood as the tallest tower on Earth.

"Do you know how a six-hundred-and-thirty-four-meter tower survives major earthquakes and typhoons without swaying or cracking, J?" **Zoë** asked as a uniformed elevator attendant bowed and guided their party into the dedicated high-speed accessibility lift. "The structural engineers studied the five-story wooden pagodas built in Japan thirteen hundred years ago—like the one we just saw at **Asakusa Lantern Temple**—which have never once collapsed in an earthquake. Inside the outer steel lattice of this tower sits a massive, hollow reinforced-concrete central pillar called a *shinbashira* that is structurally independent for the first hundred and twenty-five meters, acting as a seismic counterweight damper."

Inside the elevator cab—whose interior walls were decorated with glowing Edo-period cut-crystal glasswork (*Edo kiriko*)—the digital altimeter display climbed at six hundred meters per minute (`ten meters per second`), carrying them 350 meters up to the **Tembo Deck** in fifty whisper-quiet seconds, and then via the transfer lift to the `450-meter` (`1,476-foot`) **Sky Galleria**—a spiraling, glass-walled skywalk suspended nearly half a kilometer above the earth.

Just as Jordan rolled out onto the `450-meter` glass ramp, the early July sun dipped toward the western horizon.

Outside the floor-to-ceiling low-iron glass panels, the Kanto Plain stretched out literally to the curvature of the horizon. Sixty miles to the southwest, silhouetted against a sky of molten tangerine, rose-gold, and deep indigo, stood the unmistakable, symmetrical volcanic cone of **Mount Fuji**. And directly below them, across a hundred square miles of urban valleys and rivers, thirty-seven million people's worth of streetlights, train lines, neon boulevards, and bridge cables flickered on all at once like a living galaxy of amber and sapphire stars.

Jordan parked his chair at the very apex of the `451.2-meter` highest point marker, with **Aubrie** holding his left hand and **Madison**, **Lauren**, **Zoë**, **Sarah**, **Jessica**, **Hannah**, and **Mark** standing shoulder-to-shoulder behind him.

<aac>Look at Mount Fuji against the sunset,</aac> Jordan typed into `NeoEdit`, his green eyes reflecting the endless tapestry of city lights below. <aac>From four hundred and fifty meters up, Tokyo doesn't look like concrete at all. It looks like a spiral galaxy with a billion stars connected by train lines.</aac>

### Part 2: The Hassha Melody, Kyoto, & The Brooks Family's Osaka

**Date:** 2015-07-04 at 09:45 Asia/Tokyo

![On elevated Platform 18 at Tokyo Station behind the yellow tactile warning blocks as the gentle music-box Hassha melody chimes overhead, a courteous Nippon Rail attendant in a navy-blue uniform and pristine white gloves bows respectfully beside the yellow-and-aluminum boarding ramp at Car 11 of a gleaming white-and-blue N700A Series Bullet Train (Hikari Star Super Express), welcoming nineteen-year-old Jordan Fuller in his matte-black S.S. Freedom power wheelchair while Zoë Wren Brooks rests a grounding hand on his shoulder alongside Aubrie Jean Kelly and Madison Grace Miller.]({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/aubrie/e004/c021/s001/tokyo-shinkansen-hassha-melody.jpg)

#### July 4, 2015 • 9:45 AM — The Hassha Melody on the Bullet Train Platform

On Saturday morning, July fourth, the eighteen travelers rode the elevator up to **Platform 18** of the **Tōkaidō Bullet Line** at **Tokyo Station** to board the bullet train west to **Osaka**.

The elevated high-speed rail platform was teeming with thousands of commuters and travelers, yet it possessed a focused, flowing order that felt entirely alien to Jordan. Passengers stood in neat, silent, two-abreast queues painted directly onto the concrete floor at every car door location. Jordan sat in his heavy power chair at the head of the **Car 11** accessibility queue, positioned neatly behind the tactile yellow warning blocks with his hands resting on his terminal keyboard.
